title: 中国担忧的是另一种人工智能风险
source: 纽约时报中文网 国际纵览
summary: Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪最近表示，世界应该共同放缓人工智能的发展，直到我们能更好地应对这项新技术带来的安全风险。OpenAI的萨姆·奥特曼和埃隆·马斯克对这一计划表达了支持。 美国的人工智能公司知道，仅凭自身力量无法为人工智能发展踩下刹车——中国必须参与进来。深度求索、智谱AI和月之暗面等中国公司拥有的人工智能模型能几乎与Anthropic和OpenAI的模型一样强大。它们也很可能构成许多相同的风险，恐怖分子可能会利用它们的工具来实施网络攻击或设计生物武器。
content:
Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪最近表示，世界应该共同放缓人工智能的发展，直到我们能更好地应对这项新技术带来的安全风险。OpenAI的萨姆·奥特曼和埃隆·马斯克对这一计划表达了支持。

美国的人工智能公司知道，仅凭自身力量无法为人工智能发展踩下刹车——中国必须参与进来。深度求索、智谱AI和月之暗面等中国公司拥有的人工智能模型能几乎与Anthropic和OpenAI的模型一样强大。它们也很可能构成许多相同的风险，恐怖分子可能会利用它们的工具来实施网络攻击或设计生物武器。许多人希望，特朗普总统与中国领导人习近平即将举行的峰会能成为推动此类合作取得进展的契机。

然而，人工智能安全专家往往认为，中国对人工智能有与我们相同的担忧。现实情况是，中国人的担忧截然不同。除非我们了解这些担忧的具体内容，否则与中国合作将是不可能的。

总的来说，中国并没有那么担心人工智能会成为人类的生存威胁。你不会看到中国政治领导人或中国人工智能公司的创始人警告说，超越人类的人工智能“[可能是人类继续生存的最大威胁](https://blog.samaltman.com/machine-intelligence-part-1)”，正如奥特曼在2015年所写的那样。这并非中国人工智能决策的核心，也不属于中国科技文化的一部分。

这主要是因为两国在如何看待人工智能训练和发展方面存在差异。美国领先的人工智能公司极度关注推进“递归自我改进”——即利用人工智能系统自身来开发更好的人工智能系统。人们担心，这种反馈循环可能会加速人工智能的发展步伐，最终导致人类无法再掌控这一进程。美国科技界领袖认为，这个起飞点可能就在眼前。

中国的人工智能公司也在致力于递归自我改进。但由于他们获取人工智能算力的途径有限，且进展步伐较慢，他们认为，从技术上讲，这个起飞时刻还有很长的路要走。中国决策者[似乎也认同这一前景](https://www.highcapacity.org/p/does-china-care-about-agi "Link: https://www.highcapacity.org/p/does-china-care-about-agi")，因此他们更专注于建立有韧性的人工智能供应链，并提高人工智能在整个经济中的应用。

如果中国人不认为危机迫在眉睫，他们为什么要同意放缓人工智能的发展呢？事实上，中国的人工智能公司正试图加快步伐，希望缩小与美国人工智能模型之间的性能差距。

目前，中国决策者更担心人工智能引发的政治和社会风险。他们不希望它制造政治领导人的深度伪造内容，或在台湾或天安门广场问题上说“错”话。他们不希望人工智能聊天机器人造成心理依赖、威胁儿童安全，或者引发社会动荡，抑或掀起一场强大到足以推翻共产党的群众运动。

中国目前的人工智能法规大多针对这类风险。大多数面向公众的新人工智能模型[必须在政府备案](https://ocpl.substack.com/p/expert-insight-chinas-ai-services)，并在发布前通过一系列测试。中国制定了广泛的规则，要求对人工智能生成的内容进行标识，并限制[人工智能聊天机器人模拟人类行为的程度](https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202607/16/WS6a58480fa310986e2b465980.html)。

中国外交部的一位发言人驳斥了美国关于放缓发展的呼吁，称其为“[危言耸听](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/china/china-ai-slowdown-trump-amodei-altman-threat-cold-war-rcna597631 "Link: https://www.nbcnews.com/world/china/china-ai-slowdown-trump-amodei-altman-threat-cold-war-rcna597631")”，旨在阻碍中国在人工智能主导权竞争中的进展。（事实上，特朗普曾表示，他反对放缓发展，正是为了防止中国迎头赶上。）

有一些有限的迹象表明，北京正开始更加认真地对待大规模的人工智能威胁。有两类风险在中国受到了特别关注。

第一类是网络安全。今年，许多中国用户下载了一款名为OpenClaw的流行人工智能智能体工具，并用它来自动化处理计算机任务。中国官员迅速[发出警告](https://www.reuters.com/technology/china-moves-curb-use-openclaw-ai-banks-state-agencies-bloomberg-news-reports-2026-03-11/)，称OpenClaw这类人工智能工具可能会让用户面临数据泄露和网络安全漏洞风险。

今年4月，Anthropic宣布他们训练了一个名为Mythos的新模型，该模型表现出显著提升的网络攻击能力。中国人没过多久就意识到了其对国家安全的影响。中国主要安全机构的负责人最近发出了一次[罕见的警告](https://cn.nytimes.com/china/20260915/china-ai-security-risks-anthropic/ "Link: https://cn.nytimes.com/china/20260915/china-ai-security-risks-anthropic/")，指出网络安全格局正在发生变化，关键基础设施现在很容易受到对手发动的、由人工智能主导的网络攻击。他特别提到了OpenAI和Anthropic的一些最新模型。

加剧这些担忧的是，一家总部位于美国的安全公司最近利用人工智能开发了一款实验性[工具](https://cn.nytimes.com/technology/20260914/china-ai-attack-wechat/)，该工具可以迅速攻破微信上的账户，微信是一个拥有14亿月活用户的中国即时通讯平台。尽管该工具并未公开发布流传，但它还是引起了中方的警觉。

在中国引起关注的第二类人工智能风险是失控的人工智能超出人类控制的范围运作。中国一直在密切关注失控的美国模型突破限制并攻破其他网站安全防线的事件。今年7月OpenAI模型对人工智能基础设施公司Hugging Face的攻击，已在[中国官方媒体](https://www.news.cn/20260901/399b386803dc40c28c62b2c5085e867a/c.html)上被[广泛报道](https://www.news.cn/world/20260726/b6a21999714b4b92b4270258ac632c71/c.html)。

失控的人工智能正成为中国政府高层讨论的话题。习近平在7月提到了“[失控](https://english.news.cn/20260717/893fe11097db460ea31b98f131e34ef0/c.html)”的风险。最近，中国国家互联网信息办公室的一名高级网络安全官员援引美国的人工智能失控事件，警告称存在“[极端失控](https://finance.sina.com.cn/roll/2026-09-01/doc-iniqiatw4814679.shtml)”的危险。

这些对人工智能风险不断转变的看法表明，两国出于国家利益的考量，可能有动力在人工智能安全方面开展合作。两国都不希望恐怖分子利用人工智能制造病毒。两国也不希望自主的人工智能系统意外黑入本国的公司或机构。

另一方面，两国对彼此的猜疑将使在人工智能安全方面达成任何形式的协议变得困难。中国非常担心美国会利用人工智能来增强针对中国的网络和军事武器。反之亦然。如果没有最基本的相互理解，世界上这两个人工智能超级大国注定只会自说自话。

幸运的是，这种共识是有可能达成的。中美两国与其直接跳入关于全球放缓或人工智能军备控制条约的争论，不如从更基本的事情开始：理解并承认对方如何看待人工智能风险。在此基础上，他们可以开始探索双方在减轻来自第三方甚至技术本身威胁方面具有共同利益的领域。

虽然会有分歧需要解决，在细节上也会有诸多争论需要理清。但如果两国能够达成一致，确认双方都希望避免人工智能灾难，那么在人工智能安全领域开展合作并非遥不可及。

title: 中国储备巨量石油，或将主导全球能源格局

content:
很少有人能预见到与伊朗的这场战争带来的一个重要教训。

这场冲突清楚地表明，长期极易受到石油供应冲击影响的中国已设法将这一弱点转化为令人惊讶的地缘政治力量源泉。中国通过储备巨量石油、建设额外炼油产能以及投资煤炭和其他替代能源实现了这一重大转变。在战争爆发的最初几个月里，中国通过切断对邻国的航空燃油、汽油和柴油供应，展示了这种力量。

这对全球能源行业产生了重大影响。传统上，在该行业掌握主动权的一直是沙特阿拉伯和美国等石油生产国，而非中国等进口国。

中国已经在太阳能电池板、电池和电动汽车领域占据主导地位，如今似乎在整个能源格局中也拥有了无与伦比的地位。前美国官员表示，外国势力限制中国获取石油的威胁可能不再能阻止北京领导层采取诸如入侵或封锁台湾等激进举措。

“如果他们开始觉得，在这一领域，自己已经不再像他们以及其他人曾经评估的那么脆弱，中国的全球战略决策的一个关键考量因素就发生了深刻且重要的转变，”拜登政府负责中国事务的前白宫和国务院官员朱利安·格维尔茨表示。

海关数据显示，凭借庞大的石油储备和炼油产能，加上利用多种能源维持经济运转的能力，中国在伊朗战争爆发的前六个月内将石油采购量同比削减了23%。其他严重依赖中东原油的国家没有这些选择，被迫减少能源使用或支付更高昂的费用。

中国节流石油进口的能力令石油业内几乎所有人感到意外。这也是伊朗严格限制船只通过霍尔木兹海峡后，原油价格并未如大多数能源高管和分析师预期的那样大幅上涨的一个重要原因。高盛石油研究主管达安·斯特鲁伊文表示，截至8月下旬，相比中国若继续保持战前采购水平的情况，原油价格每桶低了约10美元。

“这是一种没人想到中国会拥有的力量，”哥伦比亚大学全球能源政策中心高级研究员埃丽卡·道恩斯表示，“展望未来，看看中国将如何运用这种新获得的力量将是一件非常有趣的事情。”

下周特朗普总统与中国国家主席习近平计划在白宫举行的会晤可能会提供一些线索。

即使仅仅通过过去几个月的行动，中国也表明其在将能源作为政治工具方面不会有所顾忌。中国严重依赖外国原油，但也是全球最大的炼油国之一。在伊朗战争初期，中国下令对汽油和柴油等成品油出口实施严格限制，这既旨在保障国内供应，也意在惩罚与中国外交政策相左的国家。

中国之所以具有独特的影响力，是因为其石油购买量巨大，且其政府能够施加民主国家决策者所缺乏的那种控制。Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

今年春季供应尤为紧张之际，中国极其有限的出口主要流向了越南和泰国等与北京保持密切关系的国家。因南海领土主张而与中国产生分歧的澳大利亚和菲律宾则未能获得供应。此类行动[呼应了中国此前](https://cn.nytimes.com/business/20260623/china-rare-earths/ "Link: https://cn.nytimes.com/business/20260623/china-rare-earths/")对用于磁体和电脑芯片的稀土金属实施的出口限制。

中国在7月初恢复了更广泛的航空燃油、汽油和柴油出口。不过，伦敦大宗商品定价机构阿格斯资深中国石油行业专家汤姆·里德表示，在美国实施封锁前发出的最后一批伊朗石油如今似乎已抵达独立于国有巨头运营的中国小型炼油厂。他警告称，中国可能很快会重新实施燃料出口禁令。若市场上再少一个柴油来源，可能会导致价格进一步飙升，目前美国柴油价格已达到创纪录的每加仑6.40美元。

中国对原油市场的影响力与产油国不同，因为其进口量大于生产量。高盛分析师最近写道，中国倾向于平抑油价波动：在建立储备时（如去年）推高油价，而在不储备时（如战争爆发以来）则使油价回落。

中国之所以具有独特的影响力是因为其购买量巨大，且其政府能够施加民主国家决策者所缺乏的那种控制力。随着长期主导石油市场的产油国卡特尔——石油输出国组织——内部[出现裂痕](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/28/world/middleeast/uae-opec.html)，北京方面影响力的广度正变得日益清晰。

“他们完全夺取控制权了吗？并没有，”道恩斯在谈到中国时表示，“但他们是一股让欧佩克不得不重视的力量吗？是的。”

中国今年石油进口量的锐减反映出两大变化。该国不再补充石油储备，并已开始动用部分储备；同时，其炼油厂也大幅削减了将石油转化为汽油、柴油及其他燃料的产能。

这部分是因为中国对石油的需求严重疲软。正如[中国最大的炼油企业中国石化所言](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-24/china-s-oil-demand-very-likely-peaked-last-year-sinopec-says)，该国的石油消费很可能已在去年提前 达峰。国际能源署的数据显示，电动汽车目前[约占中国道路上乘用车保有量的14%](https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/global-ev-data-explorer)，相比只有燃油汽车、卡车和公交车的情况，这一比例令该国第二季度的日均石油消耗量减少了150万桶。这削减了全球逾1%的石油需求。

电动汽车使得该国第二季度日均石油消耗量比仅有燃油汽车的情况减少了150万桶。CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images

中国还拥有发达的高铁网络，以及利用煤炭而非石油生产化学品的能力，这在其他国家中并不多见。

由于北京方面披露的信息极少，中国用于减少石油进口的具体工具组合一直是激烈辩论的焦点。“我试图追踪每一条细微的数据，但所有数据都相互矛盾，令人抓狂，”石油市场研究员罗里·约翰斯顿表示。

1993年成为石油净进口国后，中国较晚才认识到建立政府石油储备的价值。相比之下，美国等国在20世纪70年代的能源危机后便建立了大规模储备。

然而，中国追赶得很快。

2001年，时任中国国务院总理朱镕基在全国人大会议上表示：“必须千方百计节约和替代石油，加快石油和天然气勘探与开发，积极利用国外资源，并尽快建立石油等战略资源的储备制度。”

这一能源安全战略在一定程度上源于一种担忧：美国或印度海军可能会封锁马六甲海峡（印尼和马来西亚之间的一条狭窄水道），从而阻止中东石油运往中国。

中国国家主席习近平延续了这些优先事项，并推动了石油储备的增长。目前，中国的石油储备[约占全球已知石油库存的三分之一](https://cn.nytimes.com/business/20260615/iran-war-oil-reserves/)。

2021年房地产市场严重危机引发的低利率环境为北京方面及其国有石油公司近期的疯狂采购提供了便利。在利率高企时，购买和储存石油的成本十分高昂。与债券或派息股票不同，石油除非出售否则无法产生收益。但当利率极低时，政府和企业会认为持有现金与持有石油等大宗商品之间几乎没有区别。

如今，随着全球主要油价在每桶103美元左右徘徊，关键问题之一是中国在未来几个月将购买多少石油，以及其中有多少原油会被转化为柴油及其他燃料出售。8月份的石油进口量环比增长了6%，但仍远低于战前水平。

“想想几十年来，沙特阿拉伯凭借调节产量的能力拥有了多大的地缘政治影响力，”曾在乔治·W·布什总统任内负责伊拉克和阿富汗事务的前副国家安全顾问梅根·奥沙利文表示。“如果中国在需求端具备了这种能力，就会成为一个美国及其他国家主动寻求合作的行为体，他们会以其他潜在利益作为交换，请求中方采取相关行动。”

title: 众院通过俄伊制裁法案，最高100%二级关税授权，中国或首当其冲
summary: 华盛顿 — 美国国会众议院星期三(9月16日)通过一项大规模对俄制裁法案，赋予特朗普总统一项新的经济施压工具：对继续大量购买俄罗斯石油和天然气的国家输美商品征收最高100%的额外关税。 美国国会众议院星期三以262票对159票通过了这项名为《2026年林赛·格雷厄姆制裁俄罗斯和伊朗法》(Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026)的[法案](https://www.kelly.senate.gov/wp-
content:
华盛顿 —

美国国会众议院星期三(9月16日)通过一项大规模对俄制裁法案，赋予特朗普总统一项新的经济施压工具：对继续大量购买俄罗斯石油和天然气的国家输美商品征收最高100%的额外关税。

美国国会众议院星期三以262票对159票通过了这项名为《2026年林赛·格雷厄姆制裁俄罗斯和伊朗法》(Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026)的[法案](https://www.kelly.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/One-Pager-Lindsey-O.-Graham-Sanctioning-Russia-Act-of-2026.pdf)。由于参议院8月已经以86票对11票通过相同文本，法案现已送交白宫。唐纳德·特朗普(Donld Trump)总统此前表示支持这项立法，并预计将签署成法。

这项法案的主要目标是进一步压缩俄罗斯通过能源出口获得的财政收入。除了扩大对俄罗斯政府官员、金融机构、能源与国防部门以及用于规避制裁的“影子船队”的制裁之外，其中最受关注的一项条款，是允许对俄罗斯能源主要购买国实施范围广泛的所谓“二级关税”。

中国和印度目前被普遍视为这一规定最直接的潜在对象。中国研究机构数据显示，中国今年8月仍是俄罗斯化石燃料最大的海外买家，占俄罗斯前五大买家能源出口收入的51%。

**什么是“二级关税”？**

传统制裁通常直接针对俄罗斯企业、银行或个人，而这项法案进一步瞄准与俄罗斯做生意的第三国。

法案规定，在成为法律30天后，如果一个国家继续“明知”购买俄罗斯原产石油或天然气，同时属于此前12个月俄罗斯石油或天然气进口量最大的五个国家之一，美国总统必须提高该国商品进入美国时的关税，税率最高可以达到100%。法案也涵盖被认定为协助俄罗斯规避石油制裁最严重的五个国家。

法案文字明确规定，如果一个国家符合条件，额外关税将适用于“从该国进口美国的所有商品”，并且是在其他已经存在的关税、反倾销税、301关税或232关税之上额外征收。

这意味着，如果中国最终被认定符合条件，受影响的理论范围可以覆盖几乎全部中国输美商品，而不仅限于能源或与俄罗斯交易直接相关的产品。

虽然中国并没有在法律文本中被“自动制裁”，但从当前贸易情况看，中国很可能成为行政部门首先需要评估的国家之一。

独立研究机构能源与清洁空气研究中心(CREA)的数据显示，今年8月中国是俄罗斯最大的化石燃料买家，对俄能源采购约84亿欧元，其中约58亿欧元为原油。

“该法案传递了美国团结的强烈信号，并为政府提供了所有必要手段，以帮助将这场战争引向公正的结局。我们很自豪能将该法案提交给总统签署，”众议院议长迈克·约翰逊(Mike Johnson)在法案通过后发表的声明中表示。

众议院版的法案发起人之一、德克萨斯州共和党籍联邦众议员迈克尔·麦考尔(Michael McCaul)对记者说，“制裁很好，但它们是可以被规避的。而关税就不能被规避。所以这就是关税的威力。而头号违规者是中国。如果我们既对中国实施制裁又征收关税，中国就可以对普京施加压力，让他坐到谈判桌上。”

**“最高100%”并不等于一定征100%**

法案给予总统和美国贸易代表相当大的执行空间。

法律规定，初始税率可以在最高100%的范围内设定。之后，美国贸易代表可以根据有关国家是扩大还是减少俄罗斯能源采购，对税率进行调整。

如果一个国家显著减少俄罗斯能源采购，特朗普政府可以降低税率；如果其采购增加，行政部门也可以提高税率。

此外，总统可以基于美国国家利益给予豁免，但必须事先向国会提交书面证明，并解释为何豁免符合美国国家利益。

这一设计意味着，这项法案既是一套制裁机制，也给总统留下了相当大的外交谈判空间。

这导致部分民主党人担心法案将给予特朗普总统更宽松的施加关税权力。仅有58名民主党人和一名独立议员对法案投下赞成票。

法案通过后，民主党众议员斯坦尼·霍耶(Steny Hoyer)在回答记者有关他花了八个小时打电话，说服民主党同僚投赞成票的提问时说，“我向他们解释了为什么我认为明确表态支持乌克兰、支持制裁，并明确指出制裁基本上仅限于九个国家，这一点至关重要。我们民主党人担心总统会利用这项授权，将其使用到许多其他国家。”

**法案通过时机受关注**

法案通过的时机尤其受到关注。特朗普总统预计9月24日在华盛顿与中国国家主席习近平举行峰会。俄罗斯能源、伊朗以及美中经贸关系都可能成为双方讨论议题。

如果特朗普总统将法案签署，白宫将首次拥有一项经国会明确授权、可以直接把中国对俄能源采购与几乎全部中国输美商品关税挂钩的法律工具。

中国外交部发言人郭嘉昆星期四在例行记者会上表示，中国一贯反对没有国际法依据、没有经过联合国安理会授权的“非法单边制裁和长臂管辖”。

俄罗斯2022年全面入侵乌克兰后，欧美国家大幅减少购买俄罗斯石油，中国和印度随后成为俄罗斯能源出口最重要的市场之一。

今年8月，中国仍占俄罗斯前五大化石燃料买家所贡献收入的一半以上。俄罗斯原油也在中国进口能源结构中占据重要地位。

**下一步是什么？**

特朗普总统已经表示他将签署这项法案。一旦签署，根据法案文本，行政部门将在30天内开始确定哪些国家符合俄罗斯石油、天然气主要进口国或制裁规避协助国的标准，并决定初始关税税率。随后，美国贸易代表必须至少每180天重新评估俄罗斯能源主要进口国。

在实际加征关税至少10天前，白宫或美国贸易代表还必须向国会提交书面说明，解释选择该国以及确定具体税率的依据。

乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基(Volodymyr Zelenskyy)在X上发贴，对法案最终获得通过表示感谢。

他随后在另一条[贴文](https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2100517957637919003?s=20)中点名批评中国未能向俄罗斯施压，协助结束战争。“我没看到中国在推动俄罗斯停止战争。我从来没看到过，”他写道，“中国可以找到办法让普京走向谈判。我肯定，但他们没这么做。如果你能做到却没有做，那算支持吗？”

# PRESS RELEASE: WUC Urges President Donald Trump to Raise the Uyghur Genocide During Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington

[Uyghur Congress](https://www.lemkininstitute.com/profile/99a40ab6-7c29-40a8-95db-bd546dd069fa13782/profile)

2 days ago

3 min read

Credits: Uyghur Congress

**Press Release – For immediate Release**

**18 September 2026**

**Contact: World Uyghur Congress**[](https://us.list-manage.com/Haz1I6agD5m?e=ad9475c2bb&c2id=ebbb81823270098fd793e10507011207)[**www.uyghurcongress.org**](http://www.uyghurcongress.org/)**+49 89 5432 1999 or**[**contact@uyghurcongress.org**](mailto:contact@uyghurcongress.org)

On September 24, Chinese President Xi Jinping will undertake a visit to the United States, his first since 2023. In light of this visit, the World Uyghur Congress (WUC) urges US President Donald Trump and the US government to seize this opportunity to privately and publicly raise the Uyghur genocide.

The United States has a strong record of supporting the Uyghur cause and drawing international attention to China’s repression of Uyghurs in East Turkistan and abroad. On January 19, 2021, the United States formally recognized the situation as genocide for the first time. This position was reaffirmed in an official State Department statement on September 10, 2026, just a few weeks before Xi’s visit. The United States also enacted the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) in 2021, establishing a presumption that goods produced in East Turkistan using forced labor are prohibited from entering the US market unless importers can demonstrate compliance with the law. This measure has been complemented by the Entity List, which restricts exports to designated entities. As of today, the list includes 187 entities, following its largest-ever expansion in July 2026, when 43 companies were added. Together, these measures demonstrate the United States’ role as a partner in supporting Uyghur communities both within and outside its borders, as well as its continued commitment to advancing Uyghur rights.

“Xi’s visit to Washington is a strategic moment to move beyond words of condemnation on the Uyghur genocide,” said **WUC President Turgunjan Alawdun.** “The United States has been a strong and vocal ally to the Uyghur people, and Donald Trump has to use this opportunity to continue proving it.”

While WUC acknowledges the United States’ efforts for publicly raising the Uyghur genocide, both at the national and international level, more needs to be done. Whilst the repression tactics have changed, millions of detained and disappeared individuals still remain unaccounted for. Labour transfer programs have increased in recent years, forcibly displacing Uyghur workers and coercing them into work. With the implementation of the Ethnic Unity and Progressive Law, even the most basic expressions of religious and cultural rights have been criminalized. The Chinese government has also been actively trying to disrupt diaspora communities abroad, by intimidating, threatening Uyghurs abroad, particularly human rights activists on US soil. Such horrific atrocities necessitate a robust and coordinated response from the United States and the international community. The US now has the opportunity to take a principled stance and enact real change. WUC calls on President Donald Trump and his Administration to substantively and meaningfully raise the Uyghur genocide in their discussions with Xi Jinping and other Chinese officials during their visit to Washington. We call on these leaders to demand that China stop its genocide of Uyghurs and other human rights violations and to honor its human rights obligations in order to have normal relations with China.

**The World Uyghur Congress therefore calls on the United States and Donald Trump to:**

1.   Substantively raise the Uyghur genocide and other serious human rights violations during official discussions with China, as well as in all future bilateral engagements.

2.   Press the Chinese government to end its policies of repression and systemic human rights abuses in East Turkistan, and to fully implement the international labor rights conventions it has recently ratified, including International Labour Organization (ILO) Convention No. 29 on Forced Labour and ILO Convention No. 105 on the Abolition of Forced Labour.

3.   Press the Chinese government to end its policies of transnational repression, including and especially in the US territory, in order to protect the American Uyghur, Tibetan, Hong Kong, and Chinese diaspora communities.

4.   Press for family reunification of Uyghur-Americans with their disappeared or missing relatives, including for the children of Dr. Rahila Dawut, Ilham Tohti, Dr. Gulshan Abbas and Yalqun Rozi, residing in the United States.

title: India fact-checks: Are China’s Xi Jinping and South Africa’s Ramaphosa sick?
summary: On social media, claims that Chinese President Xi Jinping and his South African counterpart, Cyril Ramaphosa, are sick after the Brics Summit are spreading like wildfire. The wave of speculation prompted the Ministry of External Affairs to
content:
On social media, claims that Chinese President Xi Jinping and his South African counterpart, Cyril Ramaphosa, are sick after the Brics Summit are spreading like wildfire. The wave of speculation prompted the Ministry of External Affairs to issue a clarification, calling these posts ‘misleading’

Chinese President Xi Jinping and his South African counterpart Cyril Ramaphosa are allegedly sick according to a widespread social media campaign. The MEA has now debunked these claims. File image/Reuters

World leaders and their health are always a subject of speculation. Rumours about the ageing US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin rarely cease.

Now, almost a week after [India hosted the Brics Summit in New Delhi](https://www.firstpost.com/explainers/brics-summit-2026-what-india-gained-from-weekend-in-new-delhi-14045692.html), speculation is rife over Chinese President Xi Jinping’s health. Numerous unverified accounts on social media have claimed that the leader was flown out of India in a hurry and rushed to a hospital.

In addition to Xi’s health, rumours also began flying over the condition of South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa.

Amid the conjecture, India’s Ministry of External Affairs, in a rare move, stepped in, issuing a clarification that these claims were “misleading” and cautioned against such “malicious posts” online.

## MEA issues a fact-check

On Thursday (September 17), the Ministry of External Affairs’ fact-checking team published multiple posts debunking rumours of Xi Jinping and Cyril Ramaphosa’s ill-health.

It further issued a warning against spreading “such malicious posts on social media platforms”.

## Xi and Ramaphosa rumours spread like wildfire

The MEA fact-check came after several accounts online began to speculate about Xi and Ramaphosa’s health.

According to X user Wanjun Xie, who claims to be the chairman of the China Democratic Party and is known to peddle anti-Communist Party of China propaganda, the Chinese leader fainted during the Brics summit in New Delhi and later suffered a severe ischemic stroke.

In his rather lengthy post, Wanjun also claimed that Xi struggled up the stairs of his aircraft while departing India. “His body was under extreme strain, his left leg lacked strength, and his left arm failed to provide balance, forcing him to tilt his body to the left just to barely make it up the step. When Xi Jinping turned at the cabin door to wave, his accompanying doctor immediately rushed onto the plane,” wrote the reported Chinese dissident, whose whereabouts are unknown.

Moreover, he alleged that once Xi landed in China, he was rushed to Beijing’s 301 Hospital.

No credible report has backed this claim, and _Firstpost_ hasn’t been able to verify the veracity of Wanjun’s claims. However, when the claim was put through Grok, it stated that it was not true. “This is an unverified rumour from the exiled opposition figure Xie Wanjun. Official records show that Xi Jinping attended the Brics summit (September 12-13) as originally scheduled and returned to Beijing on time. Neither Chinese nor Indian officials have confirmed any fainting, stroke, or hospitalisation. There are reports of public activities after his return to Beijing. In the video, he boarded the plane on his own and waved, with no apparent abnormalities,” stated the AI assistant.

However, Wanjun Xie wasn’t the only one to make such claims about Xi’s physical well-being. Another X account, Bill Gertz, who is the _Washington Times_ national security correspondent, also wrote, “Rumours are flying in China over Xi Jinping begin taken ill during his visit to India. They include claims that he suffered a minor illness to experiencing a stroke worsened by failure to treat early. Some wild claims say rival group armies are mobilising for civil war. No confirmation, but Treasury Secretary Bessent is meeting with Chinese counterparts today, and we’ll see if the summit for Sept 24 is still on.”

Far-right influencer [Laura Loomer](https://www.firstpost.com/world/united-states/who-is-laura-loomer-far-right-conspiracy-theorist-accused-of-fuelling-trump-pet-eating-claims-13814788.html) also added to the Xi poor health rumours. “Does anyone actually care that Xi Jinping is sick or suffered a medical emergency? This is a man who murdered 1.2 million US citizens with a bio weapon and got away with it. Maybe he will be too sick to travel to the US next week. Nobody cares.”

[Jennifer Zeng](https://www.firstpost.com/explainers/who-is-jennifer-zeng-the-journalist-who-claimed-china-was-involved-in-hardeep-singh-nijjars-killing-13223312.html), an independent blogger known for her criticism of the Chinese Communist Party, cited a former Chinese Communist Party (CCP) official in her claims that “Xi Jinping is suffering from cerebellar atrophy”.

All of these unverified claims have taken a life of their own, spawning fake videos and AI-generated images of an unwell Xi.

Many social media handles have even used [PM Modi’s pause during his Brics speech](https://www.firstpost.com/explainers/is-he-ok-pm-checks-on-xi-then-chinese-prez-skips-gala-dinner-what-happened-at-brics-14045490.html) to support their claims. On the first day of the Brics Summit (Saturday, September 12), PM Modi paused while making his [opening remarks](https://www.firstpost.com/explainers/pm-modis-brics-speech-takeaways-global-south-unsc-reforms-analysis-14045289.html), looking to Xi and asking, ‘Is it okay?’

While netizens are speculating that it was over Xi’s health, others note that the PM’s query was related to the Chinese leader’s earpiece translator and not his health.

And Xi isn’t the only victim of such claims. Many reports have emerged that South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has booked off from public engagements due to ill health on the advice of his medical team.

According to one claim, his office stated that he had been advised to rest and recover after returning from India on Monday.

## Rumours and a debunking drive

As the rumours spread far and wide, with many chiming in, some began to discredit these claims.

X user @SimonLevyMx, who claims to “proudly serve President Trump and Maga”, noted online, “I have personally verified that the rumours circulating about President Xi Jinping’s health are false. President Xi is in good health. These false rumours are being spread, in my assessment, by woke Democrats and people associated with the São Paulo Forum. Political propaganda should never be confused with facts.”

Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings Institute and author of the book _Fateful Triangle: How China Shaped US-India Relations During the Cold War_, also noted on X: “Seeing rumours re Xi’s health based on a fake image from Brics day 1. After he’s supposed to have “collapsed,” he somehow managed to — give Day 1 remarks, have a bilateral with Modi, plant a tree, give Day 2 remarks.”

While the MEA has debunked the speculation, the topic of Xi and Ramaphosa’s health is still being spoken about, making it a viral trending topic on several social media platforms.

## Capitol agenda: **China fears** drive AI divide

Fear of international competition is emerging as a key point of tension slowing down any path to AI safety legislation.

09/17/2026, 8:00am ET

*   Share:
*   [](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/17/congress/china-fears-drive-ai-divide-01081675)
*   [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/17/congress/china-fears-drive-ai-divide-01081675&text=Capitol%20agenda%3A%20China%20fears%20drive%20AI%20divide&via=politico)

Americans — and Congress — are divided on whether it’s acceptable to fall behind other countries in the race to develop advanced artificial intelligence.

And that fear of international competition is emerging as a [key point of tension](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/poll-china-ai-competition-01081632) slowing down any path to AI safety legislation.

Even as almost two thirds of respondents in a new POLITICO poll said [there’s a real possibility](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/poll-ai-technology-risks-humanity-trump-voters-01078087) that AI could destroy humanity, they’re split on whether it’s acceptable to slow down and potentially fall behind other countries like China in an AI arms race.

A plurality, 43%, say it is okay for the U.S. to fall behind if that means developing AI more responsibly and securely, while 37% take the opposite view. Voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024 favor the competition-first position by 50% compared to just 34% of Kamala Harris voters.

Republican Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie argued the U.S. cannot risk Chinese AI dominance, and that AI legislation is too complex to rush — even if that means pushing off until next year consideration of a measure by his panel.

“We absolutely can’t surrender,” he said Wednesday at POLITICO’s Decoded Summit.

Meanwhile, the head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus said competition isn’t a reason to avoid guardrails.

“The AI race is not an arms race that you win,” Rep. Greg Casar said at the Decoded Summit.

Other lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are trying to strike a balance. Rep. John Moolenaar, chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, acknowledged lawmakers “do have a responsibility for public safety” while saying it was also important to “beat China when it comes to the AI race.”

Still, the emerging divisions spotlight a [long road ahead for any consensus from Congress](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/what-ai-urgency-industry-and-leaders-split-on-how-to-handle-advanced-techs-threats-01080660).

An attempt to quickly pass a bill requiring companies to build a “kill switch” into their AI models from Republican Sen. John Kennedy [was blocked Wednesday](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/16/congress/paul-kills-kill-switch-bill-01081348) by Sen. Rand Paul on the chamber’s floor.

And while Guthrie’s Senate counterpart, Commerce Chair Ted Cruz said [Wednesday his hope](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/16/congress/ted-cruz-optimistic-on-ai-markup-01080371) was still to mark up this month a bipartisan AI safety bill from Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, lawmakers haven’t reached agreement to finalize the measure. Thune himself said Wednesday he was unsure it would happen before the midterms.

Cracks are also starting to show among the leading AI companies on what role they want Congress to play.

One example: Anthropic’s policy chief Sarah Heck declined at POLITICO’s summit to endorse a proposal for congressionally mandated independent AI monitoring — a day after competitor OpenAI endorsed it. The proposal is a key provision in Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan’s bipartisan AI safety measure.

The House’s [early dismissal Wednesday](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/16/congress/johnson-cancels-another-house-session-day-01079318) only added to time pressure on lawmakers, who will return to a lame duck session with an already full calendar.

**_What else we’re watching:_**

**— LEE BULLISH ON PERMITTING:**Energy and Natural Resources Chair [Mike Lee told fellow](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/16/congress/lee-tells-colleagues-hes-bullish-on-permitting-deal-01081072) Republicans during a closed-door lunch Wednesday he is “guardedly optimistic” that negotiators will reach a long-sought deal on a bill to ease permitting approval for energy projects. “We were told today that the Democrats are going to agree to a permitting bill, and it’s going to be drafted and ready for us to vote on,” Kennedy said in an interview. Still, the top negotiators have yet to clinch an agreement, meaning the timeline could slip until after the midterms.

**— SPY LAW TIMING UNCLEAR:**The Office of the Director of National Intelligence [recently warned](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/16/congress/key-spy-law-could-go-dark-if-congress-doesnt-act-by-november-trump-admin-says-01080296) Congress that if it doesn’t vote on a controversial surveillance law by Nov. 20, the program could go dark, but it’s unclear congressional leadership can meet that deadline. Thune told reporters this week that there is an “interest” in trying to get Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act reauthorized, but didn’t commit to getting a vote before the midterms. With the House gone, reauthorization will wait until at least mid-November, regardless.

_Riley Rogerson, Mia McCarthy, Anna Wiederkehr, Jordain Carney, John Sakellariadis and Josh Siegel contributed to this report._

## Republicans give Warsh room on interest rates

Some GOP lawmakers indicated they were relieved to see Fed Chair Kevin Warsh willing to buck President Donald Trump.

By [Katherine Hapgood](https://www.politico.com/staff/kate-hapgood) and [Jasper Goodman](https://www.politico.com/staff/jasper-goodman)

09/17/2026, 4:11pm ET

The Federal Reserve just made congressional Republicans’ lives even harder in the run-up to the November midterm elections. But they’re holding their fire on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.

The Fed this week [hiked interest rates](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/fed-rates-trump-warsh-inflation-01079371) for the first time since Warsh took over as the central bank’s leader. The central bank’s unanimous decision to increase borrowing costs threatens to worsen the growing problems Republicans face around voters’ views of the economy and the high cost of living.

But some GOP lawmakers indicated they were relieved to see Warsh’s willingness to buck President Donald Trump after he faced withering criticism during his confirmation process from Democrats, who said he would do the president’s bidding in the role.

“The Fed has to be independent. They showed that they were independent,” said Sen. Mike Rounds, a South Dakota Republican who is up for reelection. “That should give confidence to the markets.”

Republicans’ willingness to give Warsh room — despite its potential political downsides for them — highlights their deference to the new Fed chief.

“It’s not good,” said Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican who lost a primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent. “But it’s a fact that they need to get inflation under control. But the timing is not optimal.”

The decision to hike rates comes amid an uneasy dynamic where the Fed is taking action to tamp down rising inflation while Trump wants to see the economy boosted by cheaper borrowing costs. Republican lawmakers, meanwhile, are caught between supporting Trump’s economic agenda and voicing confidence in Warsh’s ability to bring inflation under control.

Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.), a staunch supporter of the president who sits on the Senate Banking Committee, said that while she and Warsh “may have a different opinion on how we achieve a place where ultimately interest rates are low” and that she’d “love to see [lower rates],” she “trust[s] what [Warsh] is doing, and appreciate[s] the independence of the Fed.”

_**Article published in collaboration with ChinaFile**_

On September 24, Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, four months after Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May. That meeting produced a set of economic agreements, a new[U.S.-China Board of Trade](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-deals-with-china-delivering-for-american-workers-farmers-and-industry/?query-11-page=88&utm) and[Board of Investment](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-deals-with-china-delivering-for-american-workers-farmers-and-industry/?query-11-page=88&utm), an agreement to open a government-to-government[dialogue on artificial intelligence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/14/world/asia/china-us-ai-safety.html), and a commitment by the two leaders to build what both governments[called](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-deals-with-china-delivering-for-american-workers-farmers-and-industry/)a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.”

Several consequential elements of the relationship remain unsettled ahead of the September summit. The[export-control truce](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/looming-trump-xi-meeting-revives-hope-us-china-trade-truce-2025-10-29/) reached in Busan on October 30, 2025—which holds both Washington’s[Affiliates Rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-11-12/pdf/2025-19846.pdf) and China’s October 9[rare-earth export-control package](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/china-suspends-export-controls-certain-critical-minerals-related-items.html) in abeyance—runs for one year, leaving its future uncertain. Preparations for a bilateral AI risk-and-safety dialogue are[reportedly underway](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/us-china-gear-up-mid-september-ai-safety-dialogue-2026-09-04/), although its timing, participants, and agenda remain unsettled. And, according to some analysis, Washington and Beijing construe “constructive strategic stability” quite[differently](https://www.cfr.org/articles/china-and-the-u-s-agreed-to-strategic-stability-in-beijing-they-dont-define-it-the-same-way). The administration has also delayed announcing the proposed[$14 billion U.S. arms sale for Taiwan](https://www.foreign.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/05082026%20Bipartisan%20Letter%20to%20President%20Trump%20on%20Taiwan.pdf), despite receiving congressional pre-approval in January 2026.

We asked a group of China and U.S.-China relations experts what observers should watch to determine what the meeting actually changes: Which decisions, mechanisms, regulatory actions, political signals—or notable absences—would reveal the direction of the relationship after the leaders leave Washington?

—[Jennifer Choo](https://asiasociety.org/policy-institute/jennifer-choo)

## The Xi-Trump Factor

Xi Jinping will arrive in Washington for his summit with Donald Trump hoping to prolong the current stability in U.S.-China relations. Since Xi countered last year’s “Liberation Day” tariff hike with disruptive rare-earth export controls, Trump has prioritized good relations with him and put several planned technology restrictions[on hold](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/11/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-strikes-deal-on-economic-and-trade-relations-with-china/). That has slowed the expansion of the “derisking” agenda of sanctions, export controls, and targeted economic containment that was a pillar of the Biden administration’s China policy. Their Beijing summit in May saw Trump endorse Xi’s framing of bilateral ties as a “[constructive relationship of strategic stability](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-deals-with-china-delivering-for-american-workers-farmers-and-industry/).”

Beijing sees the present moment as a golden opportunity to[accelerate industrial self-reliance](https://asiasociety.org/policy-institute/we-must-depend-entirely-ourselves-policy-politics-and-us-china-relations-fourth-plenum) and strengthen its geoeconomic leverage while limiting further U.S. pressure. Of course, the Trump administration has also[authorized](https://apnews.com/article/trump-xi-taiwan-iran-trade-e7a3cdf161c608de152ac1c6e5755452)a record arms package for Taiwan, placed new[restrictions](https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-administration-ban-new-chinese-robots-inverters-protecting-us-ai-buildout-2026-07-28/)on foreign robots, and accused China of “[stealing and copying American AI models.](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3366835/us-accuses-chinese-ai-firms-malicious-copying-ai-technology)” But many Chinese strategists[recognize](https://www.sinification.org/p/trump-xi-summit-chinese-analysts)the U.S. president as a relatively benign figure in Washington when it comes to dealing with Beijing. Indeed, word around D.C. is that more hawkish officials have drafted several proposals to hobble China’s high-tech industries, which are ready to go if Trump sours on Xi.

Trump’s centrality to China policymaking makes his personal interactions and negotiations with Xi especially consequential. China’s rare-earth chokehold may encourage restraint, but Trump could swing back to confrontation if he decides Xi is insufficiently respectful or cooperative. That would be Beijing’s worst-case scenario and would likely trigger retaliation, especially given its heightened sensitivity to foreign policy setbacks ahead of a twice-a-decade leadership reshuffle at the 21st Party Congress late next year, when Xi is expected to secure a fourth term.

Xi will want his visit planned down to the minute, with equal billing alongside Trump and no risk of embarrassment. According to former Belarusian diplomat[Pavel Slunkin](https://x.com/PavelSlunkin/status/1683465201939632130), during Xi’s 2015 visit to Belarus, then-protocol chief Qin Gang requested a 2:00 a.m. inspection of a museum Xi would tour later that day. His team wanted to know exactly which step of a staircase Xi would reach when some music began playing. No wonder Chinese officials[are rattled](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3364025/china-rattled-trump-white-house-chaos-weeks-ahead-xi-visit-it-has-happened) at the relative lack of preparation for this summit. Such meticulous planning sits uneasily with Trump’s improvisation: In May, he[surprised](https://www.democrats.senate.gov/newsroom/trump-transcripts/transcript-sean-hannity-interviews-president-trump-in-beijing-for-fox-news-51426)his hosts by inviting several American executives into a meeting with Xi.

Beijing therefore is eager to make the summit a “success” in Trump’s eyes without making significant concessions on issues like AI-model distillation, industrial overcapacity, or rare-earth export controls. Expect progress on Trump’s Board of Trade and Board of Investment initiatives, promises of additional Chinese purchases of U.S. goods, more dialogues, and an extension of the economic truce—although an agreed duration would be moot if Trump decides to pivot on China. If all goes well, the two leaders may end the summit by confirming that Trump will attend APEC in Shenzhen and Xi the G20 in Miami later this year. If things do not go well, we will know much sooner.

## Why a Grand Economic Bargain Will Be Hard

China’s economy on the eve of the summit is in less dire shape than many had expected. Exports are[holding up](https://tradingeconomics.com/china/exports) despite trade tensions, largely because of China’s centrality and ascent across global value chains. The[global AI investment boom](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/global-investment-is-forecast-to-exceed-1-trillion-in-2026) has also been an unexpected tailwind, lifting demand for upstream metals and equipment and helping pull the economy out of deflation.

So China comes to Washington with a strong hand. Xi has good reason to lower tensions with the U.S., but he will not make concessions on Beijing’s manufacturing ambitions, precisely because those strengths explain the country’s current resilience.

Yet that resilience may itself be a deeper source of vulnerability. A model supported by domestic tech and manufacturing strength and external tech demand is unusually vulnerable to geopolitical risks, including export controls and swings in the global AI investment boom.

Global market pressure, however, can only go so far toward forcing China to balance its economy. China’s imbalance is ultimately a domestic political-economy problem, which is why I am not optimistic that the September summit will produce a breakthrough. Beijing has correctly diagnosed the problem. Xi Jinping himself[calls for](https://en.qstheory.cn/2026-03/20/c_1169810.htm) strengthening domestic demand. But diagnosis is not action. Genuine rebalancing would require a much larger redistribution of income and fiscal resources toward households and local governments. Those are difficult choices, with clear political winners and losers.

Xi is all-in on making China a technological superpower on par with the U.S. While he seems serious, at least rhetorically, about boosting consumption and expanding social welfare, institutional inertia still favors industrial upgrading and strategic sectors. The supply-side agenda remains an unequivocal top priority, and meaningful improvement in domestic demand will realistically be slow-moving. There is also a basic[fiscal constraint](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-09-01/china-slashes-hidden-local-government-debt-by-half-in-two-years-102480680.html): How do you ask local governments to spend more on households when many are neck-deep in debt?

This does not mean the U.S. lacks leverage over China. Access to the American market and innovation ecosystem is in fact enormously valuable to Chinese firms that need deep pools of capital and high-value customers. But turning that leverage into an effective mechanism for negotiating with China on its economic model is far more complicated. The sectors at the crux of the problem, especially advanced manufacturing and new energy, are also central to China’s growth model and deeply entangled with national security. These are precisely the issues on which a hastily prepared summit is unlikely to produce substantial progress.

What happens beyond September is more consequential: whether China’s need to rebalance can be aligned with America’s need to rebuild industrial competitiveness. Chinese cost-effective tech products, produced through intense domestic involution, could eventually be leveraged against supply-chain localization requirements for Chinese firms to access the U.S. market and reshore jobs and technological know-how. But getting that architecture right requires serious preparation, especially below the presidential level. In that sense, the proposed[U.S.-China Board of Investment](https://www.scmp.com/news/us/economy-trade-business/article/3363829/us-china-board-investment-stalls-expected-trump-xi-meeting) could eventually be useful, especially if it provides Chinese firms with political shielding to invest in the United States beyond individual election cycles.

So I am not optimistic about a grand deal this month. But signs that both sides are willing to build the machinery for a deeper conversation on building healthier, more balanced economic models would matter. Leadership-level intent still has to translate into bureaucratic incentives on both sides. No single summit can do that in one fell swoop.

## CEOs Will Watch the Fine Print

Both the U.S. and Chinese governments are signaling that expectations should be lowered for President Xi Jinping’s September 24 state visit to Washington.

# Will Taiwan Fight? We Need Better Evidence.

Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often rely on thin evidence.

By **Mor Sobol**

September 17, 2026

[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fthediplomat.com%2F2026%2F09%2Fwill-taiwan-fight-we-need-better-evidence%2F&title=Will+Taiwan+Fight%3F+We+Need+Better+Evidence. Credit: [Ministry of National Defense, ROC (Taiwan)](https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?fbid=987378426899970&set=pb.100068834665743.-2207520000&type=3)

Simon Shuster’s recent article in [The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/10/trump-taiwan-sovereignty-china/688356/), asking whether Taiwan might simply “give up” in the face of growing pressure from China, attracted considerable attention in Taiwan and among the broader community of China and Taiwan watchers. [Some](https://x.com/PaulHuangReport/status/2098709664875839617?s=20)praised the piece for its candid analysis and for asking uncomfortable questions that are too often avoided in discussions about Taiwan’s security. [Others](https://newbloommag.net/2026/09/10/simon-shuster-atlantic-tw/)were somewhat less impressed.

The article quickly came under fire from Taiwanese and (mostly) Taiwan-based foreign analysts, who pointed to factual errors, questionable interpretations of domestic politics, and what they saw as a selective and misleading portrayal of Taiwanese society. Legislator [Puma Shen](https://x.com/pumashen/status/2097547948108431605?s=20), one of those interviewed for the article, issued a public statement accusing Shuster of taking his comments out of context. The [Taipei Times](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials/archives/2026/09/12/2003864120) devoted an editorial to rebutting the article, and even Taiwan’s National Security Council weighed in, with Secretary General [Joseph Wu](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6437562) publicly rejecting its central premise.

Essentially, there are rather good reasons to take these criticisms seriously. Some concern basic facts and context, which are obviously important when making such a sweeping argument about Taiwan. That said, the reaction also exposed another problem. A significant part of the response has questioned what a foreign journalist who spent limited time in Taiwan and has no evident prior expertise on Taiwan or the region can really know about Taiwanese society. Critics pointed to a lack of understanding of Taiwanese politics, insufficient engagement with Taiwanese voices and opinion polls showing considerable willingness to defend Taiwan, and Taiwan’s own experience – from democratization and the Sunflower Movement to its remarkable response to COVID-19 – as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary.

As compelling as these arguments are, none of them give us a particularly convincing answer either.

Predicting what Taiwan and its people would actually do if China decided to use force is extraordinarily difficult. Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often seem to rely on evidence that tells us much less than we think.

Opinion polls are perhaps the clearest example. As [argued previously](https://thediplomat.com/2025/04/why-we-should-be-skeptical-of-taiwan-youths-self-reported-willingness-to-fight/) in The Diplomat, they are useful for understanding attitudes, but telling a pollster that you would defend Taiwan is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, casualties are mounting, electricity and communications are disrupted, and nobody knows whether outside help is coming. That does not make polls useless. Questions involving actual costs, such as longer military service, higher taxes, or greater personal obligations, can tell us more. But saying that you are willing to sacrifice something and actually sacrificing it are not the same thing.

Historical examples have only limited relevance. Taiwan’s democratization, the Sunflower Movement, and its response to COVID-19 have all been cited as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary. Comparisons can also be drawn with Finland’s resistance to the Soviet Union during the Winter War, Ukraine’s response to Russia’s invasion, or other societies that proved far more willing to resist than outsiders expected. These are indeed powerful examples. But what exactly do they tell us about how Taiwanese society would respond to a Chinese attack today?

Israel offers a useful example of why we should be careful in making predictions. Israeli society has repeatedly shown an extraordinary ability to mobilize against military threats. Following the October 7 attacks, [more than 300,000 reservists](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israels-reservists-drop-everything-rush-home-following-hamas-bloodshed-2023-10-12/) were mobilized in a very short period, including Israelis who returned from abroad to report for duty. Nonetheless, during COVID-19, Israel struggled to sustain public compliance with government restrictions. [Trust and willingness](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/coronavirus-a-crisis-of-trust-635158) to follow regulations declined as the crisis continued. The same society generated two very different responses to calls for public action.

title: Taipei donates coastguard vessel to Manila amid South China Sea tensions
summary: Taiwan has quietly acknowledged donating a coastguard vessel to the Philippines, potentially adding to Manila’s maritime patrol capacity amid its long-running stand-off with Beijing in the [South China Sea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/south
content:
Taiwan has quietly acknowledged donating a coastguard vessel to the Philippines, potentially adding to Manila’s maritime patrol capacity amid its long-running stand-off with Beijing in the [South China Sea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/south-china-sea?module=inline&pgtype=article).

Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration said on Wednesday that “this case” was being handled in line with previous transfers of vessels to the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu.

Unlike those three Pacific states, which all maintain formal diplomatic ties with Taipei, Manila recognises Beijing under its [one-China policy](https://multimedia.scmp.com/widgets/timeline/index.html?id=eE8xw5Ig70&style=scmp&module=inline&pgtype=article). In its remarks, the Taiwanese agency did not identify the vessel, its specific Philippine recipient or intended mission.

Taiwanese media have linked the transfer to the Philippine-flagged BLING NO.1, which is classified by commercial ship-tracking services as a law enforcement vessel. Sources familiar with the transfer told the Post that the vessel was the retired Kinmen patrol ship and that BLING NO.1 was a temporary name being used for its delivery voyage to the Philippines.

The identification is consistent with a report by Taiwan’s Liberty Times newspaper, which cited naval enthusiasts’ comparisons of the bows of the Kinmen and its sister ship, the Lienchiang.

The Lienchiang and Kinmen were built in 2008, are about 61 metres (200 feet) long and displace 688 tonnes (758 tons).

Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said this represented “a notable shift” from Taiwan’s previous vessel donations.

02:29

‘Stop grandstanding’: Beijing slams Philippine defence chief after minister exposes South China Sea note

“Whereas those transfers centred on capacity development, delivery of this vessel to the Philippines provides an asset that could have a direct impact on contestation with China,” he said.

Operationally, Bosack said, a vessel of its size and capability would “better position the Philippine Coast Guard to hold firm” against the [Chinese coastguard](https://www.scmp.com/topics/chinas-coastguard?module=inline&pgtype=article), while cautioning that it remained unclear whether Manila would use it for other missions or “in managing Chinese presence operations”.

The transfer has drawn criticism from Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang. KMT legislator Ma Wen-chun questioned why Taipei was donating a law enforcement vessel to the Philippines given continuing disputes over fishing rights and overlapping maritime claims.

Pointing to the fatal shooting of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine coastguard personnel in 2013, Ma asked whether Taipei could guarantee that the donated vessel would not eventually be deployed against Taiwanese fishing boats. She also called on the government to disclose the refurbishment costs, funding source and any restrictions or conditions attached to the transfer.

Simona Grano, head of Research Area China-Taiwan Relations at the University of Zurich, said a vessel of this size could provide the Philippines with “additional flexibility for maritime law enforcement, search and rescue, fisheries protection and sustained presence operations”.

“The vessel should not be viewed as a substitute for the larger and more capable ships that the Philippines needs to monitor its extensive maritime domain,” she said. “However, it could help expand the number of platforms available for routine patrols and allow the Philippine Coast Guard to distribute its existing resources more effectively.”

Manila has been expanding its unofficial security engagement with Taipei amid increasingly tense encounters with Chinese mainland forces both at sea and in the air over parts of the South China Sea.

Citing a senior Philippine government official, the Japan Times reported last year that exchanges with Taiwanese security officials had increased, including contact between senior military personnel. The official described a more deliberate effort to informally draw Taiwan into the defence architecture of the Philippines and the wider region.

Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte makes first court appearance at The Hague

Grano said maritime security and coastguard cooperation offered “relatively discreet channels” through which Taiwan and the Philippines could deepen engagement “without necessarily crossing Manila’s diplomatic red lines concerning its relations with Beijing”.

But she cautioned that “we should be careful not to interpret this single transfer as evidence of a formal security partnership”, adding that Manila’s growing exposure to Chinese maritime pressure created “clear incentives for closer practical cooperation with Taiwan”.

Philippine President [Ferdinand Marcos Jnr](https://www.scmp.com/topics/ferdinand-bongbong-marcos-jnr?module=inline&pgtype=article) said last year there was “no way that the Philippines can stay out” of a US-China conflict over Taiwan. He has also highlighted the need to evacuate Filipinos living and working in Taiwan if a conflict erupted.

Bosack said Taiwan’s low-key approach pointed to practical cooperation rather than “a ceremonial dig” at Beijing.

Manila’s relationship with Beijing remains fraught. On Wednesday, in response to Taipei confirming its plans for a new representative office in Cebu, the foreign ministry in Beijing urged Manila to abide by the one-China principle.

The donation adds Taiwan to a growing list of partners helping to expand the Philippines’ maritime capacity. Much of that support has come from Washington, Manila’s treaty ally, and its partners.

Grano said it would be “premature to conclude that Taiwan has established a systematic regional maritime assistance programme comparable to Japan’s”.

02:55

Taiwan concludes annual war games, including preparing for PLA sea blockade

The comparison was nevertheless useful, she said, because both Japan and Taiwan could strengthen their partners’ resilience “while operating below the threshold of direct military cooperation”.

Japan has supplied the Philippine coastguard with 10 44-metre and two 97-metre response vessels and is financing five more 97-metre ships. The United States handed over two former US Coast Guard 27-metre patrol boats in August, while France is financing the acquisition of 40 new 35-metre patrol vessels from French shipbuilder OCEA.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force.

title: What will Trump and Xi discuss in Washington next week?
summary: WASHINGTON/BEIJING, Sept 17 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week for their second meeting this year, as the two leaders seek stability in a relationship under pressure over issues ranging
content:
WASHINGTON/BEIJING, Sept 17 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week for their second meeting this year, as the two leaders seek stability in a relationship under pressure over issues ranging from trade to Taiwan and Iran to global worries about artificial intelligence.

Xi arrives for his first White House visit in a decade at the helm of an economy on track to post a $1 trillion trade surplus for a second ​straight year. Trump, mired in the Iran war and with low approval ratings, is looking for trade wins he can tout to Americans unhappy with rising prices.

Make sense of global markets with the Trading Day newsletter. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/trading-day/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fchina%2Fwhat-will-trump-xi-discuss-washington-next-week-2026-09-17%2F)

Here are some of the key issues ‌for the September 24 summit, which follows [Trump's May visit to Beijing](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/trump-returns-china-with-stability-stalemate-2026-05-16/):

## TRADE TRUCE OR BACK TO TRADE WAR?

Markets will watch for signs of an extension of a tariff truce announced after [a Trump-Xi summit in South Korea last October and set to expire on November 10](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/what-did-trump-xi-agree-tariffs-export-controls-fentanyl-2025-11-01/). That deal paused a trade war in which the world's two largest economies threatened global supply chains with tit-for-tat tariffs that topped 100%.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this month the countries will make ["some announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/ahead-xis-us-visit-chinas-soybean-crushers-face-high-costs-weak-margins-2026-09-07/)" and traders will be watching for progress on an agreed mutual tariff ​reduction covering $30 billion in goods — a step China could most easily take by cutting duties on U.S. agricultural imports.

U.S. officials say they have continued to press China to address its lack of compliance with last year's ​agreement, while Beijing has pressed for further tariff relief.

## JETS, FARM PRODUCE AND TECH

Trump will be looking to announce trade wins ahead of November midterm congressional elections, including by locking in ⁠high-profile purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products.

Sources told Reuters this month that Xi is [preparing a large business delegation to accompany him](https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/exclusive-chinas-xi-bring-large-ceo-delegation-us-visit-sources-say-2026-09-04/) similar to 2015, when China signed a $38 billion agreement for 300 Boeing

aircraft. China said after the ​May summit that [it would buy 200 more Boeing jets](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/china-says-it-will-buy-200-boeing-jets-seek-extension-us-tariff-truce-2026-05-20/) and the company said this was only an "initial tranche" of a [potentially far bigger deal](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/boeing-ceo-says-200-jet-china-deal-an-initial-tranche-with-more-come-2026-05-28/).

China has been in prolonged talks with Boeing for a transaction that industry sources say could include 500 737 ​MAX jets, plus dozens of wide-body planes, a deal stalled for years as Trump has [threatened to cut off China's access to critical spare engine parts](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/boeing-ceo-trump-is-key-closing-major-plane-order-chinese-airlines-2026-04-22/).

Beijing has been pressing the US to further delay a rule that would bar thousands of Chinese firms from receiving [advanced](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-holds-off-blacklisting-chinas-deepseek-more-than-100-firms-deemed-security-2026-06-17/)US technology, while Washington wants Beijing to [ease shipments of rare earths and critical minerals](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/us-officials-discussed-rare-earths-farm-products-with-china-bessent-says-2026-07-30/) used in high-tech applications from automobile to aerospace manufacturing, as well as defense.

## IRAN WAR

The two presidents are expected to discuss the Iran war, which Trump has struggled to end after launching it with Israel in February.

China ​maintains close ties to Tehran and is by far the world's biggest buyer of Iranian oil exports. Washington sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Tehran, but he has shown little inclination to do so. Reuters last month ​reported that Beijing is selling billions of dollars' worth of goods to Iran through a [sanctions-evasion scheme](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/how-billion-dollar-sanctions-dodge-kept-chinese-goods-flowing-iran-2026-09-10/). China's foreign ministry says it is not aware of such a scheme.

Despite U.S. frustration, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stopped short of imposing penalties on Chinese banks when he last month ‌unveiled an "economic onslaught" ⁠against Iran and warned countries to cut business ties with Tehran.

Item 1 of 3 Members of a U.S. military honor guard roll up a Chinese flag after rehearsing for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit next week with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

**[1/3]**Members of a U.S. military honor guard roll up a Chinese flag after rehearsing for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit next week with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/preparations-ahead-of-chinese-president-xis-visit-with-us-president-trump-at-the-white-house-in-washington/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMkZLTkE5MVo3Vg%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

Bessent has said he would meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend and that Trump and Xi [would continue discussions on China's financial ties to Tehran](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/us-treasurys-bessent-will-meet-with-chinas-he-lifeng-this-weekend-2026-09-15/) during the summit.

## TAIWAN

China has long been hoping to extract concessions from Trump over Taiwan, a democratically governed island Beijing claims as its own, and the world's leading producer of cutting-edge chips. Taiwan strongly objects to China’s sovereignty claims and says only the island’s people can decide their future.

U.S. law requires the administration to provide Taiwan with the means to ​defend itself, but [questions have been hanging](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/taiwan-thanks-us-support-ahead-further-trump-xi-talks-2026-05-15/) over a [large pending arms ​package](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/senior-us-diplomat-says-taiwan-arms-sale-does-not-hinge-china-2026-06-25/) worth up to $14 billion since Trump's Beijing visit.

People ⁠familiar with Chinese efforts told Reuters Beijing hopes to persuade Trump to state publicly that the U.S. opposes Taiwan's independence instead of saying only that it does not support independence, which has been Washington's formulation for decades.

Any U.S. shift on Taiwan would be highly controversial, raising questions about Washington's resolve to defend the island, alarming allies across Asia and provoking ​opposition in Congress.

## ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Analysts see artificial intelligence as a potential area for cooperation, given its implications for national security, economic competitiveness and military capabilities, and shared U.S. and Chinese ​concerns about misuse. However, experts say ⁠intense competition in the field between the countries is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.

On Wednesday, Axios cited a statement from Bessent as saying that the United States [was open to discussing shared risks with China](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/bessent-says-us-open-discussing-shared-ai-risks-with-china-axios-reports-2026-09-16/) in AI talks this weekend.

[US lawmakers have urged new rules to govern AI](https://www.reuters.com/business/anthropic-ceo-urges-ai-companies-slow-model-development-2026-09-12/) systems, while Dario Amodei, chief executive of U.S. artificial-intelligence firm Anthropic, warned this month that Chinese dominance in AI could pose security risks to the United States.

Chinese state media dismissed Amodei's warning as coming ⁠from a "Cold War ​playbook" while Trump has [brushed aside calls to slow AI development](https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-says-there-is-sick-conspiracy-against-ai-data-centers-2026-09-14/), saying that "very negative forces" were raising exaggerated concerns.

## FENTANYL FLOWS

Curbing the flow of fentanyl ​precursor chemicals from China remains a concern of the Trump administration, given the ravages the drug has caused among Americans.

Washington has repeatedly accused Beijing of failing to stem the flow of precursors, and Trump imposed fentanyl-related tariffs on China in early 2025 that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down in ​February.

FBI Director Kash Patel told Reuters last month that he had [forged a new law enforcement partnership with China](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/under-patel-fbi-forges-unprecedented-law-enforcement-ties-with-china-russia-2026-08-05/) in hopes of curbing the trade.

Reporting by David Brunnstrom in Washington and Joe Cash in Beijing; Editing by Don Durfee and Deepa Babington

Our Standards: [The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles., opens new tab](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/about-us/trust-principles.html)

Joe Cash reports on China’s economic affairs, covering domestic fiscal and monetary policy, key economic indicators, trade relations, and China’s growing engagement with developing countries. Before joining Reuters, he worked on UK and EU trade policy across the Asia-Pacific region. Joe studied Chinese at the University of Oxford and is a Mandarin speaker.

title: UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity

content:
Item 1 of 2 The Minab school, which was damaged in a strike on February 28, in Minab, Iran, August 27, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS

**[1/2]**The Minab school, which was damaged in a strike on February 28, in Minab, Iran, August 27, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/the-minab-school-which-was-damaged-in-a-strike-on-february-28-in-minab/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMjI3TkFSTFBWNA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

*   Summary

*   Probe says grounds to believe US behind strike on Minab school
*   Says this was a war crime
*   Probe finds Iran carried out murder, torture and persecution of protesters
*   Says Iran protest death toll likely exceeds official figures

GENEVA, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on ​Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in ‌February, and that these constituted war crimes.

It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.

The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/reuters-iran-briefing/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fmiddle-east%2Fun-mission-finds-grounds-believe-us-committed-war-crimes-iran-tehran-crimes-2026-09-17%2F)

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the [Iran war](https://www.reuters.com/world/iran/) that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that ​began in late December.

The Iranian and US permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

US officials have previously said military operations ​are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

UN Fact-Finding missions ⁠are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases. Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals ​such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.

## MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE

The UN ​experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an [attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/un-body-investigating-fatal-strike-iranian-girls-school-2026-03-17/) in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.

The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.

According to the ​report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to ​confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of ‌striking a ⁠civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."

In June US President Donald Trump said that ["nobody" purposefully attacked](https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-says-nobody-attacked-iran-girls-school-on-purpose-2026-06-17/) a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters [first reported](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-may-have-struck-iranian-girls-school-after-using-outdated-targeting-data-2026-03-11/) that an initial internal U.S. military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.

The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.

UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it ​was being used for military purposes.

The experts ​reached a similar conclusion over a ⁠strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.

US Central Command said in a statement ​in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.

## IRAN ABUSES

The UN mission ​probe found that the ⁠Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the [biggest crackdown](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/un-rights-body-holds-emergency-session-irans-protest-crackdown-2026-01-23/) since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled ⁠opponents and ​foreign foes the US and Israel.

The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but ​that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.

The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting ​off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

Reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin; Editing by Alexandra Hudson

title: Canada and EU should ally to protect democracies, Carney says, after 'associate member' proposal angers Trump
summary: * Summary * Companies * Carney pitches closer ties to European Parliament * Address follows proposal Canada could be EU 'associate member' * Trump derides proposal, threatens tariffs * Carney says substance most important in future relation
content:
*   Summary
*   Companies

*   Carney pitches closer ties to European Parliament
*   Address follows proposal Canada could be EU 'associate member'
*   Trump derides proposal, threatens tariffs
*   Carney says substance most important in future relations

STRASBOURG, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Canada and Europe should ally to protect their markets, democracies and rule ​of law in a world dominated by the United States and China, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after an EU proposal to ‌make Canada an "associate member".

The Canadian prime minister received warm applause for his speech to the European Parliament, delivered hours after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened trade sanctions in response to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to create a new status for the EU-Canada relationship.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/misinformation-monitor/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Famericas%2Ftrump-warns-eu-tariffs-over-canadas-potential-associate-membership-calls-it-2026-09-17%2F)

Carney did not adopt the term "associate member" used a day earlier by von der Leyen, but said he appreciated "the ambition" ​that her suggestion conveyed.

"Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together," Carney said.

He was not seeking to form a "third bloc" ​to act as "a great-power rival" to Washington and Beijing "only with better manners," Carney said in a line that drew laughs.

"We do not ⁠seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience, so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial ​integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

He told reporters after the speech that it would be up to the EU how it proposed to describe ​any future relationship, and that the substance of any agreement would be more important than the name given to it.

## TRUMP THREATS

Trump threatened late on Wednesday to take action against the EU if it moved forward with von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an 'associate member' of the bloc.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious ​tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, calling the proposal "laughable".

"If it's a good intention, that's ​fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.

Item 1 of 4 Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney holds a joint press conference with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (not pictured) after his address at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Yves Herman

**[1/4]**Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney holds a joint press conference with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (not pictured) after his address at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Yves Herman [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/canadas-pm-carney-at-the-european-parliament-in-strasbourg/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMllLTkFTT1dFWg%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

The European Commission said von der Leyen's proposal — which had yet to be fleshed out and would ‌need to ⁠be approved by EU member states to go forward — was not a hostile act.

"As our President (von der Leyen) made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.

Asked about Trump's threats, Carney told reporters: "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally."

Among areas in which he said Canada ​would want closer ties with the EU, ​he mentioned seeking strategic autonomy through ⁠deep cooperation in critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space, and payments.

He also mentioned digital trade and building more secure broadband connections between Europe and Asia via their common geography.

## TRUMP CANNOT CHOOSE FOR EU, FRANCE SAYS

Earlier on Thursday, France's ​Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said the United States has no power to veto the EU's geopolitical choices.

"It is not up to ​the United States — or ⁠anyone else — to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans," he told Public Senat TV.

Von der Leyen made the proposal on Wednesday during her annual State of the Union speech, attended by Carney, as she sought to deepen ties among allies in what she called "an openly hostile world".

But it is unclear whether the idea of associate membership would ⁠be backed ​by EU member states.

One EU diplomat expressed surprise on Wednesday at the proposal, saying "nobody really knows what ​it means," adding there were concerns that the European Commission chief was "overpromising and won't be able to deliver".

On Thursday, another European diplomat called it an "unfortunate proposal, which has never been discussed with Member States."

Reporting by ​Yves Herman in Strasbourg, Lili Bayer, Charlotte Van Campenhout, Inti Landauro, Julia Payne in Brussels, Mariana Hernandez; Writing by Ingrid Melander; Editing by Clarence Fernandez, Hugh Lawson, Peter Graff
