content: 李承鹏（大眼哥） X @dayangelcp · Sep 17, 2026 徐湖平安全落地了。南京博物院的事判决如下：徐湖平利用担任常务副院长、院长职务便利，为他人在承接工程、促成商业合作等提供帮助，收受他人财物，犯受贿罪，被依法判处有期徒刑三年，并处罚金人民币二十万元。 那些国宝级文物的事儿没提，提不得。在中国，要当官就得当大官，到了一定级别，好多事儿就不算事儿了。 所以金瓶梅是一部伟大作品。 李承鹏（大眼哥） X @dayangelcp · Dec 30, 2025 李承鹏最新文章：论爱国及《南京博物院之官人我要》 到了年底，没想到被一个画面给震撼到了： 爱国主义相声艺术家姜昆带领一群老艺术家，在洛杉矶豪宅拉着手风琴深情演唱《我和我的祖国》，夕阳，圣诞篝火，永不结冰的泳池……冷不丁地，像看见洪承畴在盛京拉着满清的二弦子，吟唱《我和我的大明》。 姜昆反复辟谣，却被反复证实，人们说姜老师终于创作出此生最好的相声。拿绿卡住豪宅过洋节没什么问题，但大力呼吁“中国人抵制圣诞节”、写数千字长文缅怀抗美援朝，你却坐拥美国绿卡、豪宅还把女儿留在美国读书工作定居，这“含夹量”就太高了。 这国有个不可能三角定理：正直，有钱，真爱国。正直的人怎么可能有钱，有了钱，哪能真爱国。你看在洛杉富人区住了多少贝勒、格格、衙内，开超跑住豪宅喝名酒，并不关心同胞。他们的父辈却在国内教育人民要爱国，抵制外来文化入侵……都不用去大峡谷，就能瞻仰有多分裂。 爱国越来越神经病了。为了抵制文化入侵，有些地方用鳌拜替代圣诞老人。但鳌拜是“扬州十日，嘉定三屠”的满清人哪，留辫子、穿马蹄袖，妥妥的外来文化入侵，且此鳌拜用的还是徐锦江的《肉蒲团之官人我要》版本。警方刚颁布了“私人之间转发不雅视频也是违法”，曲线爱国的群众，别一不小心搞成了聚众淫乱。 到了年底，朋友们按例催更年度总结。但今年真不想写了。刚想写小洛熙被医生害死，想起去年说过宜昌“黄疸入脑窒息致新生儿死亡”。刚准备鞭挞炫富天价耳环的黄杨钿甜，发现去年周公子、北极鲶鱼已被鞭过尸。贪官年年有，器官常常少。杭州早在2011年就喝了粪水，15年前云南鹤庆就因为污染导致89名儿童血铅超标。至于江油，你想想更波澜壮阔的翁安十万人民上街差点把县衙门烧了…… 没什么好总结，每一年是上一年的轮回，我们被锁死在某个日复一日情节雷同的系统，困在算法里，这个算法就是：温水煮青蛙，我们要爱国。 倒也有些亮点试图打破算法。除了姜昆圣诞放歌，就是南京博物院，最大亮点不是几幅字画被掉包，而是让大家看见那套行云流水的体系。庞家后人回忆：“当年文化局官员带了一大群人来我家，说庞家一向爱国的啊……”先用“爱国”动员你捐画，再找专家鉴为赝品，院长儿子低价收购“赝品”，左手递右手，市场高推。我看过一次拍卖，高潮部分，买家长跪不起痛哭流涕“与祖国失散多年的文物终于回来了，花再多的钱，我也要表达赤子之心”……后来才知道，这套表演体系他们玩过多次，半月板都磨损了。有时就由博物院高价收回。 看过《金瓶梅》就知道，“雅贿”。领导就喜欢字画。找个懂事的专家把那幅苏东坡鉴为赝品。“不值钱，高仿”。领导目光如炬，心知肚明。但见：黄烘烘金壶玉盏，白晃晃减靸仙人，南京纻缎，金碧交辉……太师却道：“礼物决不好收的，拿回去”。慌得来保叩头说道：“都是些不值钱的小东西，小的主人西门庆，进献给老爷去赏人”。太师道：“既如此……朝廷赐了几张空名告身，我安你主人做个理刑副千户，顶补千户贺金的员缺。” 来保叩谢：“小的家主举家粉首碎身，莫能报答！” 《金瓶梅》就伟大在把蝇营狗苟写出人性光芒，把殿堂写出了叫床。流转至今，当然有“老子下馆子都不给钱，吃几个西瓜算什么”的粗暴玩法，“杨卫泽市长有一次到博物馆视察，看上一件瓷花瓶，直接安排手下人拿走。博物馆负责人只好把这件瓷花瓶以破碎为由报销处理。” 格局差了，没有上升到家国情怀。 庞家后人又回忆：“曾国藩的曾侄孙女曾昭燏院长也来到我家，说蒋介石把很多国宝带去了台湾，现在国家有难，你们要鼎力相助”。看，以爱国的名义就不是打劫，而是支援国家建设。昨天刷“听海频道”：1953年，三大社会主义改造，农业社会主义改造（人民公社），手工业社会主义改造（私人作坊收为集体），资本主义工商业的社会主义改造（金融国有）。就是说十年间，捐土地、捐工坊、捐公司、捐银行，顺带捐点字画算什么，你不捐，怎么证明你爱国。 公有制是最坏的私有制，最坏的私有制也比公有制好。打着爱国旗号，到头来，都是官人我要。 刚看到一段：当年蒋介石想看乾隆武英殿版的《二十四史》。故宫博物院院长马衡板着脸，让陈布雷打条子承诺“必须一个月内归还”。陈布雷气得扭头就走，回去抱怨：“什么人一个月看得完《二十四史》，存心刁难”。蒋介石苦笑：“不是刁难，是明摆着不借给我”。 后来马衡送来一部商务印书馆的《二十四史》，说：“蒋先生要的书我送来了，若只是想看书，就是这个，若必须是乾隆武英殿版《二十四史》，那就是别有图谋”。如此公然犯上，有人建议拿下马衡。蒋介石却说：“故宫文物，只可马衡，国宝由他保管，国人放心。” 联想起南博的姚迁因追要领导“借走”的字画，身败名裂，上吊自杀。蒋介石也不把马衡搞倒搞臭抓进监狱，几幅画都抢不过来，怪不得江山也丢了呢。只是我们已不好意思再说“解放前夕，国民党反动派把大量国宝偷运到台湾”，台北故宫的国宝，是一个都没少的。 不妨事，打下台湾，一切都是我们的。 故宫创始人吴瀛捐了241件文物，仅剩170余件。宋徽宗的《鸲鹆图》，南博和底特律美术馆竟各有一件……网友眼尖，说那些文物不经细看的，库房里箱子也不敢打开细察。就是玻尔的“观察即塌缩”理论。是啊，中国文物具有波粒二象性，你观察了，就是赝品，不观察，就是真品。 还是南京博物院院长徐湖平未雨绸缪：“南博跑出去一条狗也是可以查到出处的，但文物这东西不好说，不要太在乎真伪。” 大门上明晃晃写着爱国，走进库房，满眼却是盗国。那不是博物馆，是后宫。 康生喜欢上故宫的一方唐代陶龟砚，就“借走看看”，并编入“康砚第五十三号”。他也意识到不能明抢，有一天看上了黄庭坚《梅花三咏》，当即掏出5元钱，豪爽地说“我也不能犯纪律，这画我买了”…… 还是让我们谈谈爱国吧。中国爱国史上有个反面人物，被余秋雨口诛笔伐的敦煌王道士。他其实是个好人，一路逶迤来此地修行，修缮时忽然发现大量经书画卷，步行百里上报知县，无果。又心急如焚去找道台、找学政，最后上书慈禧老佛爷，均无果。眼见这一路过去，每一级上报，就会少一些文物，苦闷之际遇上斯坦因、伯希和这两个懂行的老外。老外惊为天物，表示出钱买走。急于筹钱修缮的王道士，这才答应……这才有了敦煌文物的幸存。对了，老外没有将文物占为己有，他们不是强盗而是探险家，按协议全部上交给了英国，最终保护了文物。 还有多少人说“没有一个中国人能笑着离开大英博物馆”。 王道士晚年很后悔，喃喃说要是当初把东西全卖给伯希和，该多好，也不会被哄抢被损坏了。 大家总爱说这是缩影、那是缩影，其实文物才是一个国家的缩影。 “民国四公子”之一的张伯驹，平生两大爱好，爱文物，爱国。1936年，听说中华第一帖《平复帖》将被转卖英国，他急以4万大洋抢购陆机墨宝。焚香供帖，如奉神明。有人觊觎此帖将他绑架，他宁死不从，并告诉妻子：“宁死魔窟，决不许变卖家藏！”生生被绑了八个月，绑匪只好将赎金降至40万，这才脱身。 后来他听说传世最早的山水画《游春图》，将以800两黄金卖给外国人，怒斥：“谁转手洋人，谁就是千古罪人！”当即卖掉宅子（李莲英旧宅），换了千两黄金，仍差20两，妻子潘素摘下首饰补足，这才留住国宝。蒋介石曾提出，愿意买下这幅《游春图》。张伯驹毫不犹豫拒绝：“贵贱不卖！” 1956年，新中国号召认购公债。已负债累累的张伯驹为了支持建设新中国，将一生珍藏的8件顶级书画捐给了国家，那份清单烁古震今：陆机《平复帖》、展子虔《游春图》、杜牧《张好好诗》、范仲淹《道服赞》、赵孟頫《草书千字文》……个个是故宫“镇院之宝”。文化部长茅盾颁发20万奖金，他婉拒，慨然道：“予所收藏，不必终予身，为予有，但使永存吾土。” 张伯驹捐了半个故宫，后来还是被批斗，在操场当众下跪，沿跑道爬行，拎着铜锣到人民广场边敲边喊“我是大右派，我是牛鬼蛇神”。让我震撼的是，原以为张伯驹会形容槁木，神情萎顿。后来看了炎黄春秋写的一段……“嗯嗯！”张伯驹欣然应允，眼中光芒一闪，他那原本僵直的身躯也瞬间活跃起来，接过那铜锣和小锤子，轻快地踏出门去。街巷回荡着那阵阵锣声，以及“我是大右派”…… 最后，84岁的张伯驹生命垂危，因“级别不够”只得挤在八人病房。在污浊空气和病人呻吟中，他喃喃重复李白《上阳台帖》：“山高水长，物象千万，非有老笔，清壮可穷”……那是他捐给毛泽东的。等女儿终于拿到转院批令时，他已撒手尘寰。 我觉得张伯驹也是顶级文物。器物是死的，留在上面的故事是活的。作为直隶总督的儿子、袁世凯的表侄，翩翩浊世佳公子，倾家荡产为祖国，落得个跪操场、爬跑道，最后竟对惩罚熟练自如，眼里光芒一闪，接过铜锣，轻快地踏出门去……这里面都发生了些啥啊，吉林农场有基因改造组吗？ 所以南京博物院这事儿，我们讨论的到底是文物，还是有个东西决定了文物。讲个结局，坚决反对将文物运往台湾、力劝把个人藏品捐给国家、因表现优秀当上南博院长的曾昭燏，后来政治压力也大了起来。 1964年12月22日，看完病后的她跟司机说：“去灵谷寺散散心吧”。 司机把她拉到灵谷寺。她下车时贴心给了司机一包苹果，要司机等她。那天她一个人上了灵谷寺，上了塔顶，跳了下来。 陈寅恪为其写了首悼亡诗：高才短命人谁惜，白璧青蝇事可嗟。他是了解里面发生的事情。 所有的文物，背后都是人物。不是贩夫走卒，轮不上仓库管理员，必须是通天入地的天龙族。 忽然间，一直独家报道南京博物院事件的亚洲周刊就炸了号。此前，它被令删除所有报道，留下一段藏头诗“春水碧于天，画船听雨眠。未老莫还乡，还乡须断肠”。就是“春画未还”。 博物院水有多深，像海一样深。 金瓶梅又说：只怕睁着眼儿的金刚，不怕闭着眼儿的佛。 散朝。 李承鹏/文

title: Minimum wage for HK domestic workers rises 2.35%, but advocate says still ‘far from’ a living wage
summary: Hong Kong has raised the minimum wage for the city’s more than 380,000 foreign domestic workers by 2.35 per cent, from HK$5,100 to HK$5,220 per month, the government has announced. Domestic workers in Central. File photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The
content: Hong Kong has raised the minimum wage for the city’s more than 380,000 foreign domestic workers by 2.35 per cent, from HK$5,100 to HK$5,220 per month, the government has announced. Domestic workers in Central. File photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The government also said on Friday that the food allowance for domestic workers – which employers must pay if they do not already provide free meals – will remain unchanged at no less than HK$1,236 per month. The new minimum wage will apply to all contracts signed on or after Saturday, October 3. The government said it had carefully assessed the views of employers and domestic workers before coming to the decision of the 2.35 per cent increase. Last year, the minimum wage was upped by 2.2 per cent. “This year’s socio-economic factors are more favourable than those at the time of last year’s review,” a government spokesperson added. ‘Far from’ living wage But the rise fell short of demands by groups representing domestic workers, who have called for an increase in the minimum wage to HK$6,172 – a 21 per cent hike. The Asian Migrants Coordinating Body (AMCB) has also demanded that the monthly food allowance be more than doubled to HK$3,123 – equivalent to roughly HK$100 per day. AMCB spokesperson Sringatin said on Friday that the HK$120 increase was a result of the collective struggle of migrant workers’ movement in the city. However, “the HK$5,220 is far from the HK$6,172 living wage in Hong Kong,” she told HKFP. “The piecemeal increase will give a very little relief with our long-standing sufferings and burden because of the rapid increase of inflation and standard living [in Hong Kong],” she said. “While no increase in food allowance will mean more expenses and loss in the wage of [domestic workers] who have no food at employer’s house,” she added. See also: Hong Kong workers see real salary growth slow to 1.1% in post-pandemic low The government typically announces the adjustments to domestic workers’ minimum wage in September following an annual review, but this year’s announcement was delayed . The government says it takes into account an array of factors, such as Hong Kong’s economy, labour market conditions, affordability for employers and basic living needs of domestic workers, when reviewing the minimum wage.

title: Greenpeace urges HK gov’t to cut Po Pin Chau visitor quota after Nat. Day overcrowding
summary: Environmental NGO Greenpeace has urged the government to review its ecotourism policies and reduce visitor quotas for a popular Sai Kung trail after finding overcrowding and damage on the first day of the Golden Week holiday. Tourists stand
content: Environmental NGO Greenpeace has urged the government to review its ecotourism policies and reduce visitor quotas for a popular Sai Kung trail after finding overcrowding and damage on the first day of the Golden Week holiday. Tourists stand on the Po Pin Chau viewing platform on October 1, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The green group said in a statement that Sai Kung’s Po Pin Chau trail saw overcrowding on Thursday, which marked China’s National Day and the beginning of a weeklong holiday for the mainland. This comes in spite of a recently established reservation system for the hiking hotspo t. Crowds caused erosion along the trail, the NGO said, with plants trampled underfoot and rampant littering in the form of plastic bottles, tissues, and food remains. Some tourists were suspected of defecating on the natural beauty site, the group added. Littering on Po Pin Chau, Sai Kung on October 1, 2026. Photo: Greenpeace. Hong Kong’s Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD), which looks after the territory’s country parks, introduced a real-name booking system for the trail last month to curb overtourism. Under the scheme, visitors planning to visit between 9am and 5pm on weekends and public holidays from September through October 7 must book in advance, with entry capped at 2,000 visitors per day. Authorities earlier announced that some days of the National Day Golden Week holiday were already fully booked . The AFCD said on Facebook that around 1,160 people visited the Po Pin Chau trail on Thursday, and the overall situation was “generally smooth and well-ordered.” However, Greenpeace staff inspected the site at 8am on Thursday and found that many tourists rushed up the mountain before 9am to beat the restriction. “Some ignored safety warnings and climbed over fences to take photos, creating dangerous situations,” Greenpeace said in a Chinese-language statement. “Some took shortcuts off the main trail for convenience, trampling and damaging adjacent vegetation, and some visitors were even found defecating by a cliffside beach, raising serious hygiene concerns.” Greenpeace notices tourist suspected of defecating in Po Pin Chau, Sai Kung on October 1, 2026. Photo: Greenpeace. At around noon on Thursday, the NGO counted 64 people on the Po Pin Chau viewing platform, which was designed for only 25 people. HKFP has reached out to the AFCD for comment. ‘Conservation-first ecotourism policy’ Greenpeace has urged the government to reduce the current daily limit of 2,000 reservations for the Po Pin Chau trail, and to consider temporarily closing down damaged sections of the site or even seasonal closures to let the area recover. Tourists on the Po Pin Chau trail on October 1, 2026. Photo: Greenpeace. The group said authorities should adopt “a conservation-first ecotourism policy.” “This should include carrying-capacity studies on ecologically sensitive areas across Hong Kong to formulate corresponding management measures and ensure truly sustainable ecotourism,” the Greenpeace statement stated.

title: The PRC’s Compute Push Goes Global
summary: Executive Summary: The People’s Republic of China (PRC) is pushing its domestic computing ecosystem overseas despite U.S. export controls constraining access to high-end AI chips. Chinese firms have laid the groundwork for physical deployme
content: Executive Summary: The People’s Republic of China (PRC) is pushing its domestic computing ecosystem overseas despite U.S. export controls constraining access to high-end AI chips. Chinese firms have laid the groundwork for physical deployments of domestic hardware while pursuing “Token going global” (Token 出海), in which compute remains in the PRC while serving overseas clients. China’s compute crunch is uneven. Shortages are concentrated in frontier hardware even as aggregate computing capacity expands. This enables Chinese firms to export compute without first achieving hardware parity with foreign competitors.  Overseas expansion itself may alleviate bottlenecks by creating demand and application scenarios that accelerate the iterative improvement of the PRC’s domestic AI ecosystem. Chinese firms are languishing under a compute crunch due to U.S. export controls restricting access to high-end GPUs. Domestic manufacturers like Huawei, Cambricon, Biren Technologies, and others have yet to fill the gap. Yet, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has not waited for these constraints to disappear before pushing its domestic computing ecosystem overseas. More broadly, Chinese academics, policy elites, and industry figures have begun calling for domestic “compute going global” (算力出海), even though advanced computing power remains limited at home ( PKU Institute of Urban Governance , April 30). Shenzhen’s artificial intelligence (AI) action plan, released in early September, similarly calls for domestic foundational hardware to expand abroad as part of an integrated Chinese AI ecosystem ( Shenzhen Municipal Bureau of Industry and Information Technology , September 4). Beijing appears to be laying the groundwork to export computing power before technological and supply constraints are resolved. Chinese-language sources suggest that this contradiction stems from a simplistic conception of the PRC’s “compute crunch.” Instead of waiting for domestic supply constraints to erode, Chinese firms and policy elites appear increasingly willing to internationalize the PRC’s computing ecosystem even while those constraints remain ( China Brief , June 11). Overseas deployment can open new markets, bolster demand for Chinese technology, and establish Chinese hardware, software, and technical standards internationally. While exporting compute may entail a short-term opportunity cost at home, Chinese actors appear increasingly willing to bear that cost in pursuit of long-term technological and commercial gains. Deploying Compute Abroad Physical deployment is only one form of Chinese compute going global. Chinese analysts distinguish it from the more mature model of “services crossing the border” (服务出境), in which computing hardware remains in the PRC while domestic data centers process AI workloads for foreign customers and export the resulting tokens and services ( Zhong Lun , July 10). Even when hardware remains physically in the PRC, compute exported-as-a-service still represents a decision to devote computational resources to foreign rather than domestic demand. Computing capacity is inherently rivalrous: capacity devoted to processing foreign workloads cannot simultaneously be used for domestic workloads. The model of cross-border compute exports has already developed into a wider industry push. At the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC), one exhibitor established a dedicated English-language “Token going global” (Token出海) section that demonstrated Chinese computing power packaged into standardized tokens services and exported overseas, attracting considerable attention from foreign attendees, particularly from the Middle East ( Jiemian News , July 19; China Brief , July 22). In 2025, the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT), the think-tank under the PRC’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), collaborated with industry partners to launch a dedicated “Computing-Power Token Going Global Ecosystem Initiative” (算力词元 (Token) 出海生态计划). Its aim is to move the sector beyond experimental projects towards “standardized, efficient, and sustainable” (规范、高效、可持续) overseas expansion ( CWW , July 1). Its organizers argued that doing so could help hedge against external risks and expand services trading ( Open Data Center Committee , July 1). Importantly, Chinese firms are actively laying the groundwork for the physical deployment of advanced domestic AI hardware abroad. Huawei has drawn up plans to export Ascend-series chips, including the Ascend 950DT and 950PR AI accelerator, to South Korea and has signed distributor agreements with local partners like Hansol PNS and SK Shieldus ( Sina Finance , July 7). The company has also unveiled the Atlas 960E SuperPoD as part of its effort to address large-scale AI infrastructure demand overseas, while other Chinese companies have announced plans to deploy a “domestic computing power cluster” (出海国产算力集群) in Saudi Arabia ( SenseTime , July 20). Similar intent is emerging vis-à-vis Southeast Asia, with reports that Malaysia is considering adopting Huawei’s 910C Ascend in its sovereign AI ambitions ( Sina Technology , September 8). Chinese elites have endorsed a wider version of this push. Wang Zhongyuan (王中原) of Fudan University has argued that the PRC should assist countries in the Global South by constructing local computing infrastructure, jointly building data centers, and exporting “computing services” (算力服务) ( CASS , July 16). Song Guoyou (宋国友), deputy director of Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, is even more explicit, calling for Chinese firms to deploy “computing clusters” (算力集群) across different regions of the Global South ( National Office for Philosophy and Social Sciences , July 16). Building Overseas Markets for Chinese Compute A growing number of Chinese industry and policy elites have explicitly described internationalization as the next stage for the domestic compute industry. Li Wei (栗蔚), deputy director of CAICT’s Cloud Computing and Digitalization Research Institute, has called for accelerating the overseas expansion of the domestic computing-power industry and integrating it into the “global computing-power industrial system” (全球算力产业体系) ( People’s Tribune , July 20). Wang Chao (王超), executive director of CAS Star, the deep-tech venture capital firm founded by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, has similarly argued that domestic compute will not only serve domestic demand but also for overseas expansion ( Beijing Daily , September 23). Chinese companies have described similar ambitions. Huawei has actively touted Ascend and its Kunpeng computing platform as having created “a new choice for the world” (为世界构建了新的选择) ( Huawei Tech , February 2024). iFlytek, meanwhile, has partnered with Huawei Ascend to “cooperate deeply on overseas large-model deployments” (在海外主权大模型上深度合作) and “plant flags and seize positions around the world” (在全球插红旗、抢阵地) ( iFlytek , April 29). Other firms describe computing power going global as the “industry’s second growth curve” ( Runze Intelligence , August 28) and argue that overseas expansion “is no longer optional, but imperative” ( Sina Finance , July 29). Southeast Asia has become a particularly important potential market. One CAICT report constructed a market-entry evaluation framework for overseas expansion and identified opportunities for Chinese computing-power providers in emerging markets, especially in Southeast Asia, where they note surging demand ( CWW , May 13). One Chinese AI infrastructure company similarly concludes that compute in Southeast Asia will exceed 3GW in 2026 and 6GW in 2028, asserting that Chinese firms should leverage their accumulated technological capabilities to “rapidly enter overseas computing-power center markets” (快速切入海外算力中心市场) and “capitalize on the supply gap” (把握 … 供给缺口) in Southeast Asia’s high-end IDC market ( Runze Intelligence , August 28). Meanwhile, Sugon, another major Chinese computing-infrastructure provider, has established an ASEAN business headquarters in Nanning, Guangxi. By providing a Chinese tech stack comprising Sugon’s servers and its high-end Hygon DCU compute, PRC firms can provide a “complete solution” for Southeast Asian countries ( QQ News , September 21). Chinese hardware providers often achieve pricing advantage by undercutting foreign competitors. One Chinese estimate concludes that for equivalent computing services yielding similar inference performance, Chinese compute providers can charge just one-fifth to one-seventh as much as comparable overseas services. The price advantage is derived partly from lower electricity costs in the PRC and vertical integration of large Chinese telecommunications operators, most of which own both computing and network infrastructure ( Southern Daily , June 5). Compute Crunch Unevenly Distributed The PRC’s overseas push is happening despite domestic compute constraints. Chinese sources depict a landscape in which shortages are concentrated in select types of high-performance hardware, while the country’s aggregate computing infrastructure expands rapidly. Yang Siwei (杨思维) and Liu Rui (刘睿) of CAICT have written that the PRC’s domestic computing buildout has “laid a solid foundation for the computing-power industry to ‘go global’” (为算力产业“出海”奠定坚实基础) ( Information and Communications Technology Policy , March 2025). By the end of 2023, the PRC already possessed more than 230 exaFLOPS of computing capacity, accounting for over 25 percent of the global total. Meanwhile, intelligent-computing capacity grew 70 percent, accounting for 30 percent of the PRC’s overall computational scale. By June 2024, more than 250 intelligent-computing centers were operating or under construction nationwide ( Information and Communications Technology Policy , March 2025). Li Wei points to further growth since, claiming that the PRC has developed sufficient computing capacity to support 70 percent of domestic parallel-training demand for trillion-parameter models ( People’s Tribune , July 20). Consequently, Yang and Liu call for Chinese firms to start building “comprehensive computing-power service ecosystems” (全面算力服务生态) in emerging country markets ( Information and Communications Technology Policy , March 2025) Importantly, Chinese firms do not need to physically ship domestic AI chips abroad to internationalize domestic computing power. Developers overseas can, for example, access Ascend computing power from the PRC through PyTorch, a software framework for developing and running AI models that reduces friction when accessing hardware ( Beijing Daily , September 23). The PRC has already experimented with this model at scale. In April 2026, the Shantou Overseas Chinese Pilot Zone in Guangdong completed the PRC’s first end-to-end commercial model for “Token going global,” which included consolidating the first phase of an international Token factory with 2,000 petaFLOPS of computing capacity ( TYM , September 3). This represented a deliberate decision by Chinese authorities to add compute capacity with the express intent of serving the overseas market. Overseas users have since accessed token services produced in Shantou, which Chinese reporting describes as the first time Chinese computing resources were exported in the form of “high value-added digital services” (高附加值的数字服务) ( CWW , April 23). Zhu Jun (朱军), director of the Basic Theory Research Center at Tsinghua’s Institute for AI, described the “international Token-factory model” (工厂的建设模式) as a practical path for Chinese produced computing power and large models to expand into overseas markets ( TYM , September 3). The economics of the model are increasingly plausible as the hardware itself remains in the PRC. In Shantou, network latency to Singapore reportedly fell to just 32.7 milliseconds, allowing overseas users to submit requests to models running on Chinese infrastructure and receive outputs with low network delays ( Southern Daily , June 5). Chinese researchers have also explored architectures that reduce dependence on the most high-performance accelerators. Zheng Weimin (郑纬民), a professor at Tsinghua University and former president of the China Computer Federation, has described an inference architecture in which a 10,000-accelerator cluster might employ 9,000 domestically produced accelerators for prefill and 1,000 higher performance accelerators for generation, raising the domestic share to 90 percent. Zheng remarked that the resulting high-quality tokens could serve both domestic industries and go global, adding that the PRC had “sufficient computing capacity” (算力充足) to achieve this in addition to a clear cost advantage ( Ningbo Computer Federation , June 10). Hardware Internationalization Uplifts Entire Industry Chinese inference services explain one part of the story, yet their viability makes the planned export of advanced Chinese accelerators even more puzzling. If Chinese companies can serve overseas customers while leaving their hardware within the PRC, there is less reason for them to physically export valuable hardware to foreign markets. One answer is that overseas demand can feed back into the development of the PRC’s domestic technology ecosystem. Guo Liang (郭亮), Chief Engineer at CAICT’s Cloud Computing and Big Data Research Institute, has observed that emerging markets in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America offer market conditions that have created ample room for the PRC’s computing services to expand overseas. More importantly, he argues that transitioning from building infrastructure toward exporting capabilities and services can promote the “iterative upgrading” (迭代升级) of the PRC’s “computing-power industrial chain” (算力产业链) and drive the coordinated, concurrent uplifting of domestic AI computing clusters, large models, and AI chips ( Xinhua , July 24). Liu Xiaoge ( 刘小鸽), a deputy director of research at the Development Research Center of the State Council, has similarly argued that Token exports can create a powerful “demand-pull effect” (需求牵引效应) that helps mitigate technological chokepoints affecting the PRC’s domestic AI hardware stack. Supplying domestically produced chips for large-scale application scenarios, he argues, will create opportunities for frequent iteration that can narrow gaps with the international frontier “in both manufacturing processes and ecosystems” (制程与生态) ( State Council , May 8). Conclusion The overseas ambitions of Chinese firms do not demonstrate that the PRC has overcome its computing constraints, nor does it mean that Chinese companies can challenge Nvidia globally at a competitive scale. Chinese legal analysts have pointed out that Chinese firms targeting overseas markets should prioritize cross-border service exports from infrastructure located in the PRC before deploying physical hardware abroad ( Zhong Lun , July 10). Huawei’s own leadership has been forthcoming about these constraints. Rotating chairman Eric Xu recently acknowledged that domestic shortages prevent a “fully-fledged” rollout of Huawei Ascend abroad ( Reuters , September 17). This qualification matters. Huawei is constrained from international expansion on a “fully-fledged” scale, but this does not mean that internationalization has stopped altogether. Chinese companies and policy elites do not appear to view compute scarcity as a reason to postpone international expansion before compute parity is achieved. As time progresses, and as the PRC consolidates increasingly novel algorithmic efficiencies, its ability and willingness to export compute abroad will only grow. Notes [1] Prefill processes the input prompt while generation produces output tokens, with the two stages having different compute requirements. This allows them to run on different types of accelerators. The post The PRC’s Compute Push Goes Global appeared first on Jamestown .

title: China National Day: Hong Kong leader hails Five-Year Plan as astronaut sends greetings
summary: Chief Executive John Lee hailed the city’s first Five-Year Plan at a celebration on Thursday marking the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Chief Executive John Lee at the Wan Chai Exhibition Centre on Octob
content: Chief Executive John Lee hailed the city’s first Five-Year Plan at a celebration on Thursday marking the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Chief Executive John Lee at the Wan Chai Exhibition Centre on October 1, 2026. Photo: GovHK. Following a flag-raising ceremony at Golden Bauhinia Square, Lee told attendees at Wan Chai’s Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre that China had achieved a historic transformation to become the world’s largest manufacturer. “The formulation of a Five-Year Plan for Hong Kong is not merely about rolling out a series of policy initiatives. The Plan provides a strategic roadmap for Hong Kong, allowing us to apply our unique advantages under ‘one country, two systems,’ embrace modern trends and seize the opportunities brought by national development,” he said, according to a government press release. Citing the geopolitical landscape and rapid technological development, he said the blueprint will allow the city “to fully and swiftly seize the immense opportunities brought by national development, and to deliver more fruits of development to the benefit of our citizens.” “I am confident that as long as we, each dedicated to our respective roles, join hands and work in synergy with one another, Hong Kong will certainly be able to set out on a path to a brighter and more prosperous future. Finally, I wish our motherland and Hong Kong continuing prosperity and stability,” he added. National Day festivities on October 1, 2026 in Wan Chai. Photo: GovHK. The director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong Zhou Ji, and former chief executives Donald Tsang, Leung Chun-ying and Carrie Lam also attended Thursday’s ceremony, alongside top officials. Five-Year Plan After unveiling the plan last month, Lee denied the half-decade policy blueprint, aligning with Beijing’s practice, signalled a shift in Hong Kong’s existing system. He said the proposal would adhere to the city’s “capitalist system.” Chief Executive John Lee delivered his fifth Policy Address and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 at the Legislative Council. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. As part of the Five-Year Plan, authorities set 22 indicators labelled “anticipatory” or “binding,” adopting Beijing’s evaluation framework . Among the “anticipatory” indicators is an increase in the ratio of total domestic expenditure on innovation activities to GDP from 1.63 per cent in 2024 to three per cent after 2030, as well as an increase in the “value added” of the tourism industry by 40 to 50 per cent. Beyond economic indicators, the government also outlined goals related to diversity in universities, the ratio of medical staff to population, and environmental matters. Authorities aim to increase the share of zero-carbon energy in the fuel mix for electricity generation from 25 per cent in 2024 to 30 per cent in 2030. They also aim to lower the average concentration of PM2.5 air pollutant particles from 15 micrograms per cubic metre to below 14. Regarding the Northern Metropolis tech hub, the Five-Year Plan outlines two related indicators. Hong Kong’s border areas near Shenzhen are set to be transformed into the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis. File photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Over the next half-decade, authorities will strive for a cumulative 750 per cent increase in “spade-ready sites” in the metropolis, referring to land that has been made ready for construction work. The government also hopes to increase the number of completed housing units in the Northern Metropolis by 640 per cent. Proposed in 2021, the Northern Metropolis is a sprawling infrastructure project set to transform 30,000 hectares of land near the city’s rural border with mainland China. The tech hub promises to provide jobs, more homes, and deeper integration with neighbouring Shenzhen. However, critics have voiced concern over the HK$224 billion project’s scale and ambition, its impact on sensitive wetland habitats, and the loss of existing homes and farmland. Greetings from space Lai Ka-ying, a Hong Kong police superintendent and payload specialist currently aboard the Shenzhou-23 manned spaceflight mission, sent blessings to the country for National Day. “Taking part in the national manned space mission has given me a profound sense of the nation’s soaring strength,” she said, according to RTHK. “Every piece of precision equipment we operate here, and every scientific experiment we carry out, embodies the pride of ‘Made in China’ and ‘Created in China’… I’m deeply grateful for the nation’s care towards Hong Kong and Macao, and I treasure this opportunity.”

title: U.S., China turn transactional while Japan stays hawkish on Beijing, complicating Seoul's diplomacy
summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (right) and Chinese President Xi Jinping / Yonhap News The U.S. and China agreed during their summit on preferential tariff arrangements to apply to 30 billion dollars worth of goods each in trade and
content:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (right) and Chinese President Xi Jinping / Yonhap News

The U.S. and China agreed during their summit on preferential tariff arrangements to apply to 30 billion dollars worth of goods each in trade and investment. The two sides also reaffirmed at the summit their constructive strategic stability relationship established in May. As the U.S. and Chinese leaders agreed to steer bilateral ties toward strategic stability, the hardline China policy of the Japanese administration under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been put to a new test.While continuing strategic competition with China, the U.S. is moving toward striking deals in the economic sphere and managing conflict.

Japan, on the other hand, maintained its existing policy stance toward China on Taiwan and economic security issues, coordinating heavily with the U.S. on China matters before and after the U.S.-China summit. Diplomatic calculations for South Korea are also growing more complicated, as Seoul must sustain trilateral cooperation with the U.S. and Japan while simultaneously managing its relations with China.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a summit in Washington on September 24 and agreed to build a constructive U.S.-China strategic stability relationship grounded in respect, fairness, and mutual benefit. In the economic realm, transaction-oriented agreements materialized. The U.S. and China agreed on preferential tariff measures for 30 billion dollars worth of non-sensitive goods on each side and decided to fully launch a consultative body on trade and investment. They also agreed to continue consultations on the supply of critical minerals, including rare earths.

A posture of managing relations was also evident in announcements from the Chinese side. According to China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, President Xi stated that U.S.-China relations should be directed toward making cooperation the mainstream, managing competition within appropriate bounds, and controlling differences.

However, fundamental tensions between the U.S. and China over Taiwan have not been resolved. President Xi demanded that President Trump hold fast to opposing Taiwan independence. In effect, the U.S. and China have entered a phase of managed competition, expanding transactional cooperation in economics while holding their ground on security issues.Japan intensively coordinated on China matters with the U.S. around the time of the U.S.-China summit.

Prime Minister Takaichi held talks lasting about 35 minutes with President Trump in New York on the 22nd to discuss China issues. According to Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the two leaders exchanged views on China-related issues, including economic security, with the U.S.-China summit in mind, and agreed to continue close cooperation between the U.S. and Japan.

Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi (left) and U.S. President Trump / Yonhap News

The two leaders also agreed to strengthen cooperation in economic security sectors, including artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, and critical minerals. They reaffirmed their standing commitment to enhance the deterrence and response capabilities of the U.S.-Japan alliance to ensure peace and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region. Coordination between the U.S. and Japan continued even after the conclusion of the U.S.-China summit.

President Trump held a telephone conversation lasting about 20 minutes with Prime Minister Takaichi on the 26th to explain the outcome of the U.S.-China summit in detail. The two leaders once again discussed China-related issues across economic and security spheres, including economic security, and agreed to cooperate closely.

This reveals a dual structure in which the U.S. strikes deals with China while separately coordinating its China policy with Japan. While the U.S. simultaneously requires both economic transactions with China and the management of strategic competition, Japan faces issues tied directly to its own security—such as the Taiwan Strait and the East China Sea—giving Tokyo relatively narrower room for maneuver in its China policy.

South Korea is also directly affected by these shifts in U.S.-China and Japan-China relations. President Lee Jae-myung held a summit with President Trump in New York on the 22nd, emphasizing that the U.S.-China summit scheduled for the following day was "critical to regional affairs, including Korea-China relations," and expressing hopes for a successful meeting. This publicly underscored that shifts in U.S.-China relations are directly linked to Korea-China relations and the security environment on the Korean Peninsula.

The South Korean government continues its policy direction of maintaining the South Korea-U.S. alliance and South Korea-U.S.-Japan cooperation while steadily managing relations with China. During the South Korea-Japan summit in May, President Lee stated that to achieve regional peace and stability, it is important not only to pursue bilateral and trilateral cooperation with the U.S. and Japan, but also for South Korea, China, and Japan to respect each other, cooperate, and seek common interests. Efforts to manage South Korea-China relations are proceeding in parallel.

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi last month to discuss pending bilateral issues, including South Korea-China relations and Korean Peninsula affairs.Ultimately, diplomacy in Northeast Asia following this U.S.-China summit has become difficult to frame through a simple dichotomy of the U.S. versus China. While strategically competing with China, the U.S. is pursuing economic transactions and relational stability, whereas Japan is maintaining its existing China policy anchored to the U.S.-Japan alliance.

For South Korea, it must sustain cooperation with the U.S. and Japan while stably managing ties with China and preserving the framework of trilateral cooperation among South Korea, China, and Japan. As a phase unfolds where the U.S. and China compete while cutting deals as needed, South Korea's diplomacy toward China faces an even greater need for delicate coordination that pursues both South Korea-U.S.-Japan and South Korea-China-Japan cooperation in parallel.

Choi Young-jae

title: UN renews Haiti force mandate for six months after fresh gang killings
summary: Men of the local defense force stand guard in a cemetery during a funeral service for people killed in an armed gang attack on August 23, in Kenscoff, Haiti, September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Patrice... [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](h
content:
Men of the local defense force stand guard in a cemetery during a funeral service for people killed in an armed gang attack on August 23, in Kenscoff, Haiti, September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Patrice... [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/family-members-hold-funeral-for-victims-of-kenscoff-gang-attack/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMjVCTkE5MlRMTQ%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)Read more

*   Summary

*   GSF mandate runs until March 31, 2027, after long-planned election
*   Vote was hours after deadly gang attack following GSF patrol
*   China, Russia and Pakistan abstain over funding, personnel and efficacy concerns
*   US says about ​1,500 troops deployed, 4,000 more expected in coming months

Sept 29 (Reuters) - The United ‌Nations Security Council on Tuesday extended by six months the mandate of an international security force in Haiti intended to fight powerful armed groups that have taken control of much of the country.

Twelve nations voted to renew ​the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) and none voted against. Three nations, however, abstained: ​China, Russia and Pakistan, whose representatives cited concerns over insufficient funds, personnel ⁠and efficacy.

Sign up[here.](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/undefined?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Famericas%2Fun-renews-haiti-force-mandate-six-months-after-fresh-gang-killings-2026-09-29%2F)

The extension is intended to provide security ahead of Haiti's first election in a decade ​in December. Armed groups continue to control large parts of the Caribbean nation despite successive international deployments, and the ​force has struggled to deploy enough troops to carry out its mandate.

Haiti, whose leaders first called for international security support in 2022, had urged nations to renew the mandate for the force, which is currently at less than 30% of ​its intended size.

US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, representing one of the countries that ​proposed the motion, said that around 1,500 GSF troops are now deployed in Haiti. Waltz said the remaining 4,000 ‌are ⁠expected to arrive in the coming months.

"Seven missions have been dedicated to Haiti over the previous decades and obviously to limited success," Waltz said. "We're trying to do something genuinely different."

The vote came hours after gang members in Haiti's breadbasket region burned homes and killed at least 11 people in ​what a [local mayor said](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/haiti-gang-retaliation-leaves-least-11-dead-after-security-operation-2026-09-29/) ​was retaliation after a ⁠GSF unit killed three gang members in a push against illegal toll booths.

A month ago, another massacre in the hillside town of [Kenscoff](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/gang-attack-near-haitis-capital-leaves-30-dead-2026-08-24/) near the ​capital left at least 47 people dead and around 50 more kidnapped.

The ​GSF was ⁠launched a year ago after the prior Kenyan-led mission similarly struggled to reach its goals with voluntary contributions. Its troops withdrew early this year.

The mandate was renewed until March 31, 2027. Haiti is scheduled ⁠to ​hold the elections on December 13, and final results are ​due on March 7.

Successive transitional governments have long delayed elections due to worsening insecurity, which has now forced close to ​1.5 million people to flee their homes.

Reporting by Sarah Morland; editing by Cassandra Garrison and Sanjeev Miglani

Our Standards: [The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles., opens new tab](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/about-us/trust-principles.html)

Sarah is a British-French journalist covering news from across Latin America and the Caribbean, including gender violence, mining developments, regional finance and conflict in Haiti. She joined Reuters in 2019 and studied investigative journalism at City, University of London. Based in Mexico City, Sarah enjoys spicy food, dad rock and befriending the local cat population.

title: Taiwan seeks drone partnerships with partners amid China threat
summary: The Taiwan Coast Guard joined forces with the Ministry of National Defense and the Air Service Corps to carry out the Haian 12 military exercises in June 2025 Taiwan Coast Guard Taiwan must deepen cooperation with its democratic partners on
content:
The Taiwan Coast Guard joined forces with the Ministry of National Defense and the Air Service Corps to carry out the Haian 12 military exercises in June 2025 Taiwan Coast Guard

Taiwan must deepen cooperation with its democratic partners on developing drones which are crucial to fighting modern warfare, President Lai Ching-te said on Monday.

Taiwan's government has made defence modernisation and increased spending a core policy given stepped-up military pressure from China, which views the democratically governed island as its own territory.

Speaking in southern Taiwan's Chiayi for the groundbreaking ceremony for a new drone development centre, Lai said the site's significance has become even more prominent with changes in the international situation.

"From the Ukrainian battlefield to Indo-Pacific regional security, unmanned systems have become important combat strength in modern defence," Lai said.

"At the same time, we must deepen cooperation with democratic partners and jointly build a safer and more resilient unmanned aircraft supply chain, providing solid support for Indo-Pacific regional peace and stability," he added.

Taiwan possesses world-class semiconductor and information and communications technology capabilities, as well as a deep precision manufacturing foundation.

Taiwan's cabinet earlier this month proposed [an additional TW$145.7 billion ($4.59 billion) in defence spending](https://www.bairdmaritime.com/security/naval/unmanned-naval-systems/taiwans-46b-defence-budget-top-up-includes-suicide-drone-boats) for this year for systems including drones and anti-ballistic missiles.

Those spending plans incorporate more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, over 40,000 coastal attack drones, and the first batch of over 100 small suicide drone boats.

Lai and his government reject Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the island's people can decide their future.

_(Reporting by Yi-Chin Lee and Ann Wang; Writing by Ben Blanchard; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)_

title: Sourcing the Next Blockbuster: Big Pharma Uses Chinese Biotech
source: 欧洲政策分析中心 （CEPA） - CEPA
summary: When the US biotech innovator Moderna leveraged the same messenger RNA, or mRNA, technology that powered COVID-19 vaccines to treat melanoma, the clinical trial results marked a dramatic breakthrough. The personalized vaccine instructs the
content: When the US biotech innovator Moderna leveraged the same messenger RNA, or mRNA, technology that powered COVID-19 vaccines to treat melanoma, the clinical trial results marked a dramatic breakthrough. The personalized vaccine instructs the body to produce harmless fragments of a tumor’s unique mutations, training the patient’s immune system to precisely target and destroy the cancer cells. Scientists are now  developing  similar mRNA vaccines to overcome the uniquely resistant environments of advanced prostate cancer, and other deadly malignancies. China’s position within the biotechnology value chain has changed. Nearly half of the therapeutic mRNA cancer vaccines in the global research pipeline come from Chinese companies, with applications for pioneering treatments for diseases beyond oncology.  The old maxim of China as a copycat does not apply here. Chinese biotech firms are increasingly innovating, pioneering discovery and early clinical development. So far, the partnerships look mutually beneficial, accelerating advances and profiting both sides. But they are also fueling the rise of a potentially formidable competitor in a domain historically dominated by US and European companies.  The issue could come up at this week’s summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping. Under the 2025 Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, the US is  required  to screen deals made with certain countries that involve sensitive technology, from AI to semiconductors. Should pharmaceuticals be included? The administration needs to finalize a decision by March 2027.Chinese drugmakers completed 157 outbound licensing deals in 2025 with an aggregate potential value of approximately $135.7 billion, up from 94 deals worth $51.9 billion in 2024. Chinese regulatory data put those transactions at roughly 49% of the global total, a remarkable change for an industry once defined internationally by generics, contract manufacturing, and lower-cost production For much of the past two decades, manufacturing prowess fueled China’s rise in biotechnology. Western pharmaceutical players remained dominant in high-value discovery and commercialization, while China became indispensable to important portions of the physical supply chain.  This paradigm now looks outdated. Partnerships are entangling both and blurring the lines of the old maxim, “the West invents and commercializes while China manufactures.” Since 2023, American giant  Moderna partnered with Chinese biotech CARsgen  targeting advanced gastric and pancreatic tumors. In May 2026, Pfizer agreed to a collaboration with China’s Innovent Biologics valued at up to $10.5 billion covering 12 oncology programs. Eight originated at Innovent, while four came from Pfizer. Innovent will conduct early clinical development for parts of the portfolio, while Pfizer brings global clinical development, regulatory, and commercialization capabilities. Several programs will be jointly developed and commercialized in the US and Europe. AstraZeneca is pursuing a similar model. In January 2026, the British-Swedish pharmaceutical company  entered  into a collaboration with China’s CSPC Pharmaceutical Group covering eight obesity and type-2 diabetes diseases. CSPC  is responsible  for advancing the programs through Phase I, after which AstraZeneca will be responsible for development and commercialization outside of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau. The agreement  included  $1.2 billion upfront, and as much as $13.8 billion in additional milestone payments.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular Bandwidth emails and stay informed about CEPA's These partnerships allow China to become an increasingly important discovery player within global pharma and biotech. But it does not assure Chinese supremacy. Biotech power operates across at least three stages: manufacturing, discovery, and translation. China became formidable in the first. It is rapidly strengthening its position in the second. The US and Europe continue to possess extraordinary advantages in the third: deep capital markets, large pharmaceutical companies, multinational clinical development networks, sophisticated regulatory institutions, advanced manufacturing, and access to wealthy global markets.  Translation is not a trivial role. It is itself a source of structural power. An innovation system capable of absorbing discoveries, regardless of where they originate, can remain dominant even when it does not originate every discovery itself. The open question is whether China will eventually internalize more of the capabilities required to move a molecule from laboratory discovery to worldwide commercialization.  For now, the boom in Chinese licensing deals demonstrates the continuing strength of American and European pharmaceutical and biotech giants. A promising molecule discovered in China often becomes globally valuable because a multinational pharmaceutical company can finance late-stage trials, navigate approvals from the US Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency, manufacture at scale, and commercialize it in the US, Europe, and other major markets. But the boom in licensing deals indicates that the competitive landscape, in the long-term, may be changing in favor of China. Chinese biotech is creating assets valuable enough that some of the largest Western pharmaceutical companies are competing for access to them. Control over discovery generates licensing revenue and patents. Perhaps most importantly, discovery trains scientists and drug developers, creates proprietary datasets and platform capabilities, and attracts capital and talent. Those capabilities compound over time. A country that supplies an ingredient can potentially be replaced by another manufacturer, even if it is sometimes at considerable cost and delay. A company that owns a uniquely effective molecule or therapeutic platform cannot necessarily be substituted in the same way.  Licensing Chinese assets does not automatically translate into Chinese biotech dominance. The value of that asset remains almost entirely speculative when most of these licensing deals are signed. Not every Chinese drug candidate will succeed. Drug development remains extraordinarily risky, and the industry-wide attrition rate from early clinical development to approval is steep.  But the direction matters. China is already moving into a higher-value position within global biotech. For the US and Europe, the policy challenge is to track how many Chinese innovations survive the drug discovery pipeline to market, while preserving the capabilities that make the transatlantic biotech industry the most attractive and effective place in the world to finance, develop, test, regulate, manufacture, and commercialize  breakthrough therapeutics. In the high-stakes race to cure cancer and other diseases, the line between Western supremacy and Chinese innovation could be a bridge to cure intractable diseases like cancer — and a new source of tension. title: Hong Kong slams EU report claiming ‘deterioration of fundamental freedoms’ in the city
summary: Hong Kong authorities have hit back against a European Union (EU) report that described what it called “continuous erosions” in the city’s political freedoms and autonomy. The annual report on Hong Kong, issued on Tuesday by the European Co
content: Hong Kong authorities have hit back against a European Union (EU) report that described what it called “continuous erosions” in the city’s political freedoms and autonomy. The annual report on Hong Kong, issued on Tuesday by the European Commission and the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, highlighted a “continued deterioration of fundamental freedoms” due to “the Hong Kong government’s incessant focus on national security in the fifth year after the imposition of the National Security Law.” European Union flags in Brussels. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski, via Flickr. “The HKSAR Government strongly opposes the absurd and false contents in the EU’s so-called report,” the government said in an over 4,500-word rebuttal on Wednesday. “It is each and every sovereign state’s inherent right, under international law and international relations based on the Charter of the United Nations, to enact laws safeguarding national security,” the statement read, adding that various EU member states have also enacted national security legislation. National security trials The 37-page EU report noted ongoing legal proceedings against former pro-democracy media mogul Jimmy Lai, who was convicted on national security and sedition charges in December last year. “Lai, a British citizen, has been held in custody continuously since 31 December 2020, mostly in solitary confinement,” the EU report read. It also pointed to the case brought against Tiananmen vigil organisers the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements in China, and new prosecutions initiated against student protest leader Joshua Wong under both the NSL and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (SNSO), known locally as Article 23. The report also remarked on the charges brought against Kwok Yin-sang, the father of exiled activist Anna Kwok, who was prosecuted for attempting to deal with his daughter’s financial assets. “This was the first time a relative of a wanted activist was charged with a national security offence,” it said. The issuing of bounties on 15 overseas activists for their alleged involvement in an unofficial “Hong Kong Parliament”—including an EU citizen in Germany—represented further “extra-territorial application of the [national security law],” according to the report. People watch a video installation in the Hong Kong Museum of History, on October 1, 2024. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On LGBTQ rights, the EU report described “a mixed picture” in Hong Kong. While court rulings supported the advancement of LGBTQ rights, the legislature voted down a same-sex partnership bill introduced by the government in response to a 2023 court ruling that requested authorities to pass a framework for recognising same-sex partnerships. ‘Humane’ prison conditions In its response to the EU report, Hong Kong authorities said that the city’s national security laws meet human rights standards and have allowed the city to prosper economically. “In fact, the implementation of the HKNSL (Hong Kong National Security Law) in the past six years or so has enabled the livelihood and economic activities of the Hong Kong community at large to swiftly resume to normal and the business environment to be restored and improved continuously,” the official statement read. It also said that Jimmy Lai had received “a fair trial” before conviction, and added that the city’s Correctional Services Department always ensures that prison conditions are “safe [and] humane.” Jimmy Lai in 2020. Photo: HKFP. “Any attempt by foreign countries or external forces to undermine Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability by slandering the city will only expose their own weakness and faulty arguments and be doomed to fail,” the government statement said. Beijing inserted national security legislation directly into Hong Kong’s mini-constitution in June 2020 following a year of pro-democracy protests and unrest. It criminalised subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts – broadly defined to include disruption to transport and other infrastructure. The move gave police sweeping new powers and led to hundreds of arrests amid new legal precedents , while dozens of civil society groups disappeared . The authorities say it restored stability and peace to the city, rejecting criticism from trade partners , the UN and NGOs .

title: Trump Can Derail China’s AI Threat
summary: Trump Can Derail China’s AI Threat bbert@hudson.org Tue, 09/22/2026 - 09:34 SVG Commentary Sep 22, 2026 Washington Post Trump Can Derail China’s AI Threat The president can complicate China’s artificial-intelligence strategy if he’s willing
content: Trump Can Derail China’s AI Threat bbert@hudson.org Tue, 09/22/2026 - 09:34 SVG Commentary Sep 22, 2026 Washington Post Trump Can Derail China’s AI Threat The president can complicate China’s artificial-intelligence strategy if he’s willing to economically pressure Beijing. Thomas J. Duesterberg Senior Fellow Thomas J. Duesterberg Commentary Caption A visitor walks by a billboard at the PT Expo on September 22, 2026, in Beijing. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Thursday’s summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping presents an opportunity for Trump to take a more assertive approach to derailing Beijing’s artificial intelligence strategy. China’s aggressive attempt to capture the global markets for AI directly threatens U.S. strategic and economic interests but rests on weak financial pillars. Trump can exploit these to blunt Beijing’s global AI advance if he’s willing to dial up the economic pressure. U.S. investors are all in on AI and are devoting trillions of dollars to developing its supply chains. PricewaterhouseCoopers estimates data center spending alone in the United States will total over $15 trillion in coming decades . ING estimates that AI spending already accounts for one-third or more of domestic economic growth. But cheaper Chinese “open-weight” models — meaning their core components are publicly available — are gaining global market share and undercutting the potential returns on American investment. The Chinese program for AI mirrors Beijing’s approach to other industries, such as solar, in recent decades. Since at least 2017 , Beijing has designated AI as a “strategic technology” and unleashed its usual array of subsidies, political inducements and dubious means of technology acquisition to build its own supply chain. More than $1 trillion of specialized government investment funds have been poured into hardware and software companies over the last two decades, reducing data centers’ electricity costs by half, among other benefits. Beijing’s AI labs have allegedly benefited from the unauthorized use of leading U.S. platforms, spillovers from U.S. research centers in China and sales of OpenAI and Google models to blacklisted groups. At the same time, China’s nascent AI industry has been protected by bans and limits on consumer and corporate use of U.S. models in its domestic market. Cumulative government support for AI has resulted in much lower prices for the output of Chinese open-weight models compared with models from more advanced U.S. “frontier” labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. China is a global leader in adapting models to specific industries — including advanced manufacturing and retail markets — that do not require the more sophisticated tools developed by these frontier labs. Widespread adoption has also allowed Chinese modelers to acquire vast amounts of data to improve performance. In 2026, Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models have been downloaded more than 3 billion times; Meta’s competing Llama models, only 227 million times . The problem with Beijing’s strategy is that few Chinese models are profitable , despite their lower costs. The most valuable Chinese AI firm by market capitalization, Z.ai, saw losses grow by 59 percent from the first quarter of 2025 to the first quarter of 2026 despite broad usage in China and the United States. About 85 percent of Z.ai’s revenue came from use by Chinese state-owned enterprises. The highly touted firm Moonshot was forced to pause subscriptions to its new model because the company wasn’t able to provide sufficient compute power. Powerful American firms Nvidia and Meta are now investing in new open-weight AI models to capture the same growth potential, adding to the economic challenges Chinese AI models face. In the early years of AI development, private firms in China and venture capital firms abroad helped fuel investment in advanced technology in the Middle Kingdom. But crackdowns on successful Chinese entrepreneurs, such as Jack Ma, and on unwanted foreign investors have dampened private investment in Chinese AI. More recently, China forced Meta to abandon its purchase of Singapore-based AI firm Manus, which had been founded by Chinese entrepreneurs. A telling example of the challenge for Chinese AI is flagship firm DeepSeek’s attempt to mount an initial public offering to attract the foreign capital needed to keep improving computing power and sophistication in modeling. According to reports from a former high-level Chinese leadership insider, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng lamented in a private briefing for prospective investors that China was at least one to two years behind the U.S. in computing power and lacked the chip access to reduce the gap. The second round of private fundraising for DeepSeek’s much-anticipated IPO was suspended in mid-2026 after Liang’s private briefing was leaked . Xi has also been cracking down on financial regulators , including a former vice chairman of Beijing’s securities oversight commission, for alleged corruption, which is likely to delay any public offerings of AI companies. Chinese AI firms are now highly dependent on government support. They also need to access foreign markets, especially the U.S. and other industrialized Western markets, because domestic competition limits their pricing power. Chinese developers also admit they need more advanced American processors . The White House should continue to support U.S. investment and technology development for both open-weight and frontier models. Trump can take more substantive actions to complicate Chinese AI advancement when he meets with Xi this week. First, Chinese models should be banned from U.S. markets until reciprocal access and effective market conditions are firmly in place in China. Second, given China’s need for Western capital to drive further technological advances, Trump should renew support for limits on U.S. financing of AI infrastructure IPOs and investments in the budding Chinese AI ecosystem. China’s AI strategy is a genuine threat to U.S. interests, but it teeters atop a rickety financial foundation. If Trump is willing to deploy the tools in his economic arsenal, the United States can undermine Beijing’s AI advance. Read in The Washington Post . Enjoyed this analysis? title: ​蒋经国：你为什么非要让外蒙古独立？
