*   The Insider estimates that about a third of Latvia's socio-political Telegram channels are run by Russian propagandists posing as disgruntled locals.

*   The EU imposed an asset freeze on former RT France head Xenia Fedorova for spreading Kremlin-aligned narratives in French media after RT's EU broadcasting suspension.

*   Swiss authorities confirmed covert as well as open Russian interference before Switzerland's neutrality initiative vote, though the security secretariat doubts it had decisive impact.

*   Seznam Zprávy journalists lured a film crew working for Russian propaganda project Rybar, whose founder is EU-sanctioned, to Prague, exposing a wider European filming operation.

*   Russian actors circulated an AI-generated video of a fictitious anti-corruption raid and a cloned NV website to portray Ukraine as corrupt during US-Russia talks.

*   StopFake found that screenshots of BBC, Guardian, Independent and Al Jazeera reports blaming Ukraine for the 13-09-2026 train strike near Poland were doctored.

*   Ukraine's disinformation center says Russia-controlled TikTok networks spread AI videos of fake Jewish pilgrims claiming state-paid resettlement in Ukraine to stoke antisemitism.

*   RSF's second Propaganda Monitor report details how Beijing uses content deals, funded trips, influencers and pressure on journalists to pursue its 'new world media order'.

*   Doublethink Lab concludes Chinese influence in Zambia's 2026 election worked through institutional and media ties rather than covert manipulation campaigns.

*   Golden Owl assessed a network of personas posing as Israelis as linked to Iran's regime, carrying fraud and decline themes into Israel's election debate.

*   NewsGuard found pro-Iran accounts using months-old footage to claim, without evidence, that the US had withdrawn thousands of troops from its Gulf bases.

*   Black8Mirror hackers published fragments of alleged correspondence between Russian official Mikhail Babich and Putin's press secretary Dmitry Peskov from an archive they claim to hold.

*   Democrat Vikki Goodwin filed a police report accusing Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick of breaking a 2019 deepfake law with AI-generated ads.

*   An AI-generated art therapist persona, quoted more than 30 times by outlets including Forbes and Vice, was banned from the expert-sourcing platform Qwoted.

*   Preliminary research before Victoria's election found about three in four participants identified deepfakes, but almost half could not confidently recognise genuine political footage.

*   NewsGuard found US and Chinese chatbots broadly agreed on AI risks, but Chinese bots often evaded questions

title: Chinese AI Ambition and False Promises in Southeast Asia
summary: Chinese AI Ambition and False Promises in Southeast Asia bbert@hudson.org Wed, 09/30/2026 - 14:33 SVG Reports Oct 1, 2026 Hudson Institute Chinese AI Ambition and False Promises in Southeast Asia John Lee Senior Fellow John Lee Reports Capt
content: Chinese AI Ambition and False Promises in Southeast Asia bbert@hudson.org Wed, 09/30/2026 - 14:33 SVG Reports Oct 1, 2026 Hudson Institute Chinese AI Ambition and False Promises in Southeast Asia John Lee Senior Fellow John Lee Reports Caption Diplomatic envoys of ASEAN countries to China watch an intelligent robot during a visit to the China-ASEAN AI Application Center on July 22, 2026, in Nanning, China. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print View PDF Summary Chinese President Xi Jinping frames China’s bid for leadership in artificial intelligence as a Global South issue, promising developing economies that Beijing will champion equitable AI development and use on behalf of poorer and smaller economies. In fact, however, China is seeking to enhance its ability to exercise leverage over these economies by deepening their dependence on the Chinese AI stack. If Southeast Asian developing economies become dependent on Chinese AI offerings, they unavoidably enter into and become trapped in a Chinese AI ecosystem that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) closely monitors and controls. As with manufacturing supply chains, China will benefit disproportionately from the AI revolution while its AI offerings subject Southeast Asian economies to embedded CCP‑aligned narratives, surveillance, and engineered vulnerabilities. At the same time, Southeast Asian nations pursuing hard sovereign AI policies will find themselves isolated and unable to benefit from the AI revolution, as their region lacks the capital, infrastructure, technological capabilities, and strategic cohesion to build its own AI ecosystem. Southeast Asian nations will need to make difficult decisions about which ecosystem to work with and within—American or Chinese. History and current practice suggest that the American AI ecosystem, driven by the private sector, offers these countries better and more enduring benefits, greater freedom to pursue their own development pathway, and superior data and information-security assurances. China and the Global South Geographically, the Global South includes countries in Latin America, Asia, Africa, and Oceania located mainly, but not entirely, south of the equator (see map). However, in discussing China’s interest in the Global South, it is more useful to treat the term as a geopolitical and geoeconomic concept with specific elements and characteristics. It serves as a replacement for third world , denotes lower economic ranking and victim status, and provides an opportunity to overthrow the US-led order and begin a new one. Map. The Global South and the Global North Source: Adapted from Handbook of Statistics 2022 (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, 2022), 4–5, https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/tdstat47_en.pdf . The Global South concept offers attractive and fertile ground for China, which has the advantage of being considered a Global South nation that is highly industrialized and innovative as well as a developing and middle-income economy. The concept is also useful for China because it is amorphous and is filled with the narrative and psychology of subjugation (by the Global North) and victimhood, which Beijing can weaponize against the West. As prominent scholar Ren Lin of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences writes, “From a historical perspective, these [Global South] countries were colonized by developed countries, represented by the European countries, and this led to their poverty and weakness in modern times.” [1] China positions itself not just as a member and leader of the Global South but as the only member with better solutions and options for other members. It claims it can help them avoid further submission to, and capture by, Global North nations that continue to dominate international institutions. [2] China presents as both the leader of the resistance and as the first among equals in a fledgling, but rising, Global South order—or at least, a hybrid international order that is more empowering for the Global South and better reflects its priorities. In reality, for Beijing, the Global South is more of a concept it can weaponize against the United States than a comprehensive organizing principle for its relations with the world. China still depends heavily on the West, especially the United States, for technology, innovation, capital, and know-how and requires access to Western markets. Whether Beijing genuinely sees itself as subjugated or structurally disadvantaged by the West is unclear, as some of the regimes and elites in smaller, poorer nations do. In fact, China has spent the last three decades devising clever and cunning ways to exploit its relationships and agreements with the Global North and gain disproportionately from them. Beijing wishes to be seen as leader of the Global South so that it can benefit from interactions with the wealthier Western nations while exploiting the idea of the Global South for its own purposes. China’s Geostrategic Objectives While Beijing undoubtedly has global ambitions, the CCP is still focusing most of its efforts on securing hegemony over the maritime nations of East Asia—a region encompassing China, Japan, Mongolia, North Korea, South Korea, Taiwan, and the 11 countries that are members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). In this region, fully industrialized democracies such as Japan, Australia, and even South Korea are hardening their approach toward China. This has accelerated Beijing’s plans to target developing nations, especially in Southeast Asia, to acquire and entrench strategic support states. China’s ultimate objective is for these states to accept and internalize a creeping Sinocentric order while continuing their affairs within it, rather than resisting it. In targeting Global South economies in Asia, Beijing seeks to shape the way these nations think about economic development and the economic and strategic policies they pursue for material advancement. When they depend on China or the Chinese approach to development, they drift toward becoming strategic support states, knowingly or unwittingly. They also shrink the economic, strategic, technological, and ethical ground on which the US and its allies can sustain their power and relevance. There are other reasons why Beijing would like to use the Global South concept as an organizing principle and why it heavily targets developing economies in the region. In many of these countries, governance is poor, institutions are opaque, and relatively small and unchanging groups of elites rule. This combination provides fertile ground for China for several reasons: China excels at elite capture , offering immediate and guaranteed economic and commercial gains to these elites and their countries. In many developing economies, the elites will accept Chinese material offerings even if Beijing is the primary beneficiary. This weakens these countries, making them more reliant on Chinese largesse. These economies are often unattractive to multinational firms, making their elites desperate for guaranteed Chinese offerings, even if they are paid for in political or strategic favors. The practices of elites in many Asian Global South economies run afoul of Western democratic norms and practices. Partnership with China gives them protection and the promise of material benefits without pressure to change or reform. [3] Once these countries and their elites become reliant on Chinese capital or largesse, they are locked into the Chinese system, and leaving it carries high costs and risks. In the Xi Jinping era, the contours and content of a Chinese Global South strategy for Asia and beyond are still evolving. However, there is evidence of recent and growing interest in an updated Global South strategy to advance the CCP’s long-standing core objectives, summarized below: Maintain the viability and robustness of the CCP-led political economy and impose elements of its principles and processes on the region. Continually shrink the strategic, military, economic, political, and normative ground in the region that Washington and its allies can use to sustain, build, and demonstrate US power and influence. Induce or coerce regional states to become supportive, compliant, or, at worst, neutral. In a United Nations General Assembly address in September 2021, Xi introduced Beijing’s Global Development Initiative (GDI). Ostensibly, the initiative is not revolutionary and is meant to accelerate implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, “to steer global development toward a new stage of balanced, coordinated and inclusive growth.” [4] Priority areas for the GDI include “poverty alleviation, food security, COVID-19 response and vaccines, development financing, climate change and green development, industrialization, digital economy and connectivity.” Beijing links the GDI to the Global Security Initiative (GSI) that it announced in mid-2022, and links both to developing countries. [5] Prima facie, the GSI is more concerned with security than development. At the 2022 Boao Forum for Asia, in discussing the GSI, Xi mentioned providing “indivisible security” and building a “balanced, effective and sustainable security architecture” that opposes “exclusive” arrangements such as the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (or Quad)—a partnership between the United States, Japan, India, and Australia—and AUKUS, a security agreement between Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. [6] However, China is largely packaging the GSI as the geopolitical complement to the GDI, while presenting the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)—a Beijing-led international development effort—as a Global South program. For example, when presenting the GSI to developing nations, Beijing frames it as a broad geopolitical approach to enhance and accelerate rapid economic development and material advancement, and claims it promotes “respecting the independent choices of development paths and social systems made by people in different countries.” [7] China calls the GSI “inclusive,” contrasting it with US-led security architectures that impose Western institutions and systems on developing nations as a precondition for material assistance. As one observer has noted, the GSI comprises a “non-Western alternative and mechanism by the global south for the global south.” [8] The same can be said about the GDI and BRI. Beijing is also linking the GSI to Chinese notions of Asian approaches and Asian unity, implying that US initiatives are divisive and unsuited to the Global South’s developing needs. China’s Global South strategy is an increasingly important part of its plan to ease Washington out of its periphery and advance the Sinocentric order. The GDI and GSI provide a defense against the “bullying of the weak states by the West” and a pathway to transcend Western geopolitical constraints and norms. [9] Beijing’s Bid for Global South AI Leadership In Xi’s keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance on July 17, 2026, he explained China’s vision of AI leadership and governance in terms drawn from the country’s bid for leadership in the Global South: In China’s view, all countries should take a people-centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good. We should ensure that AI is an important driver for shared prosperity and common security. We should join hands to build a just and equitable system for global AI governance. [10] He added: We should encourage inclusiveness and promote mutual learning between civilizations. AI development and its application should not erode or undermine the diversity of world civilizations or the uniqueness of cultures of different countries. We must shape the values of AI with humanity’s common values and make good use of AI technologies to increase understanding, tolerance, exchanges, and sharing among all civilizations. We should tend to the garden of civilizations with great care to ensure that the beauty of each civilization is appreciated and shared. [11] Xi then made clear that his vision for AI leadership and governance is directed at the developing economies in the Global South: We must carry out extensive international cooperation and help Global South countries with capacity building to bridge the AI and digital divides, promote sustainable development, and prevent creating new historical injustice in AI. [12] There are several elements to note about China’s bid for AI leadership in this context. One claim is that under Chinese AI leadership, developing nations will have a greater say in the development of AI standards, in who controls and governs the use of AI, and in how the technology ought to (and ought not to) be used. When Beijing promotes “China’s long-standing emphasis on AI for good, openness and inclusiveness, and the belief that AI development should contribute to more equitable global development,” [13] it is essentially arguing against allowing the US and other Western nations to shape the future governance and ethics of AI. In Beijing’s telling, China is protecting the interests of the Global South and shielding it from Western domination, and this extends to AI. AI is thus yet another important issue for China in advancing its material and non-material power and influence at the expense of the West, particularly the United States. From the BRI—including the Digital Silk Road, which seeks to expand China’s technological dominance in important economic sectors [14] —to the GDI and GSI, the fundamental objective is to “surpass” the US and the rest of the West by advancing China’s leadership and presence in the developing world. Another element of China’s bid for AI leadership is to ostensibly work with developing economies to develop AI technologies and governance approaches. According to the Chinese framing, Beijing is working with the Global South to “counter the monopolization of technical standards and governance rules.” [15] As Xi put it in his keynote address mentioned above, “AI development should not be a solo performance by a single country [i.e., the US] but a symphony of global cooperation.” [16] China seeks to demonstrate this seeming spirit of AI cooperation with the Global South in several ways. One is by contrasting Chinese open models with the closed models offered by American companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. While these companies offer the advantage of vertically integrated and bundled, exportable AI stacks of chips, models, cloud, and software, China’s open models can be downloaded, modified, and adapted with fewer restrictions. [17] Platforms such as DeepSeek, for example, allow users to download and fine-tune the model for a specific task or build a product on top of it without paying the original developer for access. To be sure, the American firms have the most powerful and secure offerings in the market, even if Chinese open-model alternatives are catching up quickly. [18] The American models have built-in safety features that are better at preventing misuse for fraudulent activities, for example. However, they are not just more expensive, but closed in the sense that users cannot inspect or modify them. [19] The Chinese notion of AI openness goes beyond how end users can access and modify AI platforms. For the country’s entire AI ecosystem, Beijing supports an open approach—from large language models (LLMs) to embodied AI, in which algorithms are integrated into physical or virtual bodies, such as robots or sophisticated chatbots, to perform specific tasks. This approach, which makes a virtue of the necessity to play catch-up to more advanced American rivals, began with the State Council’s 2017 New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan . [20] The plan imposed a domestic open-source or open-weight approach to fast-track the development of the entire Chinese AI stack, supported by subsidies, industry funds, and local government capital. [21] From development and sourcing of chips to algorithmic and software development, Beijing oversees a system of permissive licensing, below-market pricing between AI entities across the entire AI stack, and an ecosystem that encourages collaboration rather than profit for individual firms. [22] Under legislation such as the 2017 National Intelligence Law, 2021 Data Security Law, and 2021 Personal Information Protection Law, data is to be stored in China and accessible by state authorities. This reinforces the link between data security on the one hand, and national security on the other. [23] These policies to promote domestic development of AI capabilities under state supervision are supplemented by an extensive state-backed system of acquiring and even stealing American AI technologies to feed China’s AI ecosystem. [24] The main point is that China’s state-based approach to AI seeks to replicate key elements of strategies it used to achieve dominant global market share in sectors such as solar panels, [25] electric vehicles, [26] and in developing economies, 5G: [27] Identify an industry or sector of high strategic importance. Formulate and implement a domestic blueprint to accelerate development of a national ecosystem and indigenous supply chain to fast-track Chinese industrial and technological dominance. Encourage or force Chinese firms and entities to collaborate and even share technologies or proprietary knowledge to serve national objectives. Supplement the domestic blueprint with a systematic and extensive system of intellectual-property theft, illegitimate distillation (i.e., getting smaller and cheaper Chinese models to mimic more expensive and sophisticated American models), [28] and forced technology transfers from foreign firms operating in China. Mandate an aggressive pricing strategy for Chinese firms—which are frequently offered state subsidies, tax breaks, etc.—to increase their global market share, crowd out competitors, and eventually achieve domestic and external market dominance. Increase international structural dependency on Chinese firms and entrench the dominance of Chinese AI architecture, especially in developing economies. Promote international collaboration with dominant Chinese firms in the spirit of global “openness and cooperation.” Gradually restrict external access to cutting-edge Chinese technology and models for overseas users once Chinese firms have achieved dominance. In other words, China might offer an open model to global users, but with an AI stack owned by Chinese entities and regulated by Beijing. If the platform is accessed via Chinese APIs (artificial intelligence application programming interfaces) or third-party web applications, then Beijing has access to data and other information. In summary, China’s open approach is intended to achieve two main objectives. The first is to advance technological self-reliance and global Chinese AI leadership at the expense of the United States. This is necessary to achieve the CCP’s notion of cyber sovereignty , the ability to defend and promote its preferred cyber standards for how such technologies are used and governed. [29] The second is to offer cheaper and more flexible options to global users, especially in developing economies, to make them dependent on Chinese, rather than American, offerings and thus increasingly reliant on the Chinese AI ecosystem and trapped within it. Southeast Asian Sovereign AI Aspirations Sovereign AI, [30] in the broadest terms, is a strategy for governments to reduce reliance on foreign AI technologies by developing domestic capabilities and ensuring access to critical data, technologies, expertise, and national infrastructure. From a government perspective, it is the ability to shape, deploy, and govern AI ecosystems in line with national interests and values. It implies strategic and operational control and the ability to maintain resilience in AI capabilities. [31] Southeast Asian nations are increasingly championing sovereign AI for three interrelated reasons. First, countries are seeking to benefit from AI economically. As framed by delegates to the AI for Developing Countries Forum, held in February in Bangkok, Thailand, one critical component of AI sovereignty is developing and retaining local talent so that countries are not simply consumers of AI models and applications, but creators. [32] Just as Southeast Asian countries collaborated with Western export-focused manufacturing firms in the second half of the previous century to enrich local economies, [33] they are determined to do the same with AI. Second, this strategy can help build national resilience. Sovereign AI means the ability to control AI data, computing resources, and crucially, the models operating within a country. It is intended to ensure that national AI capabilities are not excessively dependent on infrastructure, technologies, and policies developed and implemented outside Southeast Asia. Third, sovereign AI will ensure that AI applications, including LLMs, reflect a nation’s languages, cultures, and values. As one regional commentator explains, this means governmental control of data and models because the range and choice of data used, and how the models are trained, determine the AI outputs consumed by a country’s citizens. [34] While Southeast Asian countries have made some efforts to advance sovereign AI, these efforts have largely involved crafting broad declaratory statements of principles and aspirations. For example, the 2024 ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics [35] and the 2025 Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics—Generative AI [36] propose shared principles of testing, assurance, accountability, and provenance. In recent years, Southeast Asian countries have also made some efforts to further define AI principles, launch assurance initiatives, and update privacy laws. For example, Singapore has put AI assurance into practice at scale, enabling real-world testing of generative AI systems through AI Verify and the Global AI Assurance Sandbox. [37] In 2024, Malaysia issued  National Guidelines on AI Governance & Ethics [38] and also established a National AI Office to coordinate implementation and legislation. In 2024, the Philippines issued AI guidance explaining how the Data Privacy Act applies to testing, deployment, and training. [39] In 2025, Indonesia’s Constitutional Court clarified the circumstances in which a data protection officer must be appointed, strengthening oversight of high-risk processing of personal data. [40] Vietnam’s stand-alone AI law, the region’s first, [41] became effective in March 2026. [42] These are either declaratory or broad governing principles and form only an elementary basis for addressing governance issues. However, the AI stack encompasses tools, technologies, and frameworks that work together to build, train, deploy, and manage AI applications. These range from data processing and machine learning frameworks to cloud services and hardware infrastructure that enable developers and organizations to create and scale AI solutions. [43] There have been some piecemeal national efforts in the region, ranging from how and where data must be stored, [44] to demanding that American frontier companies pay for the use of local content. [45] However, with notable exceptions— such as Singapore’s open-source LLM SEA-LION, which is trained and developed using content specific to Southeast Asia—there have been few successful and scalable national or private-sector initiatives to advance Southeast Asian sovereign AI objectives in practice. Indeed, American and Chinese firms continue to dominate AI investment in Southeast Asia in model and algorithmic development and at the infrastructure level (e.g., rare earth extraction, graphics-processing-unit manufacturing, data centers, energy grids, computational power, and satellite connectivity networks). Beware Chinese AI Promises China sees an opportunity to advance its geopolitical objectives by aligning its bid for leadership over the Global South, including in AI, with the sovereign AI aspirations of developing Southeast Asian nations, meaning all Southeast Asian nations except Singapore. One example of this is the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), established in July 2026 as a Chinese initiative with headquarters in Shanghai. Its 29 members are all developing economies, including Southeast Asian countries Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, and Myanmar. Mirroring Chinese Global South initiatives and promises, WAICO aims “to fully unleash the infinite potential of AI and realize common development and common prosperity.” [46] It promotes “inclusive development” to “help Global South countries enhance capacity building and foster an ecosystem for AI innovation,” and it aims to “enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards” among Global South countries. [47] More broadly, China is promising to help advance the sovereign AI goals of developing Southeast Asian economies and has established AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN—as well as with the African Union, the Arab League, and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States—and created thousands of AI training opportunities for individuals from these regions. [48] China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published a Global AI Governance Initiative [49] in 2023 and a Global AI Governance Action Plan [50] in 2025 to promote the country’s state-supported, open-source and open-weight AI approach as the driver of shared international development and evidence of China’s support for “equal [global] rights to develop and use AI.” Beijing contrasts this with ostensibly selfish American desires to propagate US closed, proprietary models, which in China’s telling, serve only American governmental and private-sector interests. [51] China promises potential customers that: Chinese AI cloud services (offered mainly by Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei) are cheaper, better integrated, and more able to meet data localization requirements than Western competitors. Chinese open-source platforms (offered by firms such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, Tencent, Baidu, ByteDance, and Xiaomi) are more adaptable for evolving Southeast Asian requirements and will accelerate the development of local talent and solutions, in contrast to the more expensive bundled, closed American platforms. AI agents developed on Chinese platforms will be cheaper and better integrated within a Chinese AI ecosystem than Western alternatives. Beijing’s pitch is that partnering with China offers Southeast Asian nations strategic autonomy, national resilience, and better developmental and commercial pathways, and that Southeast Asian sovereign AI objectives can only be achieved through this partnership. The Chinese promises are seemingly well-aligned with Southeast Asia’s sovereign AI goals: to ensure AI technologies rapidly increase the industrial capacity of poorer nations, improve their economies, and give them greater influence in the global development of AI rules, standards, ethics, and governance. Both the United States and China see AI as the decisive technology in their economic and geopolitical competition, and both admit that they are in a two-horse race. For the moment, the United States is ahead in computing power, talent, capital expenditure, algorithm development, and deployment of models. [52] China, however, is supporting an open AI ecosystem and open-weight models to encourage growing numbers of independent developers and users to train its models and gain access to more data. Beijing sees this as the less-expensive, more-efficient, and necessary way for Chinese platforms to innovate quickly and cheaply, given their limited access to American technology and know-how. The Chinese approach is not just to catch up to American AI models in performance and even surpass them, but to win by outperforming the United States in distribution and use of platforms, even if it fails to surpass American models in performance. This focus on superior distribution and third-party use is particularly effective with developing economies, where users are seeking less-expensive, good-enough solutions that are more immediately adaptable to their needs. The problem is that growing dependency on Chinese models is not cost-free and comes with significant risks. Governments, businesses and consumers should be skeptical of Beijing’s promise that it is developing its own AI ecosystem for the benefit of all other developing economies. First, Beijing is falsely promising that increased reliance on Chinese open-weight models will support national sovereign AI agendas. China is integrating a state-backed, state-controlled AI stack that includes models, hardware, infrastructure, and governance. Chinese models from companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Baidu leverage products from state-supported semiconductor producers such as Huawei and Baidu and cloud platforms from firms such as Huawei, Alibaba, and Tencent. All Chinese entities must abide by extensive state-directed rules and standards, and all governments and firms that adopt Chinese AI platforms and models are unavoidably creating path dependencies and aligning themselves with these standards. [53] For example, both Chinese and international versions of DeepSeek must filter, adjust, and redirect discussion according to mandatory rules. The system detects and suppresses politically sensitive or “undesirable” topics. [54] For Southeast Asians, this does not mean only highly sensitive topics relating to the CCP, such as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre or the denial of Uighurs’ human rights in Xinjiang. It also means illegal Chinese claims in the South China Sea or CCP foreign influence activities in the region. What is true of DeepSeek applies to other Chinese models as well. [55] Moreover, Chinese platforms have built-in algorithmic biases imposed by Beijing. Narratives are set to align with CCP preferences, and the AI will downplay CCP failings and amplify CCP achievements. It will also manipulate answers to elevate pro-Chinese content and bury or eliminate dissenting perspectives. [56] While Chinese platforms allow independent users to download, modify, or tinker with the models using their own data and for their own purposes, the original models are preset to deliver only narratives and information acceptable to the CCP. More broadly, those who become reliant on Chinese AI platforms are buying into and spreading a digital standard defined by Beijing that cannot be modified or erased. Second, a related point is that Chinese LLMs learn primarily from data filtered through Chinese internet and cyber laws. More importantly, Chinese law requires that all AI models, training outputs, and data reflect CCP values. Southeast Asian entities that choose Chinese open models are importing, in addition to narrative and information manipulation, both the deliberate and inadvertent vulnerabilities that are built into those models. Both US and Chinese models have suffered from inadvertent security flaws. Nevertheless, Chinese models have been shown to be inferior to American models in their vulnerability, for example, to jailbreaks, which bypass ethical guidelines and prompt models to perform restricted or illegal activities. [57] More pertinent are intentional vulnerabilities, such as concealed backdoors and geopolitically motivated triggers. For example, models can be “sleeper agents,” trained to behave normally until a specific trigger condition is met. [58] An investigation of DeepSeek-R1 found that adding politically sensitive topics to coding prompts made the model up to 50 percent more likely to produce code with severe security vulnerabilities. [59] Another study found that Chinese open-weight LLMs, when prompted by a user with a US government persona, produced lower-quality and less secure code with more vulnerabilities, and a CCP-aligned political bias was apparent in both the answers and the code generated. [60] To be sure, assessments about the extent to which Chinese models are compromised are contested. [61] However, researchers have discovered in these models deliberately built-in concealed vulnerabilities that appear to be driven by geopolitical incentives, and security experts have recognized this as a significant problem. [62] The key question is whom to trust: Chinese models subject to CCP mandates, from a country that treats publicly and privately owned technology as a tool of the state, including as a means for surveillance, and as part of broader political warfare? [63] Or privately owned American firms, which do seek to maximize profits but whose primary selling point is that they offer LLM models with superior performance and security? Third, putting aside concealed vulnerabilities in coding, all Chinese AI firms are governed by legislation such as the 2017 National Intelligence Law, [64] 2017 Cybersecurity Law, [65] and 2021 Data Security Law, [66] which compel Chinese entities to adhere to the legislation even if they operate outside China. The National Intelligence Law, for example, demands that Chinese firms “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.” [67] If users access Chinese AI models through an API or a third-party interface, their queries, background data, and conversational history are held in databases that transmit the data to China-based servers or can be accessed by the Chinese government. [68] Therefore, even data localization policies championed by many Southeast Asian nations, such as placing relatively cheap Chinese data centers in Southeast Asia, do not protect a country’s information. [69] In sum, Southeast Asian countries that partner with China create pathways for Beijing to export its AI stack into the region: from hardware—chips, networks, and energy infrastructure—to software—models and data—to applications. In doing so, they become ever more reliant on Chinese capital, research, talent, and governance and security standards. Finally, China uses economic coercion to pressure countries to change their domestic and external policies far more frequently and on a far greater scale than the United States uses economic sanctions to achieve specific outcomes. In recent years, Beijing has employed economic coercion against Japan, South Korea, Australia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Taiwan, as well as countries in the Pacific, Europe, South Asia, Africa, and the Americas. [70] Government officials and experts throughout Southeast Asia reveal in private conversations that there is significant concern about the extent to which their economies have become dependent on China-centered digital infrastructure as part of Beijing’s Digital Silk Road rollout. For example, Vietnamese, Thai, and Philippine dependency on Chinese-controlled submarine cables creates anxiety, [71] and the dominance of Chinese firms such as Huawei, ZTE, ByteDance, and Alibaba in 5G in Southeast Asia is seen as worrisome, [72] even though some governments in the region embrace the domestic surveillance technologies that China offers. Southeast Asian dependency on the Chinese AI stack should also be cause for concern, and countries in the region should attempt to address it before it is too late. While US tech companies do demand certain standards and might impose some measures on users, they are far less arbitrary and geopolitically driven than coercive actions by Chinese firms, which act at the behest of the CCP. Difficult Southeast Asian Choices Singapore, the only advanced economy in Southeast Asia, has unique advantages over other nations in the region and is in an enviable position. While it does not produce cutting-edge AI chips, it is a regional hub for coordinating the manufacture of mature chips, which still constitute the lion’s share of chips being used in the AI stack. Due to strong national institutions, it is the key Southeast Asian financial and investment hub and regional supply chain organizational hub in the sector. Singapore’s access to indigenous and global talent has enabled it to create AI models such as SEA-LION. More than any other Southeast Asian economy, it is well placed to partner with leading AI firms. For example, a partnership between Google Cloud and Digital Industry Singapore launched AI Cloud Takeoff to establish AI centers of excellence in hundreds of Singapore-based enterprises to enable them to create AI applications for a specific industry, workflow, or business problem. Other Southeast Asian nations face more serious obstacles. Some governments and commentators in these countries are advocating for sovereign AI policies that are unachievable. Worse, some of them, if implemented, would leave their economies irreversibly dependent on a Chinese AI ecosystem or deny themselves benefits from global advances in AI technologies and applications. These Southeast Asian economies need to accept the reality that the United States currently dominates AI and that China will likely increasingly dominate it as well. For example, as figure 1 shows, in 2025, estimated US private investment in AI was almost US$286 billion, while Europe and China were a distant second and third, at US$21 billion and US$12.4 billion, respectively. The United States leads in total AI computing power, with 39.7 million H100 equivalents, approximately 50 percent of the global total (H100 equivalent is a standardized unit of measurement used to quantify AI computing power). The United Arab Emirates is second, at 23.1 million. [73] As of May 2025, the US accounted for about 75 percent of global GPU cluster performance, which measures how fast the system processes massive amounts of data, trains AI models, and runs complex simulations, with China second at 15 percent. [74] On the other hand, China leads in the number of data center clusters, with 230. [75] In addition, in 2024, China had the largest number of AI patents, 25,177, with the United States second at 17,307. However, the percentage of AI patents among all patents in the country is higher in the United States than in China, which means that AI is behind a larger proportion of American innovations than Chinese ones. [76] Therefore, Southeast Asian nations are advancing various notions of sovereign AI, based on controlling or influencing significant parts of the AI stack, that are not realistic, financially or technically. Trying to achieve self-sufficiency will be far too costly and will leave countries with a vastly inferior AI capability. Nor will policies to physically locate AI assets in a given country provide the level of resilience and assurance that Southeast Asian nations seek. Placing data centers within a country does not necessarily make them more secure from physical destruction or, as noted earlier, from foreign access. Moreover, aspirations to achieve collective sovereign AI for Southeast Asia, perhaps under ASEAN oversight, are also unrealistic. The existing principles for AI security and governance offer some promise of regional coordination but are not sufficient to overcome real obstacles. For example, even if Southeast Asian economies constituted one economic zone, their combined capital, depth of infrastructure and technology, and capability would be vastly smaller than the American and Chinese AI stacks. Striving for regional AI self-sufficiency would leave Southeast Asia far behind other advanced economies. Besides, Singapore would not give up its privileged status as the preferred capital and technology hub for advanced economies around the world to support the impossible objective of Southeast Asian AI self-sufficiency. Additionally, while Southeast Asian nations do cooperate on many matters, ASEAN members tend to implement different hedging strategies to extract maximum security and economic gains from advanced economies, even at the expense of fellow members. [77] Indeed, when President Donald Trump introduced his so-called Liberation Day tariffs in April 2025, Southeast Asian countries quickly moved to negotiate general tariff rates that were lower than those of neighboring countries to give themselves a relative advantage in trade with the US. So behind the veneer of Southeast Asian fraternity, these economies attempt to maximize their relative gains when dealing with larger economies on which they are dependent. And enduring animosities, lack of strategic trust, and different economic trajectories and capabilities [78] mean that the objective of forging an exclusive, cohesive, and effective Southeast Asian AI ecosystem is seductive but unattainable. What, then, are developing Southeast Asian states to do? The most practical and effective way forward involves two steps: Identify a niche in the AI stack or supply chain where they can become an important or essential hub or node. Create high-tech industrial or technology clusters within or between economies to attract international capital; accelerate development and innovation; attract skilled labor; promote knowledge transfer from abroad and diffusion from within; and reach economically viable scale. Elements of this are already occurring. For example, Vietnam has emerged as an important hub for semiconductor assembly, packaging, and testing. [79] In addition, Singapore and Malaysia could leverage the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone [80] to create an industrial or technological cluster in the region that could be extended to Indonesia’s Batam, Bintan, and Karimun. This is not about achieving self-sufficiency but about welcoming foreign investment from advanced economies and tapping into their AI ecosystems for mutual benefit. In fact, Southeast Asian economies have been doing something similar since the 1960s by harnessing the export manufacturing supply chains set up and financed by advanced economies. This is how Southeast Asia became an essential region for manufacturing electrical and electronic equipment for advanced economies, which led to vast improvements in its economies and, more broadly, underpinned increased prosperity in the latter part of the twentieth century and the 2000s. [81] AI, as an enabler and driver of future prosperity and modernization, should not be viewed differently. Southeast Asian nations—by partnering with firms from the US, Europe, Japan, and South Korea—dramatically accelerated improvements from the 1980s to the 2000s. Today, however, Southeast Asians continually complain that China is capturing ever more of the value added in regional supply chains. Chinese firms in Southeast Asia tend to bring in Chinese citizens to fill key positions, slowing or minimizing knowledge transfer, further entrenching Chinese advantages, and increasing the region’s dependence on Chinese finance, technology, know-how, and inputs. Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative is an ominous indicator of China’s intention to benefit disproportionately from the AI revolution. [82] Beijing offered Southeast Asian entities enormous subsidies and assistance, such as tax breaks and regulatory protection, to increase China’s share of production and value creation in sectors like electric vehicles, robotics, automation, and tech-intensive intermediate goods. These entities had few options but to become part of an ascendant China-centric production and supply chain ecosystem—less as partners and more as dependents. [83] In both high-value-added sectors targeted by Made in China 2025 and lower-valued-added sectors such as textiles and garments and electronic packaging assembly, Chinese firms benefited at the expense of firms in Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam. The question is whether partnering with and depending on an American AI ecosystem will offer Southeast Asian nations better and more enduring benefits, freedom to pursue their own development pathway, and greater data security than the Chinese alternative, which is burdened with geopolitical incentives and direction from the CCP. Economic history and current practice suggest that the American option is better and more prudent. Finally, the important point is that Southeast Asian governments, firms, and individuals cannot ignore the dilemma. They have to make strategic and economic choices about which ecosystem—the American or Chinese—they seek to partner with and prioritize. Some decisions will not be cost-free, and many choices are necessarily zero-sum. To be sure, many Southeast Asian nations claim that they are not interested in taking part in a geopolitical contest between giants. But to paraphrase what Leon Trotsky allegedly said about war, Southeast Asians might not be interested in geopolitical rivalry, but geopolitical rivalry is interested in them. title: BRICS: Growing Ambition, Zero Accountability
summary: Media personnel watch a digital screen showing leaders of member states gather for a family photograph during the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 13 September 2026. Credit: Arun Sankar/AFP * Wednesday, September 30, 2026 * Inter Press Ser
content:
Media personnel watch a digital screen showing leaders of member states gather for a family photograph during the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 13 September 2026. Credit: Arun Sankar/AFP

*   Wednesday, September 30, 2026
*   Inter Press Service

BRUSSELS, Belgium / MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, September 30 (IPS) - At the 18th [BRICS Summit](https://www.brics2026.gov.in/brics-document/), held on 12 and 13 September in New Delhi, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi brought together presidents Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran, along with Abu Dhabi’s Crown Prince, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, representing the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Around the table sat longstanding rivals such as India and China and, in the case of Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, states on opposite sides of an ongoing war. That the summit produced a joint declaration every member could sign was a modest multilateralist success.

The summit took place against a fast-changing backdrop. With the USA under Donald Trump an unreliable partner and often a hostile power bent on bullying others into submission, numerous states are seeking new alliances as a counterweight. BRICS, whose 11 members account for 49 per cent of the world’s population and 28 per cent of the global economy, could become a more significant forum as a result. But what is on offer is a profoundly old-fashioned, state-centric form of multilateralism, in which the people in whose name states claim to act have little say.

## A hollow declaration

At the summit, Xi called for international rules to be ‘[written by all countries](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202609/13/content_WS6aa662e4c6d00ca5f9a0d2c2.html)’, even though he leads a one-party state where increasingly only he writes the rules. Putin [urges](https://saudigazette.com.sa/article/664505/world/putin-calls-for-expanded-un-security-council-representation-for-asia-africa-latin-america) greater representation for Africa, Asia and Latin America at the UN Security Council, while routinely [wielding his veto](https://lens.civicus.org/un-security-council-new-members-old-crisis/) to stop the council acting on his war in Ukraine.

The [New Delhi Declaration](https://d2jiw2zrmmyqt8.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/12185124/New-Delhi-Declaration-2026-1.pdf)’s silences speak loudest. It is explicit on Palestine, calling on Israel to end its war on Gaza and backing a Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders. But on the war in Iran, it only urges ‘maximum restraint’ without naming the warring parties, reflecting the fact that Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE sat around the same table. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not mentioned at all, a regression from past declarations and a troubling sign that Putin has no interest in ending the fighting. The text condemns ‘indiscriminate rising tariffs’ and ‘unilateral sanctions’ without naming the USA, sparing the blushes of members such as India, which is reportedly finalising a trade deal with Washington. The declaration preserves consensus at the expense of resolve.

## Closed civic space, open defiance

Most BRICS governments have no fear of being held domestically accountable for the compromises they have made. [Civic space](https://monitor.civicus.org/) is closed in seven of BRICS’ 11 states and obstructed or repressed in the rest. Russia jails and exiles opposition voices and has made protest almost impossible. China subjects its people to mass surveillance and [crushes](https://monitor.civicus.org/explore/china-repression-continues-with-new-ethnic-unity-law-targeting-of-activists-and-silencing-of-tiananmen-anniversary-commemorations/) any expression that departs from ruling-party lines. Iran [violently suppresses](https://lens.civicus.org/interview/iran-the-unprecedented-level-of-violence-points-to-a-deep-crisis-of-legitimacy/) protest movements, including through the [death penalty](https://lens.civicus.org/backward-steps-on-the-death-penalty/). Saudi Arabia and the UAE recognise no legitimate role for independent civil society. Host and self-styled mediator India has seen Modi’s government erode press freedom, restrict civil society funding and stoke hostility towards religious minorities.

Domestic repression translates directly into a closed international forum. After 18 summits, BRICS still has no treaty, no published membership criteria, no permanent secretariat, no budget and no mechanism for civil society to hold its members to account. This is no accident. It leaves powerful leaders free to pursue their interests, and it means civil society has less influence in BRICS than in comparable blocs such as the [G20](https://lens.civicus.org/diplomacy-in-troubled-times-a-g20-summit-without-the-usa/), and much less than in UN processes.

Civil society mobilised regardless. Three weeks before the summit, over 200 delegates from farmers’ organisations, people’s movements, trade unions, women’s organisations and other civil society groups gathered in New Delhi for the [People’s BRICS Summit](https://www.counterview.net/2026/08/peoples-brics-summit-decries.html). Its resolution denounced BRICS states for reproducing extractivist, inequitable development models, and insisted that cooperation between global south states be judged by the dignity and rights it delivers to people and communities, not by the freedom it grants states and capital. It called for debt restructuring, a publicly accountable energy transition, food sovereignty, universal social security, women’s political representation and an end to the persecution of civil society activists, and for BRICS to take a clear stand against military intervention, occupation and genocide. BRICS governments chose not to listen.

## Ambition without accountability

BRICS’ biggest ambition, on display in the New Delhi Declaration, is to reshape international finance. Development of payment systems independent of the US dollar would chip away at the USA’s unique ability to sustain its power by printing more dollars, despite mountainous debt, to meet unceasing demand. But it would also let repressive states such as Iran and Russia sell oil and gas more easily, funding their repression while blunting international sanctions.

This ambition comes with no commitment to accountability. The bloc has no channel through which the people most affected by its decisions can make their voices heard, and no human rights conditions are attached to its initiatives.

None of the emerging responses to the rapidly changing international order promises to be more democratic than the current system. So far, neither BRICS nor any of the other alternatives now taking shape has matched its growing ambition with greater accountability.

_**Samuel King** is a researcher at CIVICUS: World Alliance for Citizen Participation, working on [ENSURED: Shaping Cooperation for a World in Transition](https://www.ensuredeurope.eu/), a Horizon Europe-funded project. **Inés M. Pousadela** is CIVICUS Head of Research and Analysis, co-director and writer for [CIVICUS Lens](https://lens.civicus.org/) and co-author of the [State of Civil Society Report](https://publications.civicus.org/publications/2026-state-of-civil-society-report/gender-rights-rollback-and-resistance/). She is also Professor of Comparative Politics at [Universidad ORT Uruguay](https://www.ort.edu.uy/)._

title: Press union urges police to handle all cases with ‘equal efficiency’ after same-day arrest over threats to pro-gov’t outlet
summary: Hong Kong’s biggest press union has welcomed the police’s swift response after a local newspaper received a threatening letter, urging authorities to handle similar cases at other outlets with “equal efficiency.” Hong Kong Journalists Assoc
content: Hong Kong’s biggest press union has welcomed the police’s swift response after a local newspaper received a threatening letter, urging authorities to handle similar cases at other outlets with “equal efficiency.” Hong Kong Journalists Association. Photo: Selina Cheng/HKFP. Police apprehended a suspect just hours after the editorial team of Sing Tao Probe, a consumer advocacy platform under the pro-Beijing Sing Tao News Corporation, received a threatening letter containing an unidentified white powder on Monday. The letter expressed discontent over an unpublished consumer complaint about a boardgame parlour that the suspect submitted a year ago. He also accused several media outlets of “falsely accusing” him of stalking and secretly photographing women late at night. The suspect, a 24-year-old local man, remains in police custody. The Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) condemned the incident, which it said threatened press freedom in Hong Kong. “The Association welcomes the police’s swift action in arresting the male suspect on the same day,” the HKJA said in a statement on Tuesday. “We hope the police will handle other cases threatening press freedom with equal efficiency, thereby upholding the reputation of being Asia’s finest police force, as the authorities claim to reinforce.” Multiple cases unsolved In the past several years, the HKJA has publicised several other incidents of reporters being threatened and harassed. Selina Cheng, the chairperson of the Hong Kong Journalists Association, hosts a press conference on reporters’ being intimated on September 13, 2024. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. In September 2024, the press group said during a press conference that dozens of journalists from at least 13 media outlets in Hong Kong had received emails and letters with defamatory content sent to their home addresses, workplaces, and other locations. Journalists targeted included staff from Hong Kong Free Press, InMedia, HK Feature, as well as members of the HKJA executive committee. The HKJA has reported these cases to the police, but no progress has yet been made, the press union said in the statement on Tuesday. “Multiple cases involving threats against press freedom remain unsolved,” the HKJA said. Hong Kong has plummeted in international press freedom indices since the onset of the 2020 and 2024 security laws . Watchdogs cite the arrest and jailing of journalists , raids on newsrooms and the closure of around 10 media outlets including Apple Daily , Stand News and Citizen News . Over 1,000 journalists have lost their jobs, whilst many have emigrated . Meanwhile, the city’s government-funded broadcaster RTHK has adopted new editorial guidelines , purged its archives and axed news and satirical shows. See also:  Explainer: Hong Kong’s press freedom under the national security law In 2022, Chief Executive John Lee said press freedom was “in the pocket” of Hongkongers but “nobody is above the law.” Although he has told the press to “ tell a good Hong Kong story ,” government departments have been reluctant to respond to story pitches .

title: Lawmaker floats cash lottery for newborns as baby bonus scheme extension set to cost HK$2.3bn
summary: The Hong Kong government’s plan to extend a baby bonus scheme for another three years in a bid to boost fertility and assist young families amid record-low births will cost some HK$2.3 billion, according to official estimates. A pregnant wo
content: The Hong Kong government’s plan to extend a baby bonus scheme for another three years in a bid to boost fertility and assist young families amid record-low births will cost some HK$2.3 billion, according to official estimates. A pregnant woman stands in front of a Hong Kong hospital. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The cost of extending the scheme, this time with a larger cash handout for families having a second child, has been laid out in a document submitted to the Legislative Council’s (LegCo) manpower panel. The plan was proposed in Chief Executive John Lee’s Policy Address earlier this month. On top of the existing unspent balance from the first three years of the bonus scheme, the government will seek approval from the legislature’s Finance Committee to set aside an additional HK$1.6 billion for the second round of the scheme ending on October 24, 2029. ‘Conducive environment’ The first round of the scheme, which began in 2023, granted families HK$20,000 per newborn child. For the next three years from September 16, HK$20,000 will continue to be awarded for firstborns, while second and subsequent children will earn families HK$30,000. The policy was renewed “to create a conducive environment for childbearing” as the fertility rate remains low at 0.73 in 2025, the document stated. Fewer than 30,000 babies were born in Hong Kong from July 2025 to the end of June this year, marking a record low for the city. Ten years ago, the number of births was more than double this figure. As of August 31, the government had distributed payouts totalling around HK$1.55 billion to 77,709 applicants, according to the document. Some HK$732 million of the initial commitment remains unspent and will be rolled over to the renewed scheme. The baby bonus scheme also includes larger tax breaks and priority in the public rental housing queue. Families with newborns would also be able to borrow 95 per cent of a residential property’s value for a mortgage, and pay less stamp duty. Cash lottery At the Wednesday LegCo meeting, lawmakers questioned whether the bonuses could be bolstered, with one suggesting a random multi-million dollar cash prize for new parents. Legislator and former police officer Joe Chan said that the government could collaborate with the Hong Kong Jockey Club to set up a Mark Six-style award ranging from HK$1 million to HK$4 million for newborns. Deputy Chief Secretary for Administration Warner Cheuk said the funds that the government or the club could provide would be limited, with the financial commitment amounting to an astronomical figure. A caretaker walks with a little boy in Hong Kong. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Responding to a suggestion by Election Committee lawmaker Elvin Lee, Cheuk said that the government would consider a tax break for expenses associated with hiring a foreign domestic worker, while taking into account the government’s fiscal situation. Ken Lee, representing the labour sector, suggested that the government take inspiration from the Family Planning Association’s 1975 “Two Is Enough” advertising campaign, which promoted smaller families.

title: 美驻华大使庞德伟：中国将稀土“武器化”是不可接受的
summary: 华盛顿 — 美国驻华大使庞德伟(David Perdue)表示，中国将其稀土出口的主导性地位“武器化”，并用来针对全世界。他说，美国已经向中国表示，这是“不可接受的”。上个星期在美中元首峰会以及会前谈判中，双方触及了稀土问题，但并没有公布任何具体的新协议。 庞德伟星期二(9月29日)在X平台上发表针对中国稀土管制的两则贴文，贴文内容来自于他星期日接受美国周日福克斯新闻(Fox News Sunday)采访时的表述。 庞德伟表示，中国在去年4月份针对稀土和磁体推出了出口许可制度
content:
华盛顿 —

美国驻华大使庞德伟(David Perdue)表示，中国将其稀土出口的主导性地位“武器化”，并用来针对全世界。他说，美国已经向中国表示，这是“不可接受的”。上个星期在美中元首峰会以及会前谈判中，双方触及了稀土问题，但并没有公布任何具体的新协议。

庞德伟星期二(9月29日)在X平台上发表针对中国稀土管制的两则贴文，贴文内容来自于他星期日接受美国周日福克斯新闻(Fox News Sunday)采访时的表述。

庞德伟表示，中国在去年4月份针对稀土和磁体推出了出口许可制度，并进一步将其武器化。如今，“中国规定任何为多元经营而离开中国的操作均属违法，中国可以逮捕人员，将其起诉，扣押其资产，限制其出境等。”

庞德伟所指的是应该去年4月4日中国商务部、海关总署发布公告，对七种稀土元素实施出口限制，作为对特朗普政府加征关税的反制。

今年5月，富士电机两名日本籍员工因试图将内置稀土磁体的马达以“可拆卸”的组装方式出口至中国境外，在大连遭当地海关拘留，并在6月被中国正式逮捕，目前案件仍在调查和处理阶段。

庞德伟继续表示，中国将其作为稀土单一来源的主宰性地位“武器化”，并用来针对全世界。“我们已经告诉他们这是不可接受的”。“我们不会让自己活在一个必须去到中国卑躬屈膝才能以自己的方式经商的世界。”他说。

美国对外关系委员会中国与印太研究高级研究员、前美国国安会中国与台湾事务副主任杜如松(Rush Doshi)在X平台表示，在习近平国事访问刚结束不久，庞德伟大使的评论格外引人关注。

**美中峰会触及稀土，但没有新协议**

上星期四(9月24日)，美中两国元首在华盛顿举行了备受关注的峰会。峰会前，美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特(Scott Bessent)、贸易代表杰米森·格里尔(Jamieson Greer)9月20日在纽约与中国副总理何立峰在纽约会谈。稀土和关键矿产供应是美方关注的议题，但会后贝森特和格里尔没有公布改善供应进展或新的承诺。

峰会结束后，依据白宫发布的情况说明，双方将继续致力于解决美方对于稀土及其他关键矿产供应链短缺问题的关切，目标是确保相关货物的出货量恢复至适当水平。但说明没有列出具体矿种、数量、许可安排或时间表。而中国外交部公布的峰会成果清单也没有列出稀土方面的具体承诺。

白宫5月曾表示，中国将处理美方对钇、钪、钕、铟等关键矿产供应短缺以及稀土生产和加工设备、技术销售限制的关切。

美国政治新闻网站《政客》(Politico)驻华盛顿中国事务记者Phelim Kine(中文名：老康)在X平台表示，庞德伟大使的帖子证实了“特习峰会的友好表象并没有让习近平在稀土供应链的问题上让步”。他说，“北京可以随意切断关键矿产的出口，直到美国找到其他来源。”

美国之音(VOA)就美中峰会对稀土问题的讨论以及庞德伟大使的最新表态向美国贸易代表办公室寻求回应，但截至报道发表前，尚未收到回复。

**美国全力追赶，脱离对北京稀土依赖**

庞德伟在接受周日福克斯新闻[采访](https://www.foxnews.com/media/trump-officials-warn-china-weaponizing-rare-earth-dominance-beijing-uses-critical-minerals-leverage)时说，20年前，美国在稀土磁体、商业造船和制药都占据着主导地位，但这些都在过去20年被中国夺取，“现在，特朗普政府正试图扭转这种局势，重建美国在不依赖北京的情况下的运作能力。”

目前美中没有宣布下一轮稀土谈判的时间表，已知的下一次两国高层会晤是11月在中国深圳举行的APEC峰会；特朗普和习近平预计还将在12月迈阿密的G20峰会期间会面。两国的贸易休战则已延长至2027年1月10日。

title: 中国特色还是中共特色？——从“听床政治”到制度如何变成文化
summary: 艾地声Edysen X @KA594594 · Sep 28, 2026 中国特色还是中共特色？ ——从“听床政治”到制度如何变成文化 这些年，中国政治舆论场里出现了一个颇有黑色幽默意味的词：“听床师”。某个高官几个月没有公开露面，是不是出事了？某个将领缺席会议，是不是被查了？某篇新华社通稿里少了一个名字，是不是政治排名发生变化？某领导人的座次变了，是不是失宠了？某句话突然不再出现，是不是路线调整？甚至一个镜头、一张照片、一处标点，都可能被赋予远远超出文本本身的政治含义。 一
content: 艾地声Edysen  X @KA594594 · Sep 28, 2026 中国特色还是中共特色？ ——从“听床政治”到制度如何变成文化 这些年，中国政治舆论场里出现了一个颇有黑色幽默意味的词：“听床师”。某个高官几个月没有公开露面，是不是出事了？某个将领缺席会议，是不是被查了？某篇新华社通稿里少了一个名字，是不是政治排名发生变化？某领导人的座次变了，是不是失宠了？某句话突然不再出现，是不是路线调整？甚至一个镜头、一张照片、一处标点，都可能被赋予远远超出文本本身的政治含义。 一批人因此专门研究谁露面、谁消失，谁站在谁旁边，央视镜头停留几秒，《人民日报》把谁放在第几段。蛛丝马迹被反复拼接，形成一套近乎“政治密码学”的解释体系。很多预测后来证明不过是捕风捉影；但有些时候，一些重大政治变化又确实首先以这种极为含混的方式留下痕迹。 问题并不只是：“听床师为什么这么多？”值得追问的是：为什么进入21世纪二十多年，一个拥有现代官僚体系、互联网、大数据、卫星通信和世界最大新闻宣传机器之一的国家，其最高层政治仍然能够不断制造出类似古代宫廷秘闻的公共信息环境？再进一步说：这究竟是所谓的“中国特色”，还是更准确地说，是“中共特色”？答案恐怕既不能简单归于“中国文化”，也不能把两者完全割裂。 一、“宫廷秘闻”：权力越封闭，政治越像猜谜 中国人当然不是今天才开始猜皇帝在想什么。传统王朝政治中，关于最高权力的信息从来具有极高价值。皇帝病了没有？太子还能不能继位？某个大臣为什么突然不朝？某位妃嫔为什么得宠？谁能够进宫见皇帝？一道诏书究竟出自皇帝本人，还是宦官、外戚、权臣之手？这些问题在传统政治中绝非茶余饭后的娱乐，而可能关系一个家族、一派官僚甚至整个国家的命运。原因很简单，在一个权力高度集中的政治体系中，最高统治者的个人意志可能直接改变官员命运和政策方向；而最高权力运行本身却又缺乏公开、制度化的信息渠道。 这就形成一个基本规律：权力越重要，信息越稀缺；信息越稀缺，猜测越有价值。这才是所谓“宫廷政治”真正的社会学基础，并不是古人天生喜欢八卦，是他们必须通过有限线索判断权力风向。因此才会产生门生故吏、耳目消息、密折、内廷传闻、官场风声和各种政治秘闻。从这个意义上说，今天互联网上的“听床”，确实可以在中国历史中找到久远的文化原型。 可是，如果分析到这里就停下来，把今天的一切都归结为“中国人几千年的宫斗文化”，反而会遮蔽最重要的问题。现代中国毕竟不是清朝，今天的中华人民共和国拥有宪法、国务院、全国人大、最高法院、中央军委以及庞大的现代官僚组织体系。那为什么现代政治机构之上，仍然会重新生长出如此旺盛的“宫廷秘闻政治”？答案必须进入第二层。 二、“听床”首先不是文化现象，是信息制度现象 一个人如果每天都能看到透明、稳定而可信的政治信息，通常没有必要去猜。如果高级官员的任免存在公开程序，重大政策存在公开辩论，领导人的健康与履职情况有稳定披露机制，军政高层变动能够由制度化新闻渠道及时说明，那么某个人一次缺席会议，并不会产生巨大的政治想象空间。 但是，当正式信息非常有限，而实际权力又高度重要时，任何细节都会升值。一个名字有没有出现，一个镜头有没有给到，一个排名有没有变化，都会变成信息替代品。所以，“听床师”并不是某种中国人的特殊人格类型，它首先是一个信息供求失衡产生的政治职业。正式信息越稀缺，非正式信息越值钱；透明度越低，传闻市场越繁荣；制度不给确定性，人们就会从细节里制造确定性。 这其实是一种普遍机制，并不只存在于中国。苏联时代的西方研究者也曾根据苏共领导人在红场阅兵时的站位、照片排序和《真理报》的措辞变化分析克里姆林宫权力结构，“Kremlinology”由此成为冷战时代一个著名词汇。这正说明“听床政治”的核心，不是民族性，是黑箱权力。 三、中国今天的黑箱政治，又不能只用传统帝制解释 这里就必须区分“中国特色”与“中共特色”。中国传统政治确实留下许多历史遗产：大一统国家传统、官本位、中央集权倾向、家国同构、关系网络、政治忠诚伦理，以及围绕最高权力形成的政治心理。这些不是共产党创造的，但1949年以后建立起来的政治体系，同样不能简单看作传统王朝换了一块招牌。 中国共产党首先是一个现代列宁主义政党。它拥有严密的组织体系、中央委员会、政治局、政治局常委会、纪律机构、组织部门、宣传体系、干部任命体系以及遍布国家与社会的大量党组织。按照中共自己的制度表述，中国共产党是“最高政治领导力量”，“中国特色社会主义最本质的特征”就是中国共产党领导；习近平还明确强调，“党中央作出的决策部署”，不仅党的组织、宣传、统战、政法部门要贯彻落实，人大、政府、政协、法院、检察院等机构中的党组织同样要贯彻落实。 这一制度结构显然不是秦始皇、朱元璋或乾隆留下来的。它首先属于20世纪革命政党和党国体系的政治遗产。因此，今天中国政治的秘密性，不能简单解释为“皇权传统死灰复燃”。更准确地说，是两套东西发生了叠加：传统中央集权政治留下的文化记忆，与现代列宁主义党组织结构发生了结合。于是形成了一种非常特别的现代政治形态。 四、值得研究的是：传统帝制与列宁党如何彼此改造 这也是“中国特色”与“中共特色”最有意思的交界处。中共最初当然不是一个传统意义上的王朝组织，它产生于20世纪革命时代，其组织原则、革命语言和政治结构有鲜明的国际共产主义背景。但任何外来的制度进入一个历史悠久的社会之后，都不可能原封不动。列宁主义进入中国以后，必须在中国社会中运作；与此同时，中国传统的政治观念、社会关系和权力心理也会进入这个现代组织。 两者发生相互塑造。例如，“忠诚”本来是所有政治组织都会强调的品质，但是在一个拥有悠久君臣政治传统的社会里，“忠诚于组织”“忠诚于核心”与传统政治文化中的忠君心理之间，很容易产生新的文化共振；又比如“大一统”，它本来是中国古代国家形成以后长期存在的政治理念；现代政党则可以赋予它新的民族国家与意识形态解释；再比如中央集权，传统帝国的中央集权主要依靠皇权—官僚体系，而现代党国则可以通过组织、人事、纪律、宣传和技术系统，把中央权力贯彻到传统王朝无法抵达的社会深处。 所以，今天中国政治有时看起来很“古老”，实际上其控制能力却极其现代。这正是最容易造成误判的地方：外观可能像帝制，组织技术却属于现代。 五、“皇帝政治”只是比喻，并不是准确的制度描述 今天有人习惯把中共总书记直接称作“皇帝”，把中南海政治理解成现代皇宫。这种比喻当然容易传播，也能够捕捉某些个人权力高度集中的现象，但在分析上必须保持距离。 皇帝与共产党总书记毕竟不是同一种制度职位。中国共产党目前正式制度仍然存在党章、中央委员会、政治局、政治局常委会、中央军委以及干部组织体系。党章明确规定了党的组织原则与纪律体系，并把中国共产党领导定义为中国特色社会主义制度的根本特征之一。真正值得研究的并不是“中国是不是重新有了皇帝”，是为什么一个高度现代化的组织政党，在权力越来越集中以后，会重新产生如此强烈的宫廷政治观感？这比一句“复辟帝制”更值得研究，它揭示的不是名号，是政治结构。 六、“中国特色社会主义”本身已经回答了一半问题 有意思的是，中共自己实际上并不否认“中国特色”与中共制度之间的关系。习近平明确把“中国共产党领导”定义为中国特色社会主义“最本质的特征”，并强调“党政军民学，东西南北中，党是领导一切的”。这意味着至少按照官方理论，“中国特色”不是一个脱离共产党的文化概念。它首先是一个政治制度概念；与此同时，近年来中共又进一步强调马克思主义同中国具体实际、中华优秀传统文化相结合。 这就提出了一个十分重要的问题：所谓“中国特色”，究竟有多少是中国文明自身的延续，又有多少是共产党得到政权以后重新塑造出来的？二者必须拆开来看，否则，就很容易出现一种似是而非的解释：凡是中国今天出现的问题，统统说成“中国文化如此”“中国人自古如此”。这种解释看似深刻，实际上常常偷换了因果。 七、最大的认识陷阱：把制度问题民族性化 这是讨论“中国特色”时尤其要警惕的一点。例如官员揣摩上意，可以说中国古代就有；关系社会，中国古代也有；政治避讳，中国古代有；对最高领导人的个人崇拜，古代同样能找到大量例子。于是很容易得出结论：“中国人几千年来就是这样。”但这种说法遗漏了一个最关键的变量：制度会选择、强化甚至重新生产某些文化特征。 一种文化因素存在，并不等于它必然成为社会的主导行为方式。中国历史上同时存在皇权，也存在乡约、宗族、民间自治、商人契约、士绅公共生活以及各种地方社会传统。为什么现代社会中的某些传统被放大，而另一些传统不断萎缩？这里就必须考察制度：制度奖励什么行为，什么行为就更容易扩散；制度惩罚什么行为，什么行为就更容易消失。如果直言政治风险较高，揣摩暗示就会变得理性；如果公开讨论受到限制，私下传播就会繁荣；如果权力运行不透明，关系网络就会升值；如果正式规则不足以提供稳定预期，人们就会寻找非正式信息。久而久之，本来是制度适应行为的东西，就会逐渐表现得像一种“民族习惯”。 八、制度运行久了，会制造自己的文化 这可能才是“中国特色”和“中共特色”之间最关键的一层关系。我们通常习惯把文化看作很古老的东西，把制度看作后来附着其上的东西，其实并非如此，制度本身也在不断生产文化。 七十多年足够长。一个政权持续几代人以后，社会成员会围绕它形成大量适应性行为。知道什么能说，什么不能说；知道什么时候要沉默；知道哪些文件是真政策，哪些只是宣传口号；知道什么时候风向变了；知道哪个部门真正有权；知道公开规则之外还要找谁；知道新闻报道里哪些词值得注意；知道“没有消息”有时候本身也是消息。这些都不是写在宪法或法律里的制度，但它们同样真实地塑造着社会。父母教孩子，领导教下属，体制内老人教新人，商人教商人。经过几代人的社会化以后，人们甚至会忘记这些行为最初为何产生。 制度塑造行为，行为沉淀成习惯，习惯最后被误认为文化。这才是最值得警惕的地方。 九、“听床师”成为一种制度标本 回过头来看，“听床师”其实非常有研究价值。他们并不只是互联网时代的滑稽人物，他们更像一种政治生态的边缘产物；他们存在的前提，是正式信息不足以满足社会对最高权力运行的巨大需求。而这个需求又来自另一个事实：最高层政治变化可能深刻影响整个国家。于是人们不得不寻找替代性信号。 新华社稿件、央视镜头、《人民日报》排序、会议座次、领导人活动、军方报道，甚至一个人突然消失，都可能被放进政治显微镜下。其中当然充满臆测、夸张、误判乃至自媒体流量生意。但不能因为大量“听床”错误，就认为这种现象完全没有社会学意义。值得追问的是为什么现代中国需要“听床”？如果一种政治制度能够稳定、及时、可信地解释自身的权力运行，那么“听床产业”自然会失去大部分市场。从这个意义上说：听床不是黑箱政治的原因，是黑箱政治的副产品。 十、到底什么是“中国特色”，什么是“中共特色”？ 或许可以作一个基本区分。所谓“中国特色”，首先应该指中国漫长历史中形成并持续发挥作用的社会结构、文化资源和政治传统；所谓“中共特色”，则应主要指1949年以来、特别是在列宁主义政党国家体系中形成和发展的制度结构、组织行为与政治文化。二者并不相同，但是执政七十余年以后，它们又发生了越来越复杂的重叠；有些中国传统被共产党压制，有些传统被重新解释，有些传统被制度放大。 与此同时，共产党自身创造出的组织习惯、语言体系、权力逻辑和社会行为，也已经逐渐进入中国人的日常生活。所以今天最难辨认的正是：哪些是历史留下的中国，哪些是中共塑造的中国。 十一、真正需要摆脱的是一个错误命题：“中国人就是这样” 每当看到关系社会、官本位、政治沉默、揣摩上意，有人就会感叹：“中国人几千年了，改不了。”这句话非常轻松，却可能也是最偷懒的一种历史解释，它把制度造成的行为，解释成民族无法改变的性格。 事实上，一个民族从来不是一个固定人格，不同制度会生产不同的公共人格。什么样的人容易获得奖励，什么样的人容易受到惩罚，什么样的行为能够成功，久而久之，就会塑造整个社会的行为模式。与其问中国人为什么喜欢宫斗秘闻，不如问什么样的制度不断让揣摩权力变得有价值；与其问为什么中国人喜欢听床，不如问为什么重大公共权力运行需要通过猜测才能获知？这两个问题，只相差几个字，解释方向却完全不同。 十二、中国特色还是中共特色？ 答案到这里大概已经清楚。不能把今天中国所有政治现象都归罪于几千年传统，也不能假装1949年以前不存在任何权力文化遗产。更接近现实的解释是：中国传统政治遗产、现代列宁主义党国结构以及长期执政形成的社会适应机制，共同塑造了今天的政治文化。它可以简化成一个公式：历史传统 × 党国制度 × 长期社会化 = 当代政治文化。其中真正值得特别研究的，是最后一步。 历史不会自动变成现实，只有当一种制度不断选择、奖励和复制某些行为，历史遗产才会重新获得生命。于是宫廷政治的语言回来，揣摩上意的技巧回来，政治秘闻的市场回来。这一切又通过电视、互联网、大数据和现代党组织系统，以完全现代化的方式运行。这可能正是理解当代中国政治一个重要入口。 所以，“中国特色还是中共特色？”并不是一道非此即彼的选择题。更深的问题其实是：一个现代政党如何选择性吸收传统政治资源，又如何经过数十年统治，把自己的制度逻辑重新塑造成社会文化？ 也许几十年之后，人们会把今天很多行为称作“中国人的传统”。但研究者最应该做的，是把这层坚硬的文化外壳重新剥开，许多看似千年不变的“中国特色”，未必有那么古老。 它们也可能只是一个制度存在得足够久以后， 把制度变成了习惯，把习惯变成了文化，最后又把文化伪装成了民族性。

title: Trump's Meeting with Xi Reveals Limits of Personalistic Foreign Policy
source: 芝加哥全球事务委员会
summary: Trump's Meeting with Xi Reveals Limits of Personalistic Foreign Policy ccolon Fri, 09/25/2026 - 16:44 Expectations were low heading into US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s meeting in Washington on Thursday. Analyst
content: Trump's Meeting with Xi Reveals Limits of Personalistic Foreign Policy ccolon Fri, 09/25/2026 - 16:44 Expectations were low heading into US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s meeting in Washington on Thursday. Analysts expected at least some agreement on technology competition, trade, and Taiwan to come out of the leaders’ second 2026 summit. It appears to have failed to produce anything of substance on these issues. Instead, Trump showered praise on Xi, calling the Chinese leader “strong, fit, and vibrant” (despite concerns about Xi’s health ) and touting their “truly great friendship.” The display was consistent with his approach to US foreign policy, which entails collapsing complex society-to-society interactions into personal exchanges between two leaders. But in attempting to “personalize” US-China ties, Trump has produced an incoherent diplomatic process that will fail to stabilize the world’s most important bilateral relationship. By contrast, Xi was much more disciplined in both his delegate selection and words. He reemphasized the need for “strategic stability,” once again attempting to impose guardrails on the relationship and convince the United States to avoid confrontation on Beijing’s supposed red lines , including human rights and Taiwan. Xi’s performance may have bought China some time to manage its growing list of domestic challenges , particularly the country’s ongoing economic malaise. The outcome of the summit reveals the limits of Trump’s personalistic foreign policy. While filled with pomp, ceremony , an exchange of official gifts, and an air force flyover, substantive discussions between the two leaders only lasted about 90 minutes . This may be because American preparations for the visit—which included ironing out the critical talking points negotiating positions, and tradeoffs critical to any policy discussions—were handled chaotically and at the last minute. As a result, this week’s summit is most notable for what didn’t happen. Trump did not lift his pause on a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, cementing a win for Beijing. And the two sides did not reach any agreement on protections against AI misuse, despite several reports (and confessions) of tech companies failing to impose basic safeguards on their rapidly advancing models. During the May summit, both leaders agreed to a pause in trade hostilities and export controls, albeit with mixed adherence . China had communicated a desire to extend this pause , potentially until the end of Trump’s term. But shortly after Xi’s arrival on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington would only extend it by two additional months, saying that a regular renewal would provide more opportunities to apply pressure in the future. Such ephemeral bargains are typical of a personalized and transactional diplomacy . Countries more responsive to the public and with strong checks and balances (i.e., democracies) tend to have more consistent and stable foreign policies. But Trump has shown himself to be   transactional in his policy preferences, with his personalist approach forcing even cabinet secretaries to vie for his approval of their pet projects. It is unstable ground for any durable international agreement, not least because Trump has a demonstrated willingness to renege on deals he himself made. In the past, federal departments would coordinate, make tradeoffs, and reach compromises—moderating and increasing the durability of major policy decisions by giving each actor a stake in the outcome. The lack of an interagency process today means federal departments are not reaching durable policy compromises. Instead, secretaries have strong incentives to pursue their department’s individual interests. US foreign policy therefore swings depending on who is in Trump’s favor at the given time and shifts again as conditions change. Such short time horizons are generally bad for private companies, which need greater stability to secure supply chains, garner or make investments, and gain greater market access. This is especially true when it comes to the US-China relationship and explains the presence of many American business leaders at Thursday’s state dinner. One way to stabilize individual business operations is by cutting side deals with both the US and Chinese governments. But this can mean going against broader American interests. Ultimately, the visit is unlikely to steady bilateral relations for long. The relationship is complex, multifaceted, and grounded in highly interdependent society-to-society exchanges. To be clear, these exchanges are not always positive. For example, the “ China shock ” decimated American manufacturing, generating lasting political consequences . But it is unrealistic to think that these challenges can be managed purely through short, sporadic conversations grounded in the inter-personal relationship of two leaders. While such relationships are important, they must be backed by disciplined intra-governmental coordination that is fashioned into clear negotiation objectives. September 25, 2026 Raymond C. Kuo also serves as the Marshall M. Bouton Senior Fellow for Asia Studies at the Council, focusing on US-China competition, alliance dynamics, and regional order in the Indo-Pacific.
