title: US, China buy time with trade truce as pressure builds
summary: By Beiyi Seow Washington and Beijing may have bought themselves breathing space with an extended trade truce, but analysts warn that time is running out for the world’s two biggest economies to resolve their strategic rivalry. Chinese Presi
content: By Beiyi Seow Washington and Beijing may have bought themselves breathing space with an extended trade truce, but analysts warn that time is running out for the world’s two biggest economies to resolve their strategic rivalry. Chinese President Xi Jinping (right) ​paid a state visit ‌to the US between September 23 and 25 at the invitation of President Donald Trump (right). Photo: White House. President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping concluded a pomp-filled summit Friday, with the US leader confirming they would meet twice more this year. But even as Trump and Xi “are making nice,” their countries “remain locked in a bitter competition over trade, tech, Taiwan, defense, rare earths and industrial policy,” said Daniel Russel of the Asia Society Policy Institute. Daniel Kritenbrink, a former US official now with The Asia Group consultancy, said there’s “no doubt that both leaders would like to see stability in the relationship, at least through the end of the year.” However, “you’d have to see further tangible outcomes for this truce to extend in the long run.” Some feel Beijing has “largely not lived up to the commitments it made” at earlier meetings, he added, noting many US officials “have articulated their profound frustration with the Chinese.” US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping tour the Hall of Prayer of Good Harvest at the Temple of Heaven in Beijing on May 14, 2026. Photo: The White House, via Flickr. Xi and Trump agreed to a trade truce last year during a meeting in South Korea, after a bitter tit-for-tat fight that saw tariffs soar over 100 percent at one point. As part of the agreement, Beijing agreed to buy more US soybeans and other agriculture products, and to suspend rare earths restrictions for a year. The pact was originally due to expire in November but both sides agreed this week to extend it until January 10, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. ‘Short leash’ Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that Washington views such extensions as “compliance periods.” “I think US officials would say China is doing just barely enough to maintain the agreement and no more,” Kritenbrink said. “That’s unsustainable over the long run,” he added. The brief extension “was the preferred position of the Americans,” Mary Lovely of the Peterson Institute for International Economics told AFP. She added that while Beijing would have preferred a longer rollover, the current situation points to Washington’s anxiety about the delivery of rare earth magnets and how officials “want to keep this on a short leash.” “It’s not clear anymore how much their threats of high tariffs actually move China,” she said. ‘Bitter competition’ For now, Greer said that both countries have made “progress” on other economic outcomes and expect to release more details Monday. “We want to have some subset of goods that we can trade with the Chinese on a more preferential basis,” he said. He added that both sides have agreed on products that can be left aside in future trade disputes. Greer is set to host G20 trade ministers in Wisconsin next week, with US tariff threats and the issue of excess capacity — a key concern surrounding Chinese industry — expected to be discussed. Washington and Beijing have also agreed to set up some kind of notification system for artificial intelligence threats between the two countries, Bessent said. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent (left) and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng during a bilateral meeting between the United States and China in Geneva, Switzerland, on May 10, 2025. File photo: Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, via Flickr. Peter Richardson of Counterpoint Research said the channel could be as simple as a hotline, but it will be tough to define what triggers it. “It is often very difficult to tell quickly whether an AI incident was state-directed, a rogue actor or an accident,” he said. “Given the rivalry we don’t expect this to lead to any comprehensive international framework for AI regulation, but it would be the first practical guardrail,” he added. Kritenbrink, for his part, said the summit has done “nothing to curb the competitive instincts of both sides on AI.” “I don’t think you’ll see any slowing down.”

title: Questioning Hong Kong’s lack of a banned book list is ‘soft resistance’ – outgoing nat. security police chief
summary: Questioning why the government will not release a list of books banned in Hong Kong or specify where the red lines lie for seditious content is a form of “soft resistance,” the outgoing head of the police’s national security department has
content: Questioning why the government will not release a list of books banned in Hong Kong or specify where the red lines lie for seditious content is a form of “soft resistance,” the outgoing head of the police’s national security department has said. Andrew Kan appears in Causeway Bay on June 4, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. In an interview with select media outlets just before stepping down as Deputy Commissioner of Police (National Security), Andrew Kan said that raids on bookstores and arrests of bookstore staff conducted by his department earlier this year were not an abuse of power. He also said that national security legislation was clear on what constitutes illegal acts. See also: ‘Hidden dangers lurk in every corner’: Nat. security chief tells new police recruits to root out threats early In July, Hong Kong’s national security police raided two independent bookstores and arrested five people on suspicion of sedition. Officers also seized books said to carry “seditious intention.” “Saying there is no list of banned books or that the red lines are unclear – I think that is a form of soft resistance,” Kan said. The term “soft resistance” was first mentioned in 2021 in a speech by Luo Huining, then-director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong. Since then, Hong Kong officials have cited “soft resistance” as a threat to national security, although they have not provided a clear definition of the term . Hong Kong independent bookstore Have a Nice Stay, on August 30, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Security chief Chris Tang on Monday said soft resistance was the “most malicious” threat to national security in the city. ‘We actually read the books’ The July bookstore raids , which followed the arrests of other independent bookstore operators in June, came a day after one of the businesses targeted, Have a Nice Stay, announced its imminent closure . In its closing announcement, the bookstore cited financial difficulties and “unclear red lines,” adding that authorities have never specified which books can and cannot be legally sold in the city. “We’ve taken it one step further than bookstore owners and their staff – we actually read the books,” Kan said in the interview. Before bookstores consider selling a book, they should read it or seek legal advice, Kan said. Otherwise, they should simply decide not to sell it. A woman is escorted away from ‘Have a Nice Stay’ independent bookstore by Hong Kong police on July 15, 2026. Her t-shirt reads: “I am staff of a bookstore.” Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “If we release a list of banned books now, and a new illegal title is released the next day, people will question why arrests were made if it wasn’t on the list,” Kan said in the interview. Before deciding to undertake enforcement actions, the police will consult the Department of Justice to ask if it suspects the book’s content violates national security legislation, Kan said. Conservative Christian NGO The Society for Truth and Light said after the raids in July that the government’s refusal to release a list of banned books amounts to an “abuse of power” and undermines the rule of law. It was the only civil society organisation in Hong Kong to speak out against the raids. Kelvin Kong has been sworn in as the head of the Department for Safeguarding National Security, replacing Kan as he goes into retirement.

title: The Deferential President
summary: T he 747 slowly wheeled to a stop last night on the tarmac of Joint Base Andrews, just outside Washington. Portable stairs were put in position, while a red carpet was unfurled and lined by both American and Chinese soldiers in dress unifor
content: T he 747 slowly wheeled to a stop last night on the tarmac of Joint Base Andrews, just outside Washington. Portable stairs were put in position, while a red carpet was unfurled and lined by both American and Chinese soldiers in dress uniforms. After a few minutes, Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared at the aircraft door. He paused and waved. Waiting below, staring up expectantly, was President Trump. It was a remarkable act of deference. By tradition, American presidents don’t make the 12-mile trip to the base to greet a foreign leader. They instead wait at the White House, backed by the grandeur and power of the executive mansion. But not this time. Xi did not display the same level of hospitality when Trump visited Beijing in May, and the U.S. president’s gesture suggested that he will take a conciliatory role during the closely watched summit between the leaders of the world’s foremost superpowers. Trump is not expected to push Xi on core issues, including the pace of artificial-intelligence development, Taiwan’s defense, and China’s support for Iran in its war with the United States. It was not that long ago when Trump, a self-styled international bully, could credibly claim to “ run the country and the world .” But he seems far smaller on the global stage now. His speech this week to the United Nations General Assembly, usually a signature moment on any president’s foreign-policy calendar, generated few headlines other than those about his threat to “annihilate” Iran. But even that bluster felt familiar and tired; Trump is stuck in a war he is desperate to leave, and leaders in Tehran seem to believe that he doesn’t have the political will—or the defensive munitions—to authorize a full-fledged return to the conflict. His trade war with traditional U.S. allies has pushed those nations away, leaving them to seek deals and make alliances that cut out Washington. His years-long campaign to commandeer Greenland for the United States ended with little to show for it. He can’t bring the war in Ukraine to an end. Trump’s foreign policy has never been all that coherent, his isolationism haphazardly mixed with spasms of military intervention. But now his erratic behavior—his threats and bluffs, his emphasis on making money over spreading democracy—has left the United States in retreat from the rest of the world. “Trump has dramatically accelerated the arrival of what can be described as a post-American world,” Richard Haass, who worked in four presidential administrations and then led the Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “He’s reduced U.S. influence by not standing up to our foes or standing with our allies.” T he height of Trump’s power might have been earlier this year on January 3. It was then, under the cover of darkness, that U.S. Special Forces stole into Venezuela and seized the nation’s leader, Nicolás Maduro; by day’s end, Maduro was in a grim detention center in Brooklyn. Trump had deposed a leader who defied him and, later, would get control of much of Venezuela’s oil. An unspoken message went out to other nations: Don’t cross me. You could be next. Trump turned his attention to Greenland, to Cuba, to Canada. The U.S. military seemed capable of anything. Unfortunately for Trump, he also believed that illusion. Not even two months later, he did what his predecessors had avoided and launched a full-on war with Iran. Teaming with Israel, the U.S. decapitated Tehran’s leadership and smashed much of its military. But the conflict soon bogged down. Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz . Energy prices soared. The Pentagon’s bombing campaign lost its effectiveness. Defensive munitions ran low. American bases were hit. Trump alternated among making apocalyptic threats, promising that negotiations had peace close at hand, and declaring that, actually, the war had already been won. (He sometimes did more than one in the span of the same day.) But none of it was true. [ Read: The makings of a prewar world ] The debacle in Iran, which is poised to drag down Republicans in the upcoming midterms, underscored some hard truths about America’s new standing in the world. Since beginning his second term, Trump’s message to most other nations, including longtime friends, was that they were largely on their own. He left the bulk of Ukraine’s defense to Europe while he and his negotiators continued to sweet-talk Russia. He alienated allies by launching trade wars. He warned of further military intervention in his own hemisphere. He happily accepted gifts and business investments from Gulf states, only to ignore their pleas to not attack Iran. He allowed Elon Musk’s DOGE to slash foreign aid and other U.S. soft-power programs around the globe. Nearly everywhere, America’s influence is shrinking. T his week offered a chance for a reset. For decades, presidents have traveled to New York in mid-September to address the General Assembly, huddle with world leaders and really, really snarl Manhattan traffic. In 2017, Trump shocked those gathered by threatening to wipe out North Korea because Kim Jong Un was “on a suicide mission.” The next year, dignitaries and heads of state burst out laughing when Trump claimed that his administration was one of the most successful in U.S. history. Last year, following his return to office, he angrily decreed that European migration policies and efforts to combat climate change meant that its “countries are going to hell.” Those speeches were at least memorable. This one zipped by nearly without a trace. It was short by Trump’s standards—not even 40 minutes—and included a call to rebrand “artificial intelligence” as “super intelligence.” Much of the audience sat in silence. His meetings afterwards, even with the leaders of Ukraine and Venezuela, generated few headlines. The president touted a new security agreement for more U.S. involvement with Greenland that, upon closer review, didn’t change much from the status quo and was far short of Trump’s original demand for total U.S. control. Perhaps contributing to the day’s forgettable nature: Other than for the speech, there was limited video footage because the networks boycotted the trip after Trump banned three media outlets from the White House, including the trip’s scheduled TV pooler, CNN. [ Read: The Greenland fiasco stumbles to an end ] But the UN assembly this year was, in essence, an opening act to the summit and state dinner with Xi. The anti-China rhetoric that dominated Trump’s 2016 campaign is but a distant memory; in hopes of securing a massive trade deal, he has courted his Chinese counterpart and bragged about their friendship. White House aides have offered few goals for the summit, other than to note that a number of tech leaders have been invited to the White House. Some issues may be downplayed, or ignored entirely, in an effort to continue to cozy up to Xi . Though lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have urged the president to partner with China to create AI guardrails, Trump has instead vowed to let the technology grow unchecked—in part because it is propping up the stock market and much of the U.S. economy (at most, a White House aide told me, there would be some sort of broad-strokes agreement to try to avert an AI-fueled apocalypse). He has not ruled out halting weapons shipments to Taiwan, a request high on Xi’s wish list. And Trump has shown no inclination to scold China for sending Iran supplies and intelligence. Tonight, he will extend the pageantry further and throw a glitzy state dinner for the Chinese president. Trump’s trip to Andrews last night underscored the lengths to which he is willing to go to flatter Xi; there have been only a handful of times when a president has greeted a visiting leader at the base—among them, a pair of pontiffs (the most recent was President Obama greeting Pope Francis in 2015) and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, who was welcomed by President Dwight Eisenhower at the height of the Cold War. This time, both the United States and China's anthems were played, and a cannon sounded. Xi glanced above as a pair of B-1 bombers flew overhead. Trump winced at the noise.

title: China’s Recent J-36 Heavy Stealth Tactical Jet Testing Offers New Insights Into Its Evolving Design
summary: China’s Chengdu Aircraft Corporation continues to press ahead with the development of its ‘J-36’ next-generation tailless heavy tactical jet . Recent flight testing has offered interesting new views of the still-evolving stealthy design fro
content: China’s Chengdu Aircraft Corporation continues to press ahead with the development of its ‘J-36’ next-generation tailless heavy tactical jet . Recent flight testing has offered interesting new views of the still-evolving stealthy design from the top and behind, prompting discussion about the aircraft’s features. There has also been talk recently about whether the jet might receive a laser directed-energy weapon at some point in the future. The J-36 first broke cover , along with another next-generation tailless tactical jet design generally referred to as the J-XDS , back in December of 2024 . There are understood to be at least four, and possibly five, J-36 prototypes flying now. A number of significant changes between prototypes have already been observed over the past two years, as you can read more about here . The most recent video of a J-36 test flight, seen in the social media post below, began circulating online yesterday. The footage shows the aircraft coming in to land, providing good general views of the uniquely three-engined jet with its two-seat, side-by-side cockpit configuration, especially from the rear aspect. What is seen underscores a previously observed total revision of the exhausts from a trough style to a two-dimensional thrust-vectoring configuration akin to what is found on the U.S. F-22 Raptor. This and other significant changes to the design, including the addition of divertless supersonic intakes (DSIs) all around, not just on top, first emerged last year . The clip also offers a good reminder of just how wide the aircraft is overall. Obviously one of the best video recordings of the J-36 so far seen during landing approach … But can anyone read the number under the cockpit? https://t.co/cmQ0AkdsdO — @Rupprecht_A (@RupprechtDeino) September 22, 2026 As this particular J-36 passes by, it can be seen to have a lighter-colored radome, as well as at least one relatively large lighter-colored section on top of the dorsal air intake. A similarly colored radome was first spotted on what is said to be the fourth prototype back in July. This coloring could point to the installation of actual radar in the aircraft’s nose. In TWZ ‘s first in-depth analysis of the J-36 back in 2024, we assessed that the jet’s very broad radome area could house an absolutely massive primary array. The lighter section on top of the fuselage could be an aperture for a conformal antenna tied to a beyond-line-of-sight communications and data-sharing suite. In 2024, we posited that the heavyweight J-36 could serve as an intelligence-gathering and communications relay platform in addition to performing tasks more typically associated with tactical combat jets. Reliable and multi-faceted connectivity would be key for employing the J-36 as an airborne controller for advanced air combat drones , as well. Captures from the video above highlighting the lighter-colored radome and section on top of the center of the fuselage. Chinese internet captures via X Another J-36 flight testing video that emerged on Monday, seen below, offers an additional view of the top of the jet, showing multiple lighter-colored sections that would appear to be additional conformal apertures for various antennas. There is a lighter-colored rectangular outline painted around part of the intake on top of the center of the fuselage, as well. The jet’s full paint scheme includes lighter-colored leading and trailing edges, which are critical structures on low-observable (stealthy) designs that often contain additional antenna arrays. Overall, the two-tone coloring is very much in line with what is seen on operational J-20 fighters in Chinese service today. The original J-36 prototype, at least, has notably worn a splinter-type camouflage paint scheme . China's J-36 sixth-gen fighter asserting its dominance in the sky. My prediction, the J-36 will gain initial operational capability before the American F-47 take its maiden flight. pic.twitter.com/SLmjqZ76Aw — Zhao DaShuai 东北进修 (@zhao_dashuai) September 21, 2026 A stock shot of a J-20 fighter with its two-tone scheme. PLAAF A view of the first J-36 prototype with its splinter-type camouflage scheme. Chinese internet via X Whether or not the two recent video clips show the same J-36 prototype is unclear. The possibility has now been raised that Chengdu may be using a single serial number (36011) on at least some of the J-36 prototypes , a decision that could have been made for counter-intelligence and/or deliberate misinformation/disinformation purposes. Much still remains unknown about the current or expected future capabilities of the J-36. Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) did have a placard at its booth at the 14th China International Defence Electronics Exhibition earlier this month that has prompted questions about whether the jet could be equipped with a laser directed-energy weapon. Chengdu falls under the umbrella of AVIC, which is a state-run enterprise. The Chinese-language placard in question describes a “laser weapon tracking system” with a power rating of “*00” kilowatts and a weight of “less than” 837.7 pounds (380 kilograms), per a machine translation. The way the power rating is written appears to mean that it is in the hundreds of kilowatts, which would put it firmly in a class capable of doing physical damage to objects, such as incoming missiles and drones. Furthermore, an associated graphic shows a turreted system and a computer-generated rendering of a J-36 projecting a beam. The render appears to be from a video that depicts a J-36 using a laser to destroy other aircraft. Another computer-generated video that shows a J-36 using retractable lasers to shoot down incoming missiles has been circulating online since at least last year . AVIC showed this at the 14th China International Defence Electronics Exhibition earlier this month. Chinese internet via X This appears to be a screenshot from this video, via rednote user @阿中CN. https://t.co/NX1zDOLw2v pic.twitter.com/673Zl41MM1 — 笑脸男人 (@lfx160219) September 17, 2026 It is not immediately clear how official either of the clips depicting laser-armed J-36s might be, or whether they at all reflect real planned capabilities. The full placard presented at the China International Defence Electronics Exhibition, as seen in the video below, shows a variety of different laser systems, and not just for aerial applications. AVIC has confirmed that the J-36 fighter jet is equipped with a laser defense system. pic.twitter.com/4PrSqAfOQK — Modern War Explained (@FPDefenseNews) September 17, 2026 The fielding of operational laser directed-energy weapons capable of inflicting any real physical damage has historically proven to be very challenging , and even more so within the size, power-generation, and cooling constraints presented by modern combat jets. As an example, the U.S. Air Force spent roughly a decade working on a podded laser weapon system that tactical jets could use to swat down incoming missiles under its Self-protect High Energy Laser Demonstrator (SHiELD) program . In 2024, the service confirmed SHiELD had “concluded” without achieving its goal of an actual flight test. That same year, the Air Force cancelled plans to test a laser weapon system on an AC-130 gunship. Despite important U.S. strides more recently when it comes to fielding ground-based and naval laser weapon systems , “there’s nothing that’s on the shelf right now that we are ready to put onto an airplane,” U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Douglas Wickert, the commander of the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL), told TWZ and other outlets just last week at a roundtable at the Air & Space Forces Association’s (AFA) 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Tuesday. “The solid-state lasers and the power density and the different ways that you actually – there’s actually a lot of secret sauce in that. How do you make the beam, and how do you form the beam, and how do you pulse the beam, and all that’s in development.” ‘There’s development of the laser itself, but now the power and thermal management system has progressed so much that we can provide the power needed,” Dr. Michael Gregg, head of AFRL’s Air Warfare Directorate, said at the same roundtable. “We’ve also had new designs and engines that we know have the power … to direct that power in certain areas. So, from a system perspective, it’s much more feasible because everything has matured over the last decade.” A rendering of a US Air Force F-16 fighter with a podded laser directed-energy weapon. Lockheed Martin A rendering of a US Air Force F-16C Viper fighter with a podded laser directed energy weapon. Lockheed Martin China has certainly made substantial investments of its own in laser and other directed-energy weapon capabilities across domains in recent years , and this is clearly an area of interest for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), in general. When it comes to the J-36 specifically, TWZ has explicitly highlighted in the past how the three-engine configuration could be particularly useful for producing sufficient power to support a host of advanced and electricity-hungry sensors and other capabilities, including directed energy weapons. Larger questions remain about the exact set of roles the J-36 is expected to fill, as well. The basic design is certainly optimized for straight-line performance, combat radius, and payload rather than maneuverability and agility. The jet has already caused a significant amount of debate just when it comes to taxonomy, as it does not seem to fit inside traditional definitions of ‘fighters’ and ‘bombers,’ something we have explored in detail previously . A composite of other views of the J-36 that have emerged since 2024. Chinese Internet via X “According to Yang Wei – chief designer of the J-20 –, the new [J-36] fighter can penetrate heavily defended airspace that the J-20 and comparable F-22s or F-35s must avoid, placing it a generation ahead,” Andreas Rupprecht, an analyst specializing in Chinese military aviation and TWZ contributor , wrote in a post on LinkedIn last week. “With lower RCS [radar cross section], high speed, and the capacity to control more drones, it could act as a node and command center for systems including J-20s and, especially, unmanned aircraft, while attacking high-value targets from stand-off range with long-range weapons.” “The type could therefore represent a new class of ‘fighter,'” he added. “Online terms include ‘theater-level deep-penetration command combat aircraft’ and ‘high-performance fighter,’ analogous to a cruiser ranking above a destroyer within the Navy. Recent evidence gives this theory new weight and warrants continued monitoring.” The J-36, as well as the J-XDS, reflect a larger burst of next-generation air combat developments in China in recent years. This includes an array of new crewed and uncrewed aircraft designed for operations from bases on land , as well as from the PLA Navy’s (PLAN) growing fleet of aircraft carriers and big-deck amphibious assault ships . The Chinese aviation industry’s development of a growing array of flying-wing uncrewed aircraft , some of which are very large , has been particularly notable. In turn, there is something of an emerging gap between these developments and the pace at which the U.S. military is moving along similar lines, at least publicly. Boeing’s sixth-generation F-47 for the U.S. Air Force is not expected to take to the skies for the first time until 2028, though preceding demonstrator designs have been flying for years already . The U.S. Navy still has yet to officially announce a winner of its F/A-XX next-generation carrier-based fighter competition, and the current timeline for that program producing an operational aircraft is unclear. A rendering the US Air Force has released of the F-47. USAF As an aside, based on what has emerged publicly to date, there are signs that the F-47 may reflect a distinctly different design philosophy that puts greater emphasis on maneuverability compared to the J-36, and even likely the J-XDS. As mentioned, the J-36 certainly seems much more focused on payload, range, and level flight performance. In July, TWZ published a deep dive exploring why the U.S. Air Force would pursue a sixth-generation fighter with rear-swept wings, canards, and other features despite steady trends in the opposite direction visible in Chinese designs and ones elsewhere globally. Regardless, U.S. officials have downplayed questions about China’s gaining ground in the air combat arena, or even surging into the lead in certain areas, in the past . “Chinese sixth-generation aircraft are in the nascent stages of development and expected to be operational by 2035,” the Pentagon wrote in its most recent annual report on military and security developments in China, which was published in December 2025. In the meantime, the J-36’s design is already steadily being refined, and the total fleet of prototypes has been growing, offering new insights into the aircraft’s expected capabilities and roles. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post China’s Recent J-36 Heavy Stealth Tactical Jet Testing Offers New Insights Into Its Evolving Design appeared first on TWZ .

title: 澳大利亚禁止了这些中国监控摄像头，如今它们却出现在电动汽车上。
summary: 《四角》节目为 Leapmotor 汽车在堪培拉进行试驾。（《四角》：Ron Foley） 就在数百台中国 CCTV 摄像头因监控担忧被从联邦政府大楼移除仅一年后，来自同一公司的摄像头却通过一款新型电动汽车重新回到了澳大利亚。 2023 年，Dahua Technology 制造的摄像头从联邦大楼和国防基地被移除，这一事件引发了大量头条新闻。 不太为人所知的是，随着这家监控公司在全球范围内受到制裁，它已经转向了汽车制造。 Leapmotor 品牌于 2024 年进入澳大利亚市
content: 《四角》节目为 Leapmotor 汽车在堪培拉进行试驾。（《四角》：Ron Foley） 就在数百台中国 CCTV 摄像头因监控担忧被从联邦政府大楼移除仅一年后，来自同一公司的摄像头却通过一款新型电动汽车重新回到了澳大利亚。 2023 年，Dahua Technology 制造的摄像头从联邦大楼和国防基地被移除，这一事件引发了大量头条新闻。 不太为人所知的是，随着这家监控公司在全球范围内受到制裁，它已经转向了汽车制造。 Leapmotor 品牌于 2024 年进入澳大利亚市场，作为市场上最实惠的电动汽车之一进行竞争。 另一个卖点是其技术，包括一套摄像头系统。 在 Leapmotor C10 车型中，配备了六台摄像头，可提供车辆周围和内部 360 度的视野。 其中一些摄像头由 Dahua 制造，但这并不能阻止车辆被开进某些国防基地或停放在附近。 与许多电动汽车一样，Leapmotor 的汽车的摄像头可以捕捉其周围的所有景象。（《四角》） 前国家网络安全顾问 Alastair MacGibbon 表示，电动汽车和某些联网汽车上的麦克风和摄像头使其成为理想的监控设备。 他说，一辆战略性停放在政府大楼附近的电动汽车可以记录员工进出，并绘制人们的工作时间。 "甚至可以根据员工模式的变化来确定发生了什么重要事情，"他说。 "是否有人员值守的值班室突然在某个危机发生或政府扩大行动的时间段出现？" "[这] 建立了一个细粒度的视频和电子知识网络，当将其全部纳入时，几乎是澳大利亚近乎完美的实时画面。" Alastair MacGibbon 表示，与中国有联系的车辆应被禁止进入军事基地。（《四角》：Ron Foley） 8 月的一天，《四角》节目访问了堪培拉的一个公共停车场，该停车场位于 ASIO（澳大利亚国家安全局）、国防部（Department of Defence）和澳大利亚信号局（澳大利亚的数字间谍机构）总部之间。 那里停着 22 辆电动汽车——其中近一半是中国品牌。 军事基地上的中国电动汽车 对中国电动汽车被用作实时监控设备的担忧，导致它们在国外被禁止进入军事基地。 去年在英国，中国电动汽车甚至带有中国组件的车辆被禁止进入一些敏感地点和训练基地。 在其中一个案例中，军方要求它们将车辆停放在 3 公里以外。 内政部长 Tony Burke 表示，澳大利亚已有一些规定。 "我知道有人驾驶不同类型的联网车辆进入，却被要求将车辆停放在很远的地方，"他说。 "所以，事实是，澳大利亚没有全面禁令，并不意味着没有采取大量预防措施。" 国防部拒绝说明联网车辆的具体限制。 像英国一样，中国对外国电动汽车持谨慎态度，特别是那些属于其战略竞争对手的电动汽车。 2021 年，中国禁止特斯拉（即使是上海工厂生产的）进入政治区域和某些国防基地。 "我认为这是我们应该关注的最具说明性的数据点之一，"反对派国防发言人 James Paterson 说。 "如果 [中国] 认为在其国内有风险，那么我们应该如何对待他们在此制造和运营的产品？" 《四角》节目驾驶一辆 Leapmotor 汽车在堪培拉进行试驾。 我们驾驶汽车穿过皇家军事学院（Duntroon），经过 ASIO 总部，并环绕 Russell 国防区。 《四角》节目驾驶 Leapmotor 前往皇家军事学院 Duntroon。（《四角》：Ron Foley） "当涉及到与中国有联系的车辆时，它们应被禁止进入任何军事基地、任何情报设施或任何其他类型的敏感地点和关键基础设施，"MacGibbon 先生说。 Paterson 参议员，前议会安全与情报委员会主席表示，安全机构对中国 Dahua 摄像头如此担忧，以至于他们甚至移除了那些未连接互联网的摄像头。 "让我感到不可思议的是，我们从国防基地拆除了许多 Dahua 摄像头……但我们却允许相同的技术在联网车辆中行驶，带着它们所有的摄像头、传感器和数据收集功能，"他说。 Leapmotor 在澳大利亚销售三款型号，此前曾表示其雄心是成为"汽车界的华为"。 根据向香港交易所提交的文件，Leapmotor 与一家 Dahua 子公司有持续的采购合同，该子公司同意向汽车公司供应摄像头、传感器和雷达。 《四角》节目购买了一台 Leapmotor 后摄像头，其标签上带有 Dahua 标识符（DH）。 Leapmotor 的摄像头。（《四角》：Nick Wiggins） 中国的"大规模电子监控" 虽然所有联网车辆都存在风险，但鉴于北京在境外监控和黑客攻击方面的记录，中国电动汽车被视为更具风险。 此外，其国家安全法可以要求中国公司在被要求时配合当局。 "我认为大多数人会认识到这是一个监控国家，……它表现出对大规模电子监控的兴趣，不仅在中国国内，而且在国外，"MacGibbon 先生说。 "我们真正谈论的是由这些车辆的聚合数量引起的国家安全问题，数十万辆这样的车辆，并且很快将成为澳大利亚销售的占主导地位的车辆类型。" 摄像头被移除一年后，Dahua 开始在澳大利亚销售 Leapmotor 电动汽车。（《四角》：Ron Foley） 现代电动汽车由软件驱动，该软件可远程控制和更新。 人们担心，该软件可以在车主不知情的情况下被用来开启汽车中的麦克风或摄像头。 "[中国] 不需要黑客攻击这些车辆将其变成监听设备或监控设备……这是车辆的一个功能，"MacGibbon 先生说。 Leapmotor 未对《四角》节目的提问做出回应。

title: Ex-husband, in-laws accused of murdering Hong Kong model Abby Choi appear in court
summary: The ex-husband and in-laws accused of murdering Hong Kong model and influencer Abby Choi appeared in court on Wednesday, in a gruesome case that has sent shockwaves through the city. Abby Choi in 2022. Photo: Abby Choi, via Instagram. Choi,
content: The ex-husband and in-laws accused of murdering Hong Kong model and influencer Abby Choi appeared in court on Wednesday, in a gruesome case that has sent shockwaves through the city. Abby Choi in 2022. Photo: Abby Choi, via Instagram. Choi, an influencer with more than 140,000 followers on Instagram, had shared photos from Paris Fashion Week just days before she was killed in 2023. Police discovered parts of the 28-year-old’s dismembered body at a house in suburban Hong Kong. Her death was widely reported in the city, where violent crime is relatively rare. Alex Kwong, his father Kwong Kau and brother Anthony Kwong pleaded not guilty to murder charges, judge Brian Keith told a nine-person jury on Wednesday. The three defendants, who face life in prison if found guilty, appeared calm as they attended the hearing. They are also accused of preventing the lawful burial of a body, with two of them, Alex and Anthony Kwong, pleading guilty. Choi had two children with Alex Kwong, but later divorced him and married Chris Tam, with whom she had two more children. Property dispute Prosecutors told the court on Wednesday that Choi and her ex-husband’s family had financial disputes over a luxury property she had bought for them. They said they believed Choi had decided to register the property under the name of her former father-in-law years ago to avoid paying higher taxes. Prosecution lawyer Charlotte Draycott told the court that Choi’s relationship with the Kwong family began to deteriorate in 2022 after she tried to sell the luxury flat, for which she had paid HK$60 million ($7.65 million). Kadooria, the luxury property in Ho Man Tin that Abby Choi reportedly bought. Photo: Google Maps. Prosecutors said Kwong Kau, a 68-year-old retired police sergeant, had become “extremely resentful and angry” over the attempt to sell the flat. They said he decided to kill Choi because he wanted to keep the flat and that he and his sons decided to work together. “We say three of them decided they would do it together,” said Draycott, adding that each of them “played a part” in Choi’s death and burying her body in a suburban house. The trial, which adjourned until Friday, is expected to last until December.

title: The Case for Talking to China Is Not a Case for Détente
source: 芝加哥全球事务委员会
summary: The Case for Talking to China Is Not a Case for Détente ccolon Mon, 09/28/2026 - 12:21 This article was originally published by the Financial Times . This week’s US-China summit was long on symbolism and short on substance. No big deals or
content: The Case for Talking to China Is Not a Case for Détente ccolon Mon, 09/28/2026 - 12:21 This article was originally published by the Financial Times . This week’s US-China summit was long on symbolism and short on substance. No big deals or grand bargains were reached, let alone discrete deliverables. That reflects both Donald Trump’s aversion to preparation and the economic stalemate following the 2025 trade war.  Yet this summit should not be dismissed as mere spectacle. Trump hosting Xi Jinping at the White House matters. And regular leader meetings, possibly two more at multilateral gatherings this year, keep the trade truce alive and the lines of communication open.  That is needed today. Global politics is in a strategic interregnum, moving on from the era of US dominance and a rules-based order. But to what? With two regional wars raging, the range of possible geopolitical outcomes is wider today than perhaps in any period since the 1920s. What is not uncertain is the centrality of the US-China relationship.  Washington and Beijing are in the early days of a long-term competition whose terms and boundaries are still being set. As such, more communication is better than less. Summit diplomacy, properly handled, can reduce misperception, encourage restraint, narrow differences and foster co-operation. This is desperately needed in a relationship whose list of problems, from AI to Taiwan, is expanding.  This week’s summit addressed few of these issues, but it at least bought both sides more time and stability. But the case for talking is not a case for détente: a stable arrangement based on shared strategic interests. Summits are not cost-free; they allow China to play for time and project an image of comity, if not accommodation. Time and stability are only valuable if used well.  With summits like this, Washington risks sending signals that embolden Beijing rather than deter it. This is especially true on issues like Taiwan and Japan, where Trump appears receptive to Xi’s calls for restraint. US-China relations work best with clear, consistent and credible communication about American interests, backed by leverage. But Trump has his own view of US interests: criticising allies while embracing China.  Advocates of détente misunderstand both the state of US-China relations today and Xi’s global aspirations. Ties between the two countries today rest on a fragile truce, agreed in autumn 2025 to pause the trade war. It is underpinned by mutual economic vulnerability: both can inflict serious damage on the other. Washington and Beijing both value the stability of a truce, but both are racing to reduce their vulnerability and increase their leverage. For China that means reducing exposure to US tariffs and technology controls; for the US, reducing dependence on rare earths and magnets.  Some now argue that this mutual economic vulnerability can do for Washington and Beijing what nuclear deterrence did in the cold war. That would be a dangerous mistake.    The inherent instability of the cold war’s mutually assured destruction (MAD) is often forgotten. Washington and Moscow constantly tried to escape MAD, often with risky military operations. Nuclear vulnerability was hard to escape. Economic vulnerability is far less so. Today’s stalemate—built on narrow economic vulnerabilities—is not an equilibrium. It is a race, and summits set its pace, but aren’t a finish line.   Today’s bilateral bargaining is also lopsided. China’s actions, such as pauses on export controls and soyabean purchases, can be reversed overnight. American concessions on technology cannot. China’s economic challenges explain why Xi wants calm now, but that is a reason to buy time, not to settle.  Meanwhile, strategic competition persists. Both sides are putting each other’s companies on control lists and denying access to critical technologies. China’s military coercion in Asia is intensifying, as is its support for Russia’s war in Ukraine and for Iran. No one knows where the boundaries are, until they are crossed. The summit clarified none of this and, worryingly, projected the image of a US-China “G2” condominium. That image matters all over the world but especially in Asia. Coexistence in the cold war rested not on summits and restraint alone, but on alliances and military capabilities. Détente without credible deterrence is not the basis for coexistence; instead, it invites miscalculation and instability. Trump’s affinity for Xi and dealmaking with China are also at odds with hawks in his own administration and Congress, undermining its political sustainability at home and credibility abroad.   Xi believes the US is accelerating its own decline but remains dangerous because it could lash out on the way down. His plan is not to confront Washington but to accumulate power and influence until a transition becomes inevitable. Xi needs time to make China less reliant on others and others more reliant on it, beginning with the US.  So, the real question arising from the summit is who will make better use of the breathing room it has created. Washington should use it to build alternative supply chains, align export controls with partners, rebuild its force posture, reassure Taipei, Tokyo and Manila, and insist on crisis communications that work. If Washington treats the summit as an achievement in and of itself rather than an opportunity to do more, then it has already lost the competition. September 28, 2026 Evan Medeiros China US Foreign Policy Julia Demaree / AP The Chicago Council on Global Affairs is an independent, nonpartisan organization and does not take institutional positions. The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author. About the Author Evan Medeiros Penner Family Chair in Asia Studies, Georgetown University; Former Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for Asia, National Security Council; Distinguished Nonresident Fellow, China, Chicago Council on Global Affairs Evan S. Medeiros is Distinguished Nonresident Fellow on China at the Council and also a professor and director of Asian Studies at Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service. He served for six years on the staff of the National Security Council from 2009-2015, working on Asian affairs. Reviewer ccolon

title: Gov’t refutes animal activist’s claims over stray dog culling following fatal mauling
summary: Hong Kong authorities have dismissed an animal rights activist’s claims that captured stray dogs will be subject to “convenience culling,” as eight unattended canines from Yuen Long were caught in a joint operation following a fatal mauling
content: Hong Kong authorities have dismissed an animal rights activist’s claims that captured stray dogs will be subject to “convenience culling,” as eight unattended canines from Yuen Long were caught in a joint operation following a fatal mauling incident last week. Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department personnel carrying out an operation to capture stray dogs in Yuen Long on September 21, 2026. Photo: Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said on Thursday that a five-day operation jointly conducted with the police had captured eight stray dogs in Yuen Long. Among them, three were microchipped but their licences had expired, the department said. The operation was launched in response to a suspected dog attack in Yuen Long that killed a 27-year-old woman, who suffered lacerations to her head, neck, arms and legs. Last month, a 33-year-old woman was also found dead at a licensed animal shelter in Ta Kwu Ling after being mauled by a canine. The AFCD said a frontline staff member sustained a dog bite to the hand during the operation on Wednesday, and remained in a stable condition under treatment in hospital. One registered keeper has been charged with failing to hold a valid dog licence and failing to keep their dog under proper control in public, the AFCD said. That keeper was reportedly animal rights activist Kent Luk, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter. Luk earlier told a radio programme that he is the registered keeper for close to 4,000 canines, mostly stray dogs his group has rescued on the streets. ‘Statutory timeframe’ The AFCD on Thursday also refuted Luk’s claim that captured stray dogs will be culled four days after capture. Luk made the claim during the radio programme, urging authorities against “convenient culling.” He said only animals suffering from serious disease should be put down and urged the government to review the city’s Rabies Ordinance. Dogs in Yuen Long on September 22, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “The four-day period stipulated by law is simply the statutory timeframe required for the AFCD to make enquiries and locate the keepers,” the department said in a statement on Thursday. Captured dogs will be scanned for microchips and verified for licences, and their registered keepers will be contacted, the AFCD said. Dogs whose keepers cannot be traced will be kept under observation at Animal Management Centres, it added. “Dogs that are in good health and have a gentle temperament will be transferred to the AFCD’s partner animal welfare organisations for sterilisation and rehoming. The AFCD will not release dogs without keepers back into the community so as to avoid posing public safety risks,” the department said. It can take weeks, even months, for dogs to be transferred to partner organisations, depending on the animals’ health, temperament, and the capacity of the receiving organisation, the AFCD said. Dogs in Hong Kong. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The AFCD also said that, even after being neutered, ownerless dogs can still pose risks to public safety in a high-density urban environment like Hong Kong. Animal welfare activists like Luk have advocated for a “TNR” strategy – trap, neuter, and release – to manage stray animals in the city. However, the AFCD said that registered dog owners must fulfil the commitment of taking care of the animal for life, and that abandoning a dog is an offence. Authorities are considering heavier fines for pet abandonment following a string of suspected dog attacks in the city. See also: ‘Deed, not breed’: Owners and experts push back on stigma against ‘fighting dogs’ Last month, a large dog – reportedly a Spanish mastiff – killed two smaller pet dogs in separate incidents in Yuen Long. Dog owners and professionals have said that aggression in dogs could be a result of the animals’ early experience, socialisation, the environment, and the misunderstanding of humans.

title: The Makings of a Prewar World
summary: Donald Trump offered perhaps the clearest summation yet of his worldview in an otherwise discursive address to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday. Defending the American takeover of Venezuelan oil, he invoked an old maxim: “To th
content: Donald Trump offered perhaps the clearest summation yet of his worldview in an otherwise discursive address to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday. Defending the American takeover of Venezuelan oil, he invoked an old maxim: “To the victor belongs the spoils.” He then presented Iran with a choice between accepting his terms and being driven “into hell with no chance of survival.” These remarks are the latest sign that world politics is entering an era when might makes right. Yet Trump is only one of the leaders driving this rupture from the post–World War II international order. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have also broken the order, although their methods differ profoundly—morally, legally, and otherwise. American policy may change when Trump leaves office in January 2029, but Putin and Xi may remain in power well into the next decade. A new American president will likely not be able to restore the old order or create a better one, even if they want to. Their greatest challenge will be to arrest the slide. International order is a notoriously vague and politically contested concept. Many leaders in the global South, along with Western critics, reject the idea that the United States ever consistently abided by a rules-based system. They point to Western military interventions, double standards, and the unequal distribution of power within international institutions. But the old order’s failures do not mean that its restraints were meaningless. In his first book, A World Restored , Henry Kissinger argued that a stable and legitimate order rests on a limited consensus: an understanding among the major powers about what he called the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy. Governments can compete intensely and violate rules without seeking to overturn the system itself. The danger arises when a major power becomes so dissatisfied with the limits imposed upon it that it adopts a revolutionary foreign policy. [ Vivian Salama: America’s allies are no longer waiting for Trump to leave ] Under the old international order, major powers did not, as a general rule, conquer and annex the territory of their neighbors. The global trading system was based on reciprocity, tariffs were historically low, and markets were relatively open. And, although it was the world’s strongest country, the United States exercised enough self-discipline to allow its allies to grow into genuine partners, not vassals to be constantly squeezed for concessions. Over the past decade, and decisively since the pandemic, that consensus about permissible conduct has collapsed. Putin launched the largest war in Europe since World War II with his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He more than anyone has revived the idea that countries can expand their borders through the use of force. Combined Russian- and Ukrainian-military casualties (those killed, wounded, and missing) have reached approximately 2 million people. European governments have accused Russia of an expanding campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, arson, and drone incursions below the threshold of conventional war. North Korea has intervened directly in this war, and many other nations are indirectly involved—China and Iran on the side of Russia; Europe, the United States (at least under Joe Biden), and Asian democracies on the side of Ukraine. Under Xi, China has broken the global trading system. Xi has used the power of the Chinese state to establish dominance in advanced manufacturing, reduce China’s imports as much as possible, and aggressively grow its exports. The result is that China has enormous excess capacity. Its goods flood into the rest of the world at prices impossible to compete with, leaving other countries to choose between deindustrialization and protectionism. More and more of them are selecting the latter. This policy is not as morally egregious as Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, but it has toppled a key pillar of the international economic order. Since taking office for a second term, in 2025, Trump has turned American power against U.S. allies and partners. He imposed the highest tariffs in nearly a century on Canada, Japan, South Korea, India, and the European Union and used the threat of more to extract hundreds of billions of dollars in investment pledges. He mused about making Canada the 51st state and seizing Greenland. He pushed Ukraine to sign over a share of its mineral wealth in the middle of a war for its national survival. Under Trump, the United States sees itself not as the guarantor of an alliance system of like-minded democracies, but as a dominant power that wields its influence for singular, transactional gain. Trump has broken the restraint that made American primacy tolerable to most of the rest of the world. Reports suggest that he may meet Xi and Putin for a “big three” trilateral on the margins of the Asia Pacific Economic Summit in Shenzhen in November, which could mark the formal end of the old order. The rupture has produced an international environment that feels ever more like that of a prewar period. This does not mean that a major conflict is inevitable. But if one occurs, future historians will not find its causes sudden or mysterious. They are in plain sight. [ Listen: Trump battles against an economy of his making ] The major powers are building up their militaries and racing to master drone warfare and artificial intelligence. Trump’s lack of commitment to alliances, especially in Europe, raises the prospect that an aggressor may calculate that it can act without triggering much of a U.S. reaction. Meanwhile, America’s rivals are more and more aligned as they integrate their military production, share sensitive technology, and assist one another in battle. The shift has generational and psychological drivers. Putin, Xi, and Trump are elderly, sometimes erratic, insulated in information bubbles, and animated by ideological visions of national revival. The moment may feel like a closing window—a now-or-never opportunity to remake the world while they still can. A future American president may promise to build a new and improved international order. But Xi and Putin will have little reason to accept the restraints that Washington wants to restore, and although American allies may welcome a return to a more internationalist U.S. foreign policy, they will harbor doubts that it will survive the next election. Rather than promising what they cannot deliver, aspiring presidents should level with the American people. The international order has come to an end. The next president will inherit one of the most unforgiving international environments since 1945. Their task will be to stop the deterioration, inject some stability into world affairs, and begin to lay the foundation for a better future, even if that is not achievable in the short term.

title: This Is Taiwan’s New 105mm 8×8 Mobile Gun System
summary: Taiwan has provided the first public look at its new 105mm 8×8 mobile gun system in action, with the domestically developed vehicle engaging moving and stationary targets during a live-fire demonstration in southern Taiwan. The vehicle is b
content: Taiwan has provided the first public look at its new 105mm 8×8 mobile gun system in action, with the domestically developed vehicle engaging moving and stationary targets during a live-fire demonstration in southern Taiwan. The vehicle is being developed as Taiwan continues to modernize its ground forces in response to the growing capabilities and increasingly frequent military activity of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) around the island. During the demonstration, held by the Republic of China Army (ROCA) at a training area in Tainan today, the vehicle reportedly engaged a moving target at approximately 0.75 miles and a stationary target at around 0.6 miles. It also fired against targets positioned 90 degrees to the side of the vehicle while operating on a gentle slope, demonstrating the gun system’s ability to engage targets while the vehicle is positioned on uneven terrain. pic.twitter.com/dn6lHDbf5k — 青年日報 Youth Daily News, ROC(Taiwan) (@YDN_NEWS) September 23, 2026 Eight wheels. Six-wheel steering. One 105mm gun. Definitely not your average ride. #ROCArmedForces #MobileGunSystem #MadeInTaiwan pic.twitter.com/oaHsyMNtev — 國防部 Ministry of National Defense, ROC(Taiwan) (@MoNDefense) September 23, 2026 The vehicle subsequently fired its 7.62mm coaxial machine gun simultaneously with its main gun as part of a scenario intended to demonstrate engagement of multiple targets, including simulated amphibious assault vehicles. 台灣105公厘獵豹輪型戰車實彈射擊 https://t.co/cHaXthUCfA pic.twitter.com/aKBBzoVsKz — 新‧二七部隊 軍事雜談 (New 27 Brigade) (@new27brigade) September 23, 2026 An apparent weapon malfunction was also recorded during the demonstration. One of the 105mm rounds initially failed to fire, according to reports . The crew waited approximately two minutes in accordance with safety procedures before reloading the weapon, after which the vehicle fired normally. Maj. Gen. Chen Chien-chung, head of Taiwan’s Arsenal 202, the Production and Manufacturing Center of the Armament Bureau, said an investigation would be conducted into the misfire. The 155 mm infantry fighting vehicle showcased to media before entering production phase. pic.twitter.com/DBhs66aw5Q — Taepodong (@stoa1984) September 23, 2026 Despite the incident, the demonstration provided an important look at a vehicle that Taiwan is developing specifically around the country’s geography and battlefield requirements, including a potential amphibious invasion by the Chinese PLA . A new direct fire support variant of the Clouded Leopard 8×8 infantry fighting vehicle was first publicly displayed at the Taipei Aerospace & Defense Technology Exhibition in 2023. It passed initial combat readiness testing with the ROCA in October 2023, and it was authorized for mass production in April 2024. A pre-production prototype of the Taiwanese 105mm 8×8 mobile gun system. Ministry of National Defense The production configuration has undergone significant changes since then. Its height has been reduced by approximately 12 inches, bringing the overall vehicle height to below 9 feet 10 inches. Its turning radius has also been reduced from 36 feet to 26 feet. The reduction in turning radius was achieved by providing steering to three pairs of wheels, rather than two pairs on the earlier configuration. Those changes are especially relevant to Taiwan, where large sections of the island feature restrictive terrain, dense urban development, narrow roads, drainage channels, and other obstacles that can limit the movement of heavy armored vehicles. Taiwan’s 105mm 8×8 mobile gun system takes part in a live-fire demonstration in Tainan on September 23, 2026. Photo by CHENG Yu-chen / AFP Taiwanese officials specifically highlighted the system’s suitability for culverts and urban areas, as well as the challenging terrain of Hualien and Taitung on the island’s mountainous east coast. The vehicle’s principal weapon is a 105mm gun. The weapon can fire the general-purpose ammunition already developed for tank guns, in addition to ammunition developed specifically for the new system. The ROCA displayed armor-piercing, anti-personnel, and training ammunition during the demonstration. The gun also offers useful ammunition commonality with Taiwan’s older, but sill active M60A3 and CM11 tanks. A Taiwanese soldier inspects an M60A3 tank during an overnight cross-region deployment from Hualien during the annual Han Kuang military exercises in Yilan on August 9, 2026. Photo by Chiang Ying-ying / POOL / AFP That compatibility potentially gives the vehicle access to an existing ammunition ecosystem while allowing Taiwan to develop specialized rounds for its particular requirements. Against a PLA assault , the 105mm system would provide mobile direct firepower against amphibious vehicles, armored personnel carriers, fortifications, and other ground targets, complementing Taiwan’s heavier tanks and other anti-armor weapons. Its wheeled configuration also allows the vehicle to rapidly reposition along Taiwan’s road network, giving commanders a mobile source of direct firepower that could respond to amphibious landings and reinforce threatened sectors. The system falls into the same broad category as other modern 8×8 mobile gun systems, including Italy’s Centauro family and Japan’s Type 16 Mobile Combat Vehicle . Italian soldiers of the 6th Cavalry Regiment, Aosta Mechanized Brigade, observe their sector of fire with a Centauro B1 tank destroyer while conducting a simulated assault during Saber Junction 17 at the Hohenfels Training Area, Germany, May 2017. U.S. Army photo by Pfc. Zachery Perkins Less successful was a mobile gun system version of the U.S. Army Stryker , also with a 105mm gun, but the service divested that in 2021 because of problems with its dated cannon and autoloader. The U.S. Army then received the M10 Booker Combat Vehicle . Armed with a 105mm main gun, the Booker is a tracked vehicle with a much higher degree of armor protection and off-road mobility, but this, too, was canceled in 2025 , amid cost and weight increases. A Stryker Mobile Gun System fires a 105mm round. U.S. Army A wheeled 105mm gun system can provide substantial direct-fire capability while offering advantages in road mobility and potentially lower logistical demands. It also lacks the combination of protection, cross-country mobility, and heavy armament associated with a tracked main battle tank . For Taiwan, this kind of vehicle provides a comparatively compact armored platform able to move rapidly between positions and bring heavy direct firepower to areas where larger vehicles could face mobility constraints. If fighting reaches Taiwan’s cities , the ROCA regularly trains for the challenges of urban warfare . The service has also demonstrated unusual measures to conceal and protect its armored vehicles, including disguising tanks and other vehicles as scrap piles or civilian construction equipment to complicate PLA targeting. Taiwanese personnel get off a subway car in Taipei carrying a Stinger missile during the annual Han Kuang exercise. Military News Agency/Taiwan Ministry of National Defense capture via Focus Taiwan The vehicle’s development is also being influenced by the threat of battlefield drones . Taiwanese military officials say the system is expected to receive additional counter-drone capabilities before entering mass production. One planned modification is an anti-drone cage around the vehicle. More ambitious changes could involve the installation of a larger-caliber automatic weapon. Reportedly, the vehicle could eventually receive another machine gun or larger-caliber automatic cannon, with the 30mm M230 chain gun identified as one possible option. The proposed weapon could use canister-type ammunition designed to disperse numerous fragments against small drones. Adding dedicated counter-drone equipment to the mobile gun system would therefore give the vehicle another role beyond direct engagement of conventional ground targets. Taiwan’s new 105mm mobile gun system during a demonstration in Tainan on September 23, 2026. Photo by CHENG Yu-chen / AFP The prominence of counter-drone measures in the planning of the vehicle also reflects the increasingly contested environment in which Taiwan’s armored forces would have to operate. In a conflict with China, armored units have to operate under the threat of persistent surveillance and attacks from a wide range of uncrewed systems, making concealment, mobility, dispersion, and organic counter-drone capabilities very important to any change of survival. Questioning just how long any armor would last in a full-on invasion scenario is absolutely relevant. As we have seen in Ukraine, the drone threat alone has sidelined even the most capable armor . At the same time, Taiwan is working toward its own drone-heavy battlefield doctrine, part of a broader plan to turn the island into a “hellscape” for any invading force. Overall, the September 23 demonstration offered a useful glimpse into the thinking behind Taiwan’s indigenous armored vehicle program. As part of a wider modernization of ROCA armor, the service has also received 108 M1A2T Abrams tanks, broadly equivalent to the  M1A2 SEPv3  version — or System Enhancement Package version 3 — which you can read more about  here . With production of 178 series examples of the new vehicle scheduled to begin in 2027, Taiwan’s new 105mm mobile gun system is moving toward becoming a significant component of the island’s domestically produced armored fleet. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post This Is Taiwan’s New 105mm 8×8 Mobile Gun System appeared first on TWZ .

title: China says opposes ‘illegal’ US sanctions on Iran airlines
summary: China said on Tuesday it opposed “illegal” US sanctions on Iranian airlines, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened potential measures in a televised interview. An Iran Air Airbus A330-200. Photo: Wikicommons. Bessent told
content: China said on Tuesday it opposed “illegal” US sanctions on Iranian airlines, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened potential measures in a televised interview. An Iran Air Airbus A330-200. Photo: Wikicommons. Bessent told CNBC that “all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world” in a matter of days under the weight of American sanctions, as the Trump administration seeks to ramp up pressure on Tehran. Beijing — a top economic partner and diplomatic backer of Iran — slammed the threats on Tuesday, calling such measures “illegal”. ‘Illegal unilateral sanctions’ “China consistently opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that lack a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news conference. The criticism comes just before US President Donald Trump’s summit starting Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at Zhongnanhai in Beijing on May 15, 2026. Photo: The White House, via Flickr. The United States and Iran have been at war since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a broad offensive. Tehran countered by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for energy transit, causing global oil prices to surge as the conflict spread in the Middle East. ‘Economic D-Day’ The United States imposed sanctions this month on “all remaining Iranian airlines” that had yet to face such penalties. The Treasury Department also took aim at targets for supporting Iran’s aviation sector, including firms based outside Iran. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent at the World Economic Forum in Davos-Klosters, Switzerland, on January 20, 2026. Photo: World Economic Forum, via Flickr. “If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said in the interview. He had previously vowed the United States would declare “economic D-Day” on Iran and pledged to choke off Tehran financially. Bessent’s comments came a day after he met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng for economic talks, laying the groundwork for the meeting between the two countries’ leaders this week.

title: China confirms Xi to visit US this week for Trump talks
summary: China’s leader Xi Jinping will visit the United States this week for talks with President Donald Trump, Beijing confirmed Monday, expressing hope they will strengthen “strategic stability” between the world’s two largest economies. US Presi
content: China’s leader Xi Jinping will visit the United States this week for talks with President Donald Trump, Beijing confirmed Monday, expressing hope they will strengthen “strategic stability” between the world’s two largest economies. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping attend a welcome ceremony at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on May 14, 2026. Photo: The White House, via Flickr. Washington had already made clear that the leaders would meet in a bid to find common ground on trade disputes, artificial intelligence and broader strategic issues including Trump’s war in the Middle East. Xi will make a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, a government statement said. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the two leaders would “have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development”. Beijing would “work with the US to enrich the substance of the relationship of constructive strategic stability between China and the US… (and) properly manage differences”, he added. Trump will personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday before their meetings the following day, a US official confirmed. The US leader was greeted by China’s vice president when he landed in Beijing for his state visit in May. “I’ll be discussing almost everything with him,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday. The simmering trade war between the two countries is a key concern: while both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement. Vice Premier He Lifeng, China’s top negotiator for trade, is in the United States for meetings with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The two discussed creating a communication channel for AI concerns when they met on Sunday. A robot is displayed at the Hong Kong Productivity Council’s AI exhibition in Kowloon Tong on May 21, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Warnings of an AI apocalypse have hung heavy over the upcoming meeting, as both countries race for technological supremacy. “The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries,” Bessent said. Such notifications are for potential “incidents”, or a situation “that rises up to a national security level from AI”, he said. Long shadows Trump’s Iran war casts a long shadow too, as China seeks to avoid US sanctions against countries dealing with Tehran. China is one of Iran’s top economic partners and diplomatic backers, buys much of Tehran’s oil output and has sought to mediate in the war that has entered its seventh month. However, analysts caution that expectations for the Trump-Xi summit are low. “One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year,” former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell told AFP. The threat of military confrontation over Taiwan, the self-ruled island that China claims, looms large as well. Taiwan celebrates National Day on October 10, 2024 with an annual military flypast. Photo: I Chen Lin/Office of the President. In July, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that improving ties between their two countries “requires action” as he issued a warning about Taiwan. Taipei relies heavily on Washington’s support to counter growing pressure from China. In June, Rubio said a massive $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan was “under review”, with Trump calling it a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China. China’s negotiating arsenal includes its dominance in the supply of rare earths, critical materials used for high-tech products that are vital to US manufacturers. Beijing successfully pressured Washington to back down from its sky-high tariffs last year after imposing stringent controls on exports of rare earths.

title: US lawmakers hold hearing on plight of jailed media tycoon Jimmy Lai, as Hong Kong slams ‘hypocrisy’
summary: Hong Kong authorities have condemned US lawmakers for holding a hearing on jailed pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai and colluding with “anti-China and destabilising elements” to demand his release ahead of a planned summit between Chines
content: Hong Kong authorities have condemned US lawmakers for holding a hearing on jailed pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai and colluding with “anti-China and destabilising elements” to demand his release ahead of a planned summit between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. Jimmy Lai in 2020. Photo: HKFP. The government said in a statement on Thursday that it “firmly rejected” members of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), a US government agency that monitors human rights in China. After a hearing with Lai’s son Sebastien on Wednesday, CECC leaders introduced a bill aimed at securing the release of Lai and other “democracy advocates, journalists, former legislators, and civil society leaders” imprisoned in Hong Kong. Claire Lai was also scheduled to testify alongside her brother but pulled out due to a recent cancer diagnosis. “Jimmy Lai was sentenced to an appalling 20-year prison sentence simply for exercising his God-given rights and standing up for the people of Hong Kong,” CECC chair Senator Dan Sullivan said. “He should be released immediately.” Co-chair Representative Chris Smith called Lai’s sentence “unjust, politically motivated [and] an affront to free speech and human dignity.” ‘Nothing to do with freedom of the press’ Lai was sentenced in February to 20 years in jail, following his conviction on foreign collusion and sedition charges under the Beijing-imposed national security law. The 78-year-old was accused of using his newspaper, Apple Daily, to lobby foreign nations to impose sanctions, blockades, or other hostile activities upon China and Hong Kong. He was also accused of inciting hatred against the authorities with op-eds published in the now-shuttered tabloid. “The [Jimmy] Lai Chee-ying case has nothing to do with freedom of the press at all,” the Hong Kong government statement read, adding that “defendants have used journalism as a guise to wantonly create social conflicts, incite social antagonism, incite hatred and glorify violence, bringing harm to our country and Hong Kong.” “These countries and their politicians, including the so-called CECC, display their hypocrisy and double standards by pointing fingers at the HKSAR for our work in safeguarding national security,” it said. Ninety legislators were sworn in for the eighth term of Hong Kong’s Legislative Council on January 1, 2026 as the new term begins on the same day. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. In a separate statement , Hong Kong’s Legislative Council also condemned what a spokesperson called “maliciously provocative political maneuvering and alarmist talk by some politicians.” ‘Humanitarian grounds’ Lai’s son and daughter, Sebastien and Claire Lai, have lobbied Western governments to press for their father’s release, alleging that he is being held in solitary confinement without air conditioning and his health is deteriorating. The CECC and the United Nations have called for Lai’s release on humanitarian grounds, citing his age, health, and the impact of the years he has already spent in detention. The Hong Kong government statement also hit back at these claims, stating that “medical services received by Lai Chee-ying in custody are undoubtedly adequate and comprehensive,” and the Correctional Services Department “has been providing adequate medical attention.” From left: Claire Lai and Sebastien Lai, children of jailed Hong Kong publisher and pro-democracy activist Jimmy Lai, speak during a visit to the office of Agence France-Presse (AFP) in Washington, DC, on December 2, 2025. Photo: Mandel Ngan/AFP. Xi Jinping is due to meet US President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday next week, four months after Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May. Trump said he mentioned Lai’s case during their summit in May, but Xi signalled that Lai’s release was “unlikely.” Freeing Lai is a “tough one for him to do,” the US president said.

title: Planned AI ‘City Brain’ system not meant for surveillance – top Hong Kong official
summary: A planned HK$200 million artificial intelligence (AI) “City Brain” system designed to improve urban management and emergency response is not meant for surveillance, a top Hong Kong official has said. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric
content: A planned HK$200 million artificial intelligence (AI) “City Brain” system designed to improve urban management and emergency response is not meant for surveillance, a top Hong Kong official has said. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan. File photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan addressed privacy concerns about the AI system at a Thursday press conference – one day after Chief Executive John Lee delivered the city’s first Five-Year Plan and the final Policy Address of his term. The city brain “isn’t meant for surveillance,” said Chan, who is heading the task force overseeing the project, to be formed in the fourth quarter of 2026. “It’s just about monitoring traffic and urban conditions , not monitoring individuals, crime, or catching thieves,” Chan said. He added: “In the past, if a water pipe burst was detected, you’d wait for it to burst or get repaired. Now, it’s different. Through the city brain, this data is handed, for instance, to the Transport Department so they can deploy immediately.” The government aims to complete the first stage of the system’s development in the first quarter of 2028. It is expected to take six to nine years before the city brain system reaches full operational capacity. Buses outside department store Sogo in Causeway Bay. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The City Brain software system was pioneered by Chinese tech giant Alibaba in Hangzhou in 2017. Since then, the urban AI has spread to cities throughout the Chinese mainland. It was also later launched in Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur. The platform promises to centralise real-time data from a variety of sources – CCTV cameras, tracking systems, smart sensors, government databases, social media and mobile apps – and then use this information to optimise traffic lights, waste management, and other aspects of urban governance. System integration The digital infrastructure of the Security Bureau’s Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre is scheduled for integration in the first phase. Workers clear up Wong Tai Sin MTR station on September 8, 2023, after Hong Kong was hit by record-breaking rainfall. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The project will also prioritise integrating the Civil Engineering and Development Department’s AI Landslip Warning System, the Drainage Services Department’s AI Flood Monitoring System, the Transport Department’s Real-time Traffic Signal Adjustment System, and the Highways Department’s Flood Early Warning System. The police force will also set up a new “Inter-departmental Major Incident Platform” to centralise real-time data from all units when handling major public incidents.

title: 众院中国问题特设委员会举行听证，讨论以进口管制应对中国产业政策与供应链风险
