content:
美国和台湾官员在美中元首峰会结束后分别强调，美国的对台政策没有改变。唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统星期六(9月26日)证实，他与中国国家主席习近平在白宫会谈时曾谈及台湾，但双方并未在这一议题上花费太多时间。

特朗普的表态受到台湾方面高度关注。在此之前，白宫和北京分别公布的峰会成果文件都没有将台湾列为双方达成的共识或具体成果。不过，中国政府发布的会谈纪要援引习近平的话说，希望美方坚持“反对台独”的立场并“慎重处理台湾问题”。但中方后来公布的成果清单没有将台湾列入其中。

特朗普星期六上午在白宫回答记者提问时证实，台湾的确是会谈议题之一。

“谈了，谈了，”特朗普说。“我们没有花太多时间讨论台湾。他非常了解我对此的感受。”

特朗普没有进一步说明双方谈话的具体内容，也没有透露他向习近平表达了什么立场。

**美方官员强调政策不变**

美国国务院中文发言人贾博(Jakob J. Lengacher)此前接受美国之音(VOA)采访时表示，美国的对台政策没有改变。

“美国重视的是亚太地区以及台湾海峡的和平与稳定，”贾博说，“美国反对任何一方单方面改变现状。我们将继续确保一个自由、开放、和平与稳定的亚太地区。”

美国驻中国大使庞德伟(David Perdue)也在峰会结束后表示，特朗普政府的台湾政策没有改变。

庞德伟接受美国财经媒体CNBC采访时说，美国仍致力于以《台湾关系法》、美中三个联合公报和对台“六项保证”为基础的一中政策。他说，尽管北京一直试图推动美方改变相关措辞，但美国“没有改变措辞，也没有改变立场”。

**台湾通过多重渠道了解会谈内容**

台湾外交部次长陈明祺星期天在台北表示，无论是美方官员的公开表态，还是台美之间的非公开沟通渠道，都显示美国对台政策没有改变。

“我们从各种管道，也都得到美方我们的朋友一再跟我们确认，美国对台政策保持不变，”陈明祺说。

陈明祺是在出席一场由“中华亚太交流协会”主办的有关特习峰会的座谈会前接受媒体采访时作上述表示的。他表示，台湾方面仍在通过既有渠道了解特习会涉及台湾议题的具体内容，并强调台美之间各层级沟通保持畅通。

台湾中央社援引陈明祺的话说，北京长期试图推动美国采用“反对台独”的表述，但从美方公布的峰会文件来看，这一主张并未获得美国认可。台湾外交部此前也表示，北京有关台湾的说法属于中方单方面立场，不能代表台湾人民。

**对台军售仍受关注**

外界同时关注，特习会是否触及美国对台军售问题。峰会结束后，美中双方公布的成果文件都没有提到相关军售安排。

陈明祺表示，美方了解台湾的防务需求，也了解台湾加强国防投入的决心。台湾外交部正继续就军售等安全议题与美方保持沟通。

出席同场座谈会的台湾行政院陆委会副主委沈有忠也在会前接受媒体采访时表示，特习会在台湾、人工智能、稀土出口管制和科技竞争等问题上没有取得明显突破。根据台湾方面的评估，美中台局势仍呈现“三个不变”：美中战略竞争的基本结构不变、美国对台政策不变，以及台湾与国际社会维护台海和平与现状的立场不变。

据中央社报道，沈有忠还推测，北京可能试图把台湾问题与伊朗问题联系起来，寻求某种交换。不过，美国驻华大使庞德伟在峰会后明确表示，美方不会把伊朗问题与美国对台湾的承诺挂钩，二者是彼此独立的议题。

title: Chaplains and Commissars: An Analysis of the People’s Liberation Army’s Political Work System and the Will to Fight
source: 亚利桑那州立大学的《小战争杂志》
summary: Abstract : This paper posits that the People Liberation Army’s (PLA) political work system, in addition to its role in the dual-commander system and enforcing party loyalty, are also relied upon to raise esprit de corps and nurture soldiers
content: Abstract : This paper posits that the People Liberation Army’s (PLA) political work system, in addition to its role in the dual-commander system and enforcing party loyalty, are also relied upon to raise esprit de corps and nurture soldiers’ “will to fight.” To elucidate this point, the paper uses a metaphor from Liu Cixin’s The Dark Forest to explicitly compare political commissars to the US chaplain corps, while also highlighting the differences between Western and Chinese conceptions of will to fight. In potential future conflicts, Western forces can reduce the PLA’s will to fight by undermining belief in the chain of command and CCP more broadly. “In the military, you have political commissars and we have chaplains.” This comparison, proposed by a character in Liu Cixin’s The Dark Forest, compares the role of political commissars (政委) in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to that of chaplains in western militaries. On the surface, the two roles seem to be extremely dissimilar. Most analyses of political commissars in Western military literature focus on the two main roles of the political commissar: ensuring loyalty to the party, and the dual-command structure (双首长制) of the political commissar and the traditional commander. By comparison, chaplains primarily offer religious support to soldiers and advise commanders on the impact of religion within their formation and operational mission requirements. However, Liu’s metaphor posits a third role of the political commissar, one that is adjacent to the role of the chaplain: to raise esprit de corps and increase the will to fight. The idea of “will to fight” is a central concept in western military thought, dating back to Clausewitz , who used this term in defining an enemy’s power as: “the sum of available means and the strength of the Will.” While defining the “will to fight” is notoriously difficult, this paper will use RAND’s definition: “the disposition and decision to fight, act, or to persevere when needed.” Understanding any enemy’s will to fight is crucial in analyzing and understanding combat effectiveness. Chinese conceptions of will are rooted in fostering belief in the efficacy of the chain of command and the CCP, whereas Western military concepts such as “spiritual readiness” view will as an individual function as well. This paper argues that Chinese leaders view the role of the political work system, to include political commissars, as strengthening party loyalty while also simultaneously raising the will to fight among soldiers. Chinese conceptions of will are rooted in fostering belief in the efficacy of the chain of command and the CCP, whereas Western military concepts such as “spiritual readiness” view will as an individual function as well. In a potential future conflict, Western militaries can target the PLA’s “will to fight” by reducing belief in the PLA’s Chain of Command and the CCP more broadly. The People’s Liberation Army and the Political Work System Chinese Communist leaders have always recognized the power of the military and the role they play in achieving political objectives. Mao Zedong himself famously said that “political power grows out of the barrel of a gun (枪杆子里面出政权),” and Xi Jinping often talks about the need for the PLA’s absolute loyalty to the party. Many of Xi’s actions can be seen as conforming to this world view. In speeches he talks about the need to “confirm officer’s eternal obedience to the words of the party, and to walk with the party (确保官兵永远听党话、跟党走).” The political work system (总政治部) is the primary mechanism that the CCP uses to ensure the enforcement of party loyalty in its officers. In theory, the political commissar and the unit commander are positioned as co-equals, but in practice, structural advantages give the political commissar more power over the direct military commander. At the core of the political work system are the Party Standing Committees (PSC) and the PLA’s dual command structure. The PSC only exists above the regimental level and is responsible for daily decision making. This organization is chaired by the regimental political commissar with the unit commander serving as the deputy secretary, who are also the two leading figures in the dual command structure. Most political officers have military backgrounds and are chosen from junior military officers who are also Communist party members. In theory, the political commissar and the unit commander are positioned as co-equals, but in practice, structural advantages give the political commissar more power over the direct military commander. For starters, there is the aforementioned asymmetry in the PSC. Secondly, political commissars are often responsible for providing feedback to the military commander’s supervisor, a direct conflict of influence that ensures military commanders are adhering to the political commissar’s “ advice.” Thus, in reality, this structure does not naturally lend itself to war-fighting, and is instead reflective of the CCP’s intense insecurity about keeping control over the PLA. As Xi Jinping has stated, the party must be present at every level of leadership to ensure there is no room for corruption. Thus, the political work system is found at every echelon, to include the regimental, battalion, and company level. The regimental level consists of political commissars, while the battalion level has political directors (教导员) and the company level has political instructors (指导员). Political workers at the squad level are known as small group leaders (党小组长). Members of this last group are not considered political officers but are still part of the political work system . Officers in each of these positions are responsible for implementing CCP policies, enforcing party discipline, and overseeing political education. These political officers also work in tandem with their commander counterparts to make decisions, a practice in line with traditional Marxist philosophy on collective leadership. The political work system has also recently undergone wide ranging reforms that go beyond simply “enforcing the party line.” These reforms are broken into seven sections. While two of these sections are focused on “strengthening party loyalty” (强化政治忠诚) and “abiding by party principles,” (恪守党性原则) the remaining five sections are focused on re-defining personal conduct and shaping operational priorities (with a heavy emphasis on fairness in personnel management and “reinforcing a people-centered mindset” (树牢群众观念). This last point especially focuses on addressing soldier grievances and raising esprit de corps. Thus, these reforms point to an expanded purpose beyond only serving as a party apparatus. Chaplains, Political Commissars, and the Will to Fight Many scholars have used The Dark Forest to analyze 21 st century Chinese geopolitical thinking , with the title of the book even lending itself as the name of an explanation to the Fermi Paradox . “The Dark Forest Hypothesis” postulates that space is like a dark forest, where civilizations must keep quiet to avoid encountering other, potentially hostile civilizations. Likewise, much has been written about this book and its larger value in terms of understanding China’s strategic environment, yet it also has much to say on the PLA’s larger war fighting philosophy and Chinese conceptions of “will” and esprit de corps. While Liu’s metaphor about political commissars and chaplains is intriguing, it is not particularly appropriate to compare the two positions. The role of the Chaplain in western militaries, while tied to esprit de corps, is markedly different from that of the political commissar. Chaplains are responsible for providing spiritual care and emotional guidance while also working to build resilience among soldiers. To put it simply, there is not an analogous figure in the PLA’s military structure. Western militaries, including the United States, use chaplains to emphasize spiritual readiness in war fighting and increase the will of individual soldiers to fight. The chaplain system exists as a result of the First Amendment of the US constitution, specifically the “ free exercise clause ,” which prohibits the infringement of religious beliefs. Thus, as the US military bases the legitimacy of its chaplain corps off the constitution, it follows that a self-described atheistic state would not have religious advisors. The CCP views no need for “spiritual fitness,” and has effectively replaced this with absolute adherence to the party. In fact, major organized religion is a threat to the Party, and is often subject to intense repression – Muslims in Xinjiang , Christians across China , and Falun Gong are just a few examples. The United States views “will” as partially an individual function, encouraging soldiers to fight in combat and overcome personal hardships. Alternatively, Chinese leaders view “will” and esprit de corps as a means to achieving political objectives – the “greater purpose” that soldiers are fighting for is to achieve the party’s larger aims – as well as ensuring soldier’s overall loyalty to the party over any other loyalties. A key concept in US military conceptions of warfare is that of spiritual readiness/fitness. As defined in FM 7-22 , “Spiritual readiness develops the personal qualities a person needs in times of stress, hardship, and tragedy.” Likewise, the United States Army includes “ Spiritual Fitness ” as one of the five pillars of fitness (It should be noted that spiritual fitness is not tied to any religion). These ideas drive the idea of what motivates an individual soldier to fight, shaping the “will” that Clausewitz describes, and Chaplains are the key drivers of this spiritual readiness. By comparison there is no conception of “spiritual readiness” or “spiritual fitness” in the PLA. Instead, the CCP uses Marxist-Leninist thought and obedience in the party to instill their vision of “esprit de corps” – Maoist ideas of responsive leadership, where the leader is continually responding to feedback of subordinates, are meant to serve as a way for soldiers to give input and feel valued by their individual commander. In this vision, it is the feedback mechanism between leader and subordinate, Party and military, that shapes the “will to fight.” It is instead through the lens of obeying the party as raising esprit de corps that Liu Cixin describes the “political commissar,” highlighting how China’s conception of the will to fight is different from the US. The United States views “will” as partially an individual function, encouraging soldiers to fight in combat and overcome personal hardships. Alternatively, Chinese leaders view “will” and esprit de corps as a means to achieving political objectives – the “greater purpose” that soldiers are fighting for is to achieve the party’s larger aims – as well as ensuring soldier’s overall loyalty to the party over any other loyalties. Conclusion & Implications for Future Conflict Ultimately, what is worth noting is that the lack of a spiritual dimension in PLA doctrine creates a distinct difference between American and Chinese conceptions of the “will to fight.” In any future potential conflict, US and coalition forces should focus on reducing belief in both the chain of command and the CCP. There are a myriad of themes and narratives the US can emphasize, to include: identifying past failures and economic struggles, contrasting Xi’s rule with leaders such as Zhu Rongji, Jiang Zemin, and Hu Jintao, and highlighting the purging of leaders with wartime experience such as Zhang Youxia. The US can only undermine PLA “will” by understanding what motivates them. The CCP’s political work system is a crucial component in fostering the PLA’s “will to fight,” and understanding this concept provides critical insights into their war-fighting mechanisms and philosophies. The PLA bases its leadership philosophy on Maoist ideas of “collective leadership;” this collective leadership also ensures that the PLA is fully implementing the CCP’s policies, even if it could potentially degrade combat effectiveness. In light of the political commissar’s multi-faceted role, comparing “chaplains and commissars” is a fraught effort – the two positions are simply too disparate, with starkly different responsibilities. Whereas a chaplain is primarily concerned with raising esprit de corps and increasing morale, political commissars have direct command responsibility and a political dimension that chaplains do not. However, recent reforms continue to expand the purpose of the political work system, to include shaping leaders’ conduct and defining how they should interact with subordinates. This understanding provides crucial insight into PLA conceptions of warfighting, without endorsing any belief system over another. The PLA views the will to fight as increasing faith in the chain of command, whereas the US military has a personal dimension as well. Whether or not one of these is more effective is up for debate; concepts such as “spiritual fitness” and “spiritual readiness” are notoriously difficult to objectively measure and thus under-researched. Likewise, just because these concepts exist does not mean the US does not need to cultivate belief in the chain of command and the US government. Ultimately, what is worth noting is that the lack of a spiritual dimension in PLA doctrine creates a distinct difference between American and Chinese conceptions of the “will to fight.” The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not reflect the official policy or position of the USAICOE, Department of the Army, Department of Defense, or the US Government. The post Chaplains and Commissars: An Analysis of the People’s Liberation Army’s Political Work System and the Will to Fight appeared first on Small Wars Journal by Arizona State University .

title: 25 岁女游客在仙本那度假遭袭，虽奋力逃脱躲入丛林，但全身遭蚊虫叮咬溃烂
summary: 25 岁中国女游客黄女士，住进马来西亚旅游胜地仙本那的一家度假村后，她怎么也没想到，最先要防范的人，竟然是度假村的安保人员。 当地时间 9 月 19 日凌晨 3 点左右，黄女士正在房间熟睡，突然被动静惊醒。 她睁眼后惊恐地发现，一名18岁外籍安保男子站在床边，正在脱她的衣服，还抓住了她的手。 黄女士随即开始反抗，可她的力量明显处于下风。于是，黄女士没有继续硬拼，而是一边周旋，一边偷偷拿到手机，随后哄骗男子去洗澡。 机会只有几秒钟，洗澡的位置靠近房门，对方打开水阀后，她借着手机
content: 25 岁中国女游客黄女士，住进马来西亚旅游胜地仙本那的一家度假村后，她怎么也没想到，最先要防范的人，竟然是度假村的安保人员。 当地时间 9 月 19 日凌晨 3 点左右，黄女士正在房间熟睡，突然被动静惊醒。 她睁眼后惊恐地发现，一名18岁外籍安保男子站在床边，正在脱她的衣服，还抓住了她的手。 黄女士随即开始反抗，可她的力量明显处于下风。于是，黄女士没有继续硬拼，而是一边周旋，一边偷偷拿到手机，随后哄骗男子去洗澡。 机会只有几秒钟，洗澡的位置靠近房门，对方打开水阀后，她借着手机的光找到门锁，开门就跑。 黄女士说，自己以前练过长跑，一开始确实是跑得比对方快。可逃到监控覆盖的最后一片区域时，她还是被追上，对方一把拽住她的头发，将她拽倒在地，手机也摔了出去。 求生欲驱使黄女士爬起来继续跑，最后冲进度假村附近的丛林，躲到半山腰。从凌晨3点半到早上8点，她一个人在雷雨交加的丛林中藏了将近5个小时。 那几个小时并不好受，黄女士后来回忆，热带雨林里的蚊虫不停叮咬她的皮肤和伤口，她一度觉得很绝望。直到天亮后，她才被度假村工作人员发现。 9月22日，黄女士告诉媒体，自己已经完成伤情鉴定，也当面指认了嫌疑人。她称，对方承认了相关行为。 然而，她全身多处皮肤因蚊虫叮咬出现溃烂，仍在接受治疗。 警方随后介入，根据新京报报道，马来西亚警方在9月19日晚于度假村区域内抓获一名男子，这名男子就是度假村的保安，今年才18岁。 中国驻哥打基纳巴卢总领馆也已与黄女士、酒店及警方取得联系，正在跟进案件处理。 最让人后怕的是，从她逃出房间、被拽倒、再躲进树林，整个过程没触发任何警报，也没有一个巡逻人员出现。 黄女士住的并非廉价旅店，涉事度假村每晚房价超过1000元人民币。 有媒体调查称，仙本那部分千元级度假村在招安保人员时，并不做背景审查，年纪很小的外籍人员不用提供无犯罪记录就能上岗。 也正因为这样，事件曝光后，度假村安保和人员审查问题也被推上风口浪尖。不过截至相关报道发布时，涉事度假村尚未就这些问题公开回应。 黄女士这边刚脱险，泰国度假胜地芭堤雅又传出一起中国女性遇险案。 当地警方称，3名中国女子此前应征所谓“高薪伴游”工作，抵达一栋两层别墅后，却被4名同为中国籍的男子控制。 受害人向警方表示，她们遭到囚禁和性侵，对方还向她们在中国的亲友索要巨额赎金。 其中一名女子找到机会，用一部不在自己手中的手机向朋友发出求救讯息，还特别提醒：“绝对不要回复，否则会陷入危险。”她同时发出了别墅的准确定位。 9月23日凌晨，春武里府移民局、邦拉蒙警察局和观光警察等单位出动超过20人包围别墅。 二楼卧室里那名女子穿着睡衣，浑身是伤，吓得不轻，看到警察破门才松了口气。 警方进入屋内后救出3名女子，并控制4名男子。现场还发现一条疑似用于绑人的长铁链、多盒保险套，以及毒品吸食工具。 警方表示，4名男子当时都无法出示护照，初步怀疑他们非法入境。警方正在围绕非法入境、非法拘禁、集体性侵及恐吓勒索等方向继续调查，不等于已经确认全部罪名成立。

**中美AI竞赛：世界变得更危险还是更安全？**

Published 2026年9月25日

关于人工智能（AI）及其潜在危险的警告，近年来可谓接连不断。

美国最大的人工智能公司之一——Anthropic——的一名顶尖AI安全研究人员警告说，这项技术正以惊人的速度发展，未来十年内，AI“可能导致全人类灭绝”的概率高达10%。

这样的担忧引发了要求美国采取协调一致行动、放缓AI发展速度的呼声。但与此同时，也有人质疑是否真的有必要为AI设置监管“护栏”。美国总统特朗普就是其中之一。他认为，如果美国放慢AI发展的步伐，反而可能把美国在这一技术领域的主导地位拱手让给竞争对手。

与此同时，中国的AI产业也在与美国几乎同步加速发展，尽管美国一直试图限制中国科技发展的速度。

深度求索（DeepSeek）、月之暗面（Moonshot）等中国AI服务表明，中国的竞争者在能力上可能已经与美国前沿AI实验室旗鼓相当。

在本期《Asia Specific》节目中，BBC与嘉宾将共同分析中美两国在AI技术发展过程中面临的挑战、两国在AI监管与发展等问题上的分歧。

title: China Appears To Be Building A Mothership For Large Uncrewed Submarines
summary: For the past six months or so, a curious-looking vessel with a very boxy superstructure has been taking shape at a shipyard in the Chinese city of Shanghai. A new satellite image lends credence to an earlier assessment that this is a mother
content: For the past six months or so, a curious-looking vessel with a very boxy superstructure has been taking shape at a shipyard in the Chinese city of Shanghai. A new satellite image lends credence to an earlier assessment that this is a mothership to support China’s growing fleets of ever-larger submersible drones , though it could also have other roles. TWZ obtained the image of the ship in question, which was taken on September 10, from Vantor . Since then, it has also received an overall coat of gray paint, pointing to future service with the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN). It is some 669 feet (204 meters) long and around 98 feet (30 meters) at its widest. In terms of basic length and width, the vessel being built now is very roughly comparable to China’s Type 071 amphibious warfare ship . However, it appears to be much taller overall than the Type 071. The full September 10, 2026, image of the ship in question. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Another more recent view of the ship showing its new gray paint job. Chinese internet via X The new ship has been under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard on Changxing Island in Shanghai since at least April. This yard produces a variety of naval vessels, including surface combatants and amphibious assault ships, as well as commercial designs. The September 10 image, which shows the ship from the stern, is interesting for a number of reasons. It notably confirms that the design not only has a well deck, but that it is sized around what looks to be a large cradle-like platform visible in the shot. The very roughly 164-feet (50-meter) long rectangular platform has an arch-shaped structure at one end and two teardrop-shaped ones at the other, as well as six pillars, three on each side, in between. The teardrop-shaped structures, in particular, point to the platform being at least a semi-submersible, as they would help with stability and otherwise guide the flow of water while being pulled along. A closer look at the stern end of the ship, showing the opening for the well deck and the cradle-like platform. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor An even closer look at the platform. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor An earlier satellite image of the ship under construction taken on August 24, 2026, which also shows the cradle-like platform being built. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor The satellite image also clearly shows six large struts extending from the top of the stern end of the superstructure, each one which is paired with a shorter strut, for a total of 12. Earlier this month, independent naval analyst H.I. Sutton, who tracks undersea warfare developments in particular, posited that these struts could be used to lower a platform or some other similar structure below the hull of the ship. He also assessed that they could be used as part of a larger system capable of moving payloads between decks internally. This would help account for the configuration of the core superstructure, especially how high it is all the way from the front to the back. Overall, signs point to the inside of the superstructure being largely hangars and other open work spaces, allowing for multiple large UUVs to be carried and supported. Individual UUVs would be launched and recovered, one at a time, via the cradle. A closer look at the struts protruding from the top of the ship. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor In making his assessment, Sutton drew specific attention to a previously shown rendering of a proposed Chinese scientific research vessel with a roughly similar strut-based system at the stern for deploying submersibles and other large payloads. However, on that design, the system was entirely exposed rather than contained with an extended superstructure. The rendering of the proposed scientific research vessel with a system for deploying payloads at the stern that features four struts. Chinese internet via H.I. Sutton The platform seen immediately behind the ship being built at the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard aligns with Sutton’s assessment about the purpose of the struts. At the same time, launches and recoveries could also be conducted in a more traditional manner via the well deck. The design of the cradle-like platform would seem to suggest the latter option is at least part of the plan. The general idea of launching and recovering payloads through the bottom of the hull of a ship , including through moon pools , is hardly new. As another point here, Russia is known to have highly specialized mothership submarines that can carry crewed midget submarines and large uncrewed submersibles attached underneath their hulls, and that are also capable of launching ultra-long-range nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed torpedoes . The idea of deploying and retrieving large UUVs via well decks using cradle-like systems is something being explored by other navies globally, including in the United States . All that being said, a large specialized ship built for the purpose of launching and recovering very large underwater vehicles in an operational capacity is unique. The image from September 10, as well as other recent views of the ship, highlight other features that are now taking shape. This includes a large opening on the starboard side, which could be for launching and/or recovering lifeboats or other watercraft, or moving payloads to and from the pier while docked, as well as a multi-pronged mast on top of the bridge. An additional part of the ship’s superstructure extends behind the bridge area, and there is what looks to be a hangar inside. There is no attached helipad present now, but one could well be added later on somewhere on top of the superstructure. Many naval auxiliaries , as well as commercial ships designed for offshore support and other specialized tasks , have open helipads on raised frames attached to different parts of the superstructures. A closer look at the area of the superstructure around the bridge, showing the multi-pronged mast on top and what looks to be the opening to a hangar. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Though there is growing clarity about the ship’s design, many questions do remain about the full breadth of its intended purpose. In Sutton’s view, the PLAN has a need, just in general, for a dedicated mothership to support its growing uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) fleets . The PLAN is pursuing various tiers of UUVs to perform a host of different missions, including intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), as well as mine-laying, special operations support, and even launching direct attacks on enemy vessels. Larger and larger UUV designs have been steadily emerging in China , which could require more specialized launch and recovery options to be feasibly employed operationally, especially from other vessels at sea. Deployment and retrieval at sea could, in turn, support very long duration missions far from China’s own shores. “With smaller UUVs, even up to 20 meters like the AJX-002 and HSU-100 paraded in Beijing last year, they are road mobile. Truck mounted cranes should be sufficient for getting them in and out of the water making operations much simpler. With these latest, much larger XXLUUVs [extra-extra large uncrewed underwater vehicles] however, China will start to need dedicated port facilities,” Sutton wrote previously on his website . “Until now China has been using floating docks to house the two XXLUUV prototypes being tested on Hainan . One of these docks was purpose built while the other may have been taken up from general use.” A Chinese AJX-002 UUV, or a mockup thereof, seen ahead of a major military parade in Beijing in 2025. Chinese internet via X China's naval unmanned systems. Consisting of (in order), AI enabled unmanned submersible (HSU-100), used for detection and attack. Unmanned patrol boat. Unmanned mine-laying/attack submersible (AJX-002), this was previously mistaken for a nuclear powered torpedo. Because the… pic.twitter.com/Mlj55XLNBH — Zhao DaShuai 东北进修 (@zhao_dashuai) September 3, 2025 “This arrangement also has a significant drawback: each floating dock can only carry a single XXLUUV,” Sutton added. “Or if more than one, then they both need to be placed in the water at the same time. Because the whole dock floods, there cannot be one undergoing maintenance while another is being launched or recovered.” A mothership vessel able to discreetly deploy and recover large uncrewed and crewed submersibles and other large payloads underwater could be tasked with more specialized missions, including cutting cables , retrieving objects from the seabed , and other kinds of undersea espionage. There is overlap here with more benign roles, such as submarine rescue, salvage, and even deep-sea scientific research. There is also the matter of servicing an expanding array of Chinese underwater infrastructure , including sensor and communications networks . As something of a corollary, Russia’s spy ship Yantar is officially described as an oceanic research vessel. In China, the line between military and non-military assets and capabilities, including ships, is often very blurry, to begin with, as TWZ regularly highlights. This dichotomy was observed right at the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard around the end of last year after pictures of a commercial cargo ship being used to showcase a new family of containerized weapons, sensors , and other systems went viral online. It is also worth pointing out that the boxy and largely enclosed design of the ship now being built at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard will inherently make it difficult to observe any activities onboard. This will have the additional knock-on effect of helping keep any payloads, as well as the crew, shielded from the elements. This could be valuable for operations in harsher locales, including waters in and around the Arctic, an ever-more strategic part of the world where China is working to be more engaged . We also do not know if the apparent mothership vessel is intended to be a one-off or part of a larger class. It could be a stepping stone to broader plans or be part of an already extensive fleet of bespoke naval auxiliaries , as well as unique ostensibly commercial vessels , in service in China today. The PLAN’s aforementioned UUV ambitions will bring along significant test and evaluation requirements, as well as the need to support actual future operations. If nothing else, evidence is only growing that the new ship under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard is intended to serve, at least in part, as a mothership for large submersible drones. title: Chinese Culture Is Not the Obstacle: Taiwan, Democracy, and the CCP’s Narrative War
source: 亚利桑那州立大学的《小战争杂志》
summary: For decades, a persistent argument in China studies has held that democracy is fundamentally incompatible with Chinese civilization. China, this argument suggests, has always valued hierarchy over equality, order over political competition,
content: For decades, a persistent argument in China studies has held that democracy is fundamentally incompatible with Chinese civilization. China, this argument suggests, has always valued hierarchy over equality, order over political competition, and centralized authority over individual political rights. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has eagerly embraced this interpretation of history, arguing that one-party rule is not merely a contemporary political choice, but the natural, immutable expression of Chinese culture. This argument deserves closer examination. The question is not whether the CCP has created an effective authoritarian system. It clearly has. Since Deng Xiaoping’s economic reforms, China has demonstrated that a form of state capitalism and digital authoritarianism can coexist. However, economic modernization did not automatically produce political liberalization , directly challenging the Western assumption that wealthier societies inevitably become democratic. As economist Tyler Cowen observed in his analysis on China’s historical experience suggests democratization is far from inevitable. China lacks a sustained, unbroken tradition of liberal democracy on the mainland, economic growth has been decoupled from political reform, and fervent state-sponsored nationalism has provided the Communist Party with an alternative source of legitimacy. Yet, this thesis rests on a critical flaw: the assumption that the CCP’s self-serving interpretation of Chinese history represents Chinese civilization itself. It does not. China’s modern history is not a story of a civilization inherently rejecting democracy. It is a story of repeated, courageously fought attempts at constitutional reform and representative government that were repeatedly interrupted by foreign invasion, political fragmentation, economic weakness, and revolutionary authoritarianism. China’s Forgotten Democratic Tradition During the nineteenth century, Chinese intellectuals and leaders confronted an existential national crisis. Western military power, rapid industrialization, and imperial expansion threatened China’s very survival. In response, the Self-Strengthening Movement sought to modernize China’s military, education, and industrial base while preserving Chinese cultural identity. The core lesson was profound: Chinese reformers did not view foreign institutions as inherently incompatible with Chinese civilization; they believed China could adapt external structural ideas to revitalize itself. Following China’s defeat in the Sino-Japanese War of 1895, reformers such as Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao advocated for a constitutional monarchy and rapid institutional modernization. Though crushed by conservative factions at court, the Hundred Days Reform of 1898 revealed that constitutionalism was being actively debated among China’s intellectual and political elites. This impulse was not confined to the mainland. In 1895, when the Qing Dynasty ceded Taiwan to Japan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki—a transfer executed with great relief by the imperial court—local elites on the island declared the Republic of Formosa . Though short-lived, this nascent republic reflected an early commitment to self-governance and representative principles for the island’s diverse population of indigenous tribes, Hokkien, Hakka, and Han Chinese settlers who had previously fled Qing misrule. Subsequent constitutional reforms by the late Qing dynasty between 1905 and 1911 went even further. Provincial assemblies were established, local elections were held, and plans were drawn up for national representative institutions. While these efforts ultimately collapsed alongside the dynasty, their failure was the result of acute political instability—not cultural rejection. The United States, Europe, and Japan all experienced eras when democratic institutions failed, collapsed, or succumbed to authoritarianism. Few historians would argue that those historical failures proved democracy was incompatible with Western or Asian civilization. China should be judged by the same analytical standard. Sun Yat-sen and the Republican Vision The 1911 Revolution provides the clearest historical challenge to the notion that representative governance is foreign to Chinese political thought. Dr. Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of the Republic of China, envisioned a political system built upon the Three Principles of the People ( Sān Mín Zhǔyì ): Nationalism, Democracy, and Popular Welfare. Sun sought to fuse classical Chinese political philosophy with modern constitutional governance. Crucially, Sun did not believe China had to abandon its cultural identity to become democratic; he believed democratic governance was essential for China’s national revival. The Republic of China ultimately failed to establish a stable, lasting democracy on the mainland. However, the causes were geopolitical and structural: warlordism, Japanese invasion, economic collapse, and a brutal civil war. Institutions rarely survive when state infrastructure collapses under the weight of total war. The failure of early Chinese democratic experiments does not prove that Chinese culture rejected democracy; it demonstrates the extreme difficulty of building democratic institutions under catastrophic conditions. Taiwan’s Answer My own understanding of this issue has been shaped not only by studying China from afar, but by experiencing Taiwan firsthand. Having studied at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University, learned Mandarin, and returned during my time at Harvard’s Weatherhead Center for International Affairs to complete a Cross-Strait strategic analysis for the Chief of Staff of the Army—and later collaborating with defense professionals involved in counter-political warfare—those experiences shattered the conventional wisdom. Taiwan does not resemble a society that abandoned Chinese civilization in order to become democratic. It represents a society that carefully preserved its rich Chinese heritage while cultivating world-class democratic institutions. Taiwan shares with mainland China a common language, deep Confucian influences, shared cultural traditions, and much of the political legacy of the early Republic of China. Yet, Taiwan has transformed into one of the world’s most vibrant, consolidated democracies. As documented in Freedom House’s Taiwan Profile , the island boasts fierce political competition, peaceful transfers of power, an uncompromised free press, and a thriving civil society. If Chinese civilization itself prevented democracy, Taiwan’s political transformation would be a logical impossibility. Taiwan is not evidence that Chinese culture was abandoned; it is living proof that Chinese culture was never the obstacle. The CCP’s Narrative Advantage: Political to Cognitive Warfare The Chinese Communist Party’s greatest ideological achievement has been convincing Western observers that the Party and Chinese civilization are one and the same. They are not. The CCP has constructed a sophisticated strategic narrative: that criticizing one-party rule is equivalent to attacking China itself. In this formulation, democracy is framed not as a viable political alternative, but as a corrosive foreign import incompatible with Chinese identity. This is far more than traditional diplomacy; it is an active campaign of political and cognitive warfare. As detailed in recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) on CCP Cognitive Warfare . Beijing intentionally weaponizes grey-zone disinformation to alter public perception, seeking to shift the core global debate: From: “Should a single political party maintain permanent authoritarian control over China?” To: “Can Chinese people govern themselves democratically?” Taiwan completely dismantles Beijing’s cognitive trap by proving that Chinese identity and democratic governance are mutually reinforcing. Why Taiwan Matters to the United States The geopolitical importance of Taiwan extends far beyond its geography or its dominant role in the global semi conductor supply chain though both are undeniably critical to national security. Taiwan matters because it presents an alternative, highly successful vision of China’s future. Beijing argues that centralized authoritarian rule is the sole authentic expression of Chinese civilization. Taiwan proves that Chinese identity and democratic freedoms can flourish side-by-side. For the United States, Taiwan’s security is not merely a matter of defending an island chain or balancing power in the Indo-Pacific. It is directly tied to preserving a favorable strategic and ideological order. A Chinese conquest of Taiwan would not only alter the military balance in Asia; it would validate Beijing’s claim that authoritarianism is the natural political destiny of Chinese society, severely eroding confidence in democratic resilience globally. Conversely, Taiwan’s survival demonstrates that political systems are choices—not civilizational inevitabilities. American military, economic, and political support for Taiwan is about deterrence against unprovoked aggression, but it is also about preventing an autocratic state from forcibly extinguishing the most successful example of Chinese democracy in history. Conclusion The question is not whether Chinese civilization can sustain democracy. Taiwan answered that question decades ago. The real question is why the Chinese Communist Party insists that democracy is incompatible with Chinese identity. History demonstrates that the true obstacle to democracy in China is not Confucian culture, historical memory, or an inherent rejection of human rights. The obstacle is a political system that has tied national identity to permanent one-party rule. Taiwan represents something far more consequential than a regional flashpoint. It represents proof that Chinese civilization does not belong exclusively to authoritarianism. For that reason, defending Taiwan is not simply a strategic necessity for the United States—it is the defense of a vital principle: that no government has the right to claim sole ownership over an entire civilization’s political future. The post Chinese Culture Is Not the Obstacle: Taiwan, Democracy, and the CCP’s Narrative War appeared first on Small Wars Journal by Arizona State University .

title: 4 Chinese nationals arrested in Papua New Guinea human trafficking bust
summary: Four Chinese nationals are suspected of forcing 39 people to work in an online scam operation from a living room in the capital of Papua New Guinea, police said Wednesday. Police bust of the alleged trafficking ring’s property in downtown P
content: Four Chinese nationals are suspected of forcing 39 people to work in an online scam operation from a living room in the capital of Papua New Guinea, police said Wednesday. Police bust of the alleged trafficking ring’s property in downtown Port Moresby. Photo: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary. The victims, all Indonesians, were coerced into the work at a three-bedroom property in downtown Port Moresby in which they were held, a police source told AFP. “The victims are still being interviewed,” he said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give details about the case. “At the time of the bust many were hard to communicate with because of language barriers, thus investigators will have to sit with Indonesian officials to assist with interviews.” ‘Deeply disturbing’ Police rescued the 39 people being held against their will in a “complex people-smuggling enterprise”, Police Commissioner David Manning said Tuesday. “There will be no leniency for those who traffic and exploit people,” Manning said. “It is deeply disturbing that such alleged crimes could occur in our country.” Four Chinese nationals were arrested in the operation, and would likely face significant charges, he said. Manning said a people-smuggling network in Papua New Guinea and abroad had been dismantled in a Police Transnational Crime Directorate intelligence operation. More arrests were expected. Port Moresby viewed from Touaguba Hill. Photo: Wikicommons. “Those detained may be connected to a wider transnational human trafficking syndicate operating between Southeast Asia and the Pacific,” said Deputy Commissioner Donald Yamasombi, who led the police operation. Papua New Guinea police will work closely with international partners “to identify and dismantle any offshore components of this criminal network”, he said. Police said they were working with the Indonesian embassy in Papua New Guinea to take care of the rescued victims.

title: Fact Check Team: How AI agents can run foreign influence campaigns across social media
summary: WASHINGTON (TNND) — Artificial intelligence is changing how foreign influence campaigns can operate online — allowing some actors to automate tasks that previously required large numbers of people. [Video 13](blob:https://wjla.com/c7b320bc-
content:
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Artificial intelligence is changing how foreign influence campaigns can operate online — allowing some actors to automate tasks that previously required large numbers of people.

[Video 13](blob:https://wjla.com/c7b320bc-fab7-488e-b3c1-dcb168c6a2a6)
AI-generated content and fake online personas are not new. U.S. officials have previously warned that foreign actors. (TNND)

A recent report from[The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/18/technology/iran-china-autonomous-ai-influence-campaigns.html)found that Iran and China, along with private Israeli companies, have used AI agents in novel social media influence campaigns. The technology allowed agents to perform multiple steps of an operation, including creating accounts, generating posts and coordinating activity across platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok.

AI-generated content and fake online personas are not new. U.S. officials have previously warned that foreign actors, including Iran, have used generative AI and inauthentic personas in attempts to influence Americans and sow discord. What researchers say is different about these newer campaigns is the degree of automation.

## How does an AI influence campaign work?

AI agents are software systems that can complete a series of tasks with less direct human involvement.

Maryland seniors could face major long-term care insurance hikes

According to The New York Times, hundreds of AI agents were used in some of the newly identified campaigns. They created networks of fictitious accounts, generated political and current-events content and coordinated messages online.

In the Iranian operation, the AI-generated accounts presented themselves as ordinary Americans living in major U.S. cities. The accounts posted memes and political commentary, tagged journalists and politicians, and promoted messages critical of the Republican Party. The accounts accumulated nearly 80,000 followers during the first half of 2026.

That number, however, should not be interpreted as 80,000 Americans being persuaded by the operation. The reporting establishes the number of followers, but it does not establish how many people believed the content or changed their political views as a result.

## Why does this matter?

One concern is that foreign actors can exploit political divisions that already exist in the United States.

Instead of simply producing a piece of propaganda, an automated system can potentially create an entire network of accounts [designed to make a particular viewpoin](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/e50be2e51e7695dc4b1366a37a245a597377d3b5/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf)t appear more widespread than it actually is.

Researchers have also warned that AI can make these operations cheaper and easier to scale. The FBI and CISA previously warned that foreign actors could use generative AI and fake personas to conceal their involvement and attempt to sow discord among Americans.

The technology is not limited to one political side. Foreign influence operations can promote different messages depending on the audience and the strategic objective. Researchers have identified efforts aimed at increasing distrust and polarization rather than simply supporting one political party.

How far can the content spread?

In a separate analysis, the [Institute for Strategic Dialogue](https://www.isdglobal.org/digital-dispatch/how-pro-iran-networks-gained-a-billion-views-on-war-propaganda/) documented more than one billion views generated by two coordinated pro-Iran networks on X during the first month of the Iran war.

The networks circulated false, misleading and AI-generated material. ISD's analysis found that recommendation algorithms, reposting by larger accounts and coordinated amplification helped some of the content reach large audiences.

[Video 14](blob:https://wjla.com/5c2bc38b-80fb-4b08-8fe6-804eb7b87f07)
The use of AI in foreign influence operations isn't itself new. AI has been used for years to generate articles, images, videos and social media posts. (TNND)

But again, views are not the same thing as persuasion. A post receiving millions of views tells us how widely it was seen or counted by the platform's metrics; it does not establish how many people believed it or changed their opinions.

## What is actually new?

The use of AI in foreign influence operations isn't itself new. AI has been used for years to generate articles, images, videos and social media posts.

The newer development is agentic AI — systems capable of carrying out multiple tasks with less human intervention.

Anthropic's [September 2026 threat-intelligence report](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/e50be2e51e7695dc4b1366a37a245a597377d3b5/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf)similarly documents the expanding use of AI in malicious influence operations and other forms of abuse.

For social media users, that means a post that looks like it came from an ordinary person may not necessarily represent an authentic grassroots political conversation.

The documented campaigns show that foreign actors are experimenting with ways to automate that process. But determining whether those campaigns actually change Americans' political beliefs requires evidence beyond follower counts, views or the existence of fake accounts.

title: Flawed AI-linked intelligence report almost led to US military boarding Chinese ship in Middle East – report
summary: The US military came close to boarding a Chinese vessel in the Middle East earlier this year based on a flawed intelligence report prepared with the help of artificial intelligence, CNN said Friday. The US and Chinese flag. File photo: Tom
content: The US military came close to boarding a Chinese vessel in the Middle East earlier this year based on a flawed intelligence report prepared with the help of artificial intelligence, CNN said Friday. The US and Chinese flag. File photo: Tom Grundy/HKFP. US intelligence indicated the ship was carrying nuclear weapons-related components, leading American forces to prepare to intercept it, the broadcaster reported, citing four anonymous sources familiar with the incident. But the operation was called off after officials determined that an AI chatbot used by an analyst had misidentified the material the ship was carrying. CNN quoted one source as saying the intelligence report was “entirely false” but “almost started a war.” It did not specify what the vessel was actually carrying or where it was bound. US Central Command — which is responsible for American forces in the Middle East — did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reported incident. The CNN report comes after a furor erupted earlier this month when a researcher publicly resigned from leading AI firm Anthropic over fears that the technology could escape human control. Another Anthropic employee, who did not resign, said publicly that “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and that he thought the chances were greater than “10 percent within the next decade.” Despite the warnings, US President Donald Trump and some of his key allies have voiced opposition to drastically curbing the development of artificial intelligence. US President Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks on the economy at Mount Airy Casino Resort in Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania, on December 9, 2025. Photo: The White House, via Flickr. In a separate incident involving the US military and China, Politico reported Friday that F-35 jet parts — including a sensitive stealth canopy for a cockpit — were diverted to Hong Kong and are now missing, raising fears that Beijing had obtained sensitive American military technology. The parts were headed from Australia to the United States for repairs when the diversion occurred, the US outlet reported, adding that it was unclear why the parts were rerouted or where they are now. A spokesperson for Lockheed Martin, which manages the F-35 supply chain, said the company could not discuss specific shipments because of “security reasons.” “Lockheed Martin follows all US regulations established by the Department of War and regulated by the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) regarding the shipment of aircraft components,” the spokesperson said. “Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 program and the security of our allied partners.”

title: Advocates call for stronger consent laws as Hong Kong to criminalise persistent child sexual abuse and ‘cyberflashing’
summary: A campaign group has continued to urge the government to impose limits on a defence allowing a sexual assault suspect to claim they mistakenly believed they had been given consent, after authorities announced stronger protections under upco
content: A campaign group has continued to urge the government to impose limits on a defence allowing a sexual assault suspect to claim they mistakenly believed they had been given consent, after authorities announced stronger protections under upcoming sexual offences reforms. Booklets published by Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women on sexual assault and sexual law reform. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The group, which calls itself We Are X , after the placeholder name assigned to sexual assault survivors in court, said that it welcomed the Security Bureau’s move to propose the criminalisation of persistent child sexual abuse and sending digital pictures of one’s genitals without consent, known as “cyberflashing.” Hong Kong authorities are seeking to introduce dozens of new offences to Hong Kong’s archaic sex laws, including provisions to protect mentally impaired people, expand the scope of rape, and redefine consent during sexual activity. We Are X’s Friday statement read: “We would like to remind the public that the purpose of creating this offence is to provide children who endure persistent sexual abuse with an avenue to seek legal recourse and receive comprehensive protection.” The campaign group called on the government to make meaningful changes regarding what they called the stringent and unreasonable burden of proof placed on survivors. Loopholes The group had previously expressed concerns that defendants could still be acquitted by arguing that they had an “honest but mistaken belief” that consent was provided. “We are X” and the Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women jointly host a press conference on July 8, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. It “remains concerned” that the government has maintained it is up to the courts to decide whether a defendant’s “mistaken belief” is reasonable, the statement said. That approach fails to address situations where a defendant relies on the “mistaken belief” defence even in cases where “vitiating factors” — such as force, fear, unconsciousness, or deception — are involved, the group said. “We earnestly hope the Government will… ensure the law accurately reflects the reality of sexual violence and establishes an objective and effective legal framework for assessing ‘sexual consent’ within the judicial system,” the statement read. The Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women (ACSVAW) had a similar response, saying in a statement that the current approach contains “severe legal loopholes,” adding that defendants have been acquitted after claiming they believed consent was given based on “absurd or unreasonable grounds.” The association said that the defendant must be barred from raising the “mistaken belief” defence if they failed to take steps to ascertain the victim’s consent. Hong Kong is now mulling radical reform of sex crime laws for better protection of sexual assault survivors. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A limit must also be imposed if the defendant was reckless as to whether there was consent, and if the defendant was in a state of self-induced intoxication. We Are X also called on the government to step up publicity and education efforts addressing misconceptions about false accusations or a lowered conviction threshold. The government itself has said that prosecution and conviction thresholds will remain unchanged. It also continued to suggest that the government change the word “rape” in its sex crime laws to “sexual assault by penetration.” The clearer terminology would help the public understand that the offence covers all types of non-consensual penetrative sexual assault, regardless of gender, it said.

title: War By Other Means
source: 亚利桑那州立大学的《小战争杂志》
summary: Abstract Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz during Operation Epic Fury was achieved not by force but by inducing private war-risk insurers to withdraw coverage, a tactic this article calls insurance-market weaponization. The mechanism p
content: Abstract Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz during Operation Epic Fury was achieved not by force but by inducing private war-risk insurers to withdraw coverage, a tactic this article calls insurance-market weaponization. The mechanism produced blockade-equivalent effects without a shot fired at the US Navy and left no legally cognizable state authority, and the same logic is transferable to any chokepoint served by a concentrated insurance market, including Malacca, Bab-el-Mandeb, and the waters around Taiwan. When Israeli and American forces struck Iran’s Natanz and Fordow enrichment sites on February 28, opening what has become known as Operation Epic Fury , most analysts expected the ensuing crisis to unfold as a familiar contest of missiles, mines, and tanker escorts in the Persian Gulf. Instead, within seventy-two hours, the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed to commercial shipping without a single Iranian vessel intercepting a tanker and without Tehran ever declaring a blockade. The mechanism responsible deserves more attention from the security community than it has received. Lloyd’s of London syndicates and the war-risk insurers known as Protection and Indemnity clubs, without whose coverage no commercial vessel can legally load, finance, or sail through a conflict zone, simply withdrew from the Strait days after the strikes began. No tanker owner will risk a cargo and hull worth hundreds of millions of dollars without that coverage. The result was a chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil and gas trade shut down not by force, but by actuarial judgment. The Mechanism: Insurance as a Weapon Call it insurance-market weaponization: the deliberate use of military action and calibrated threats to make private insurers conclude, on their own commercial logic, that a strategic waterway is no longer worth covering. Iran did not need to sink a ship or lay a mine. It needed only to make the possibility credible enough that underwriters in London would rather walk away than price the risk. Figure 1 . The insurance-weaponization mechanism. The five-stage causal chain by which military signaling induces private underwriters to withdraw war-risk coverage, producing a blockade-equivalent chokepoint closure without a formal declaration of blockade or the interdiction of a single vessel. The dashed bracket marks the attribution gap this sequence opens: a coercive effect that is commercially real but has no legally cognizable state author. Source: Author’s elaboration. The Attribution Gap This gap matters because it appears deliberate. The right of transit passage through international straits is guaranteed under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea , and customary international law bars a blockade of neutral shipping absent a formal declaration of belligerency. None of that reaches a private insurer’s independent decision to stop covering a route it judges too dangerous. Iran issued no blockade declaration and interdicted no vessel. The rules governing when a state can be held responsible for private conduct do not extend to a firm’s own commercial judgment unless a government is shown to be directing it, and Tehran was careful never to cross that line. What results is an attribution gap: a coercive effect that is entirely real but has no legally cognizable author. Figure 2 . Two paths to a closed chokepoint. A comparative institutional map contrasting the classical blockade pathway, in which a state’s formal act triggers direct attribution under the law of the sea, with the insurance-market pathway demonstrated during Operation Epic Fury, in which the same commercial-closure effect is produced through an underwriter’s independent commercial judgment rather than state action, leaving existing deterrence and accountability frameworks with no point of purchase. Source: Author’s elaboration. Why the Old Toolkit Doesn’t Work For planners, this is the part that should be most unsettling. Every tool Washington and its partners normally reach for in a Gulf disruption – strategic reserve releases, emergency production increases, price caps – addresses a shortage of oil. None of it addresses a shortage of insurance. The International Energy Agency’s release of 400 million barrels , the largest in its fifty-year history, and Washington’s commitment of 172 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, barely moved prices, because tankers still could not legally sail without coverage that no longer existed. Goldman Sachs has warned that oil could exceed its 2008 record if the insurance freeze persists, regardless of how much physical crude sits in a reserve somewhere. Even a ceasefire will not fix this quickly. Lloyd’s syndicates and P&I clubs reassess risk through their own internal governance, on their own timeline, driven by actuarial confidence rather than diplomatic announcements. A war can end at the negotiating table months before insurers are willing to underwrite transit through the strait again, a lag that conflict-termination scholarship has never had to account for, because no earlier coercive instrument worked this way. The Asymmetric Appeal What makes the tool attractive to a state like Iran is its asymmetry. A formal blockade risks legal exposure, invites international condemnation, and can be met with naval countermeasures. Sanctions require years of multilateral coordination to bite. Insurance-market weaponization requires none of that. It cost Tehran a handful of strikes, including a drone attack on Qatar’s Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal that forced QatarEnergy to declare force majeure on its export contracts, plus enough missile signaling to keep underwriters nervous. In return, Iran achieved the commercial-closure equivalent of a blockade at a fraction of the military and legal price. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s insistence that any settlement compensate Tehran for strikes on civilian sites suggests Iran sees time, not territory, as its primary asset: every week the strait stays commercially closed is a week that inflation eats into Washington’s political runway and Beijing’s patience with an unstable oil market wears thinner. That political runway is shorter than it looks. Goldman Sachs projects that even a six-week disruption would push US inflation about a percentage point above its pre-war forecast, enough to turn energy prices into a domestic political liability. When Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled Washington’s openness to easing sanctions on Iranian oil exports even as strikes continued, that was not mixed messaging. It was an administration managing the gap between military objectives that require months and a domestic economy that can tolerate only weeks. Israel’s own war aims run on a different clock. Dismantling Iran’s regional proxy network, the stated objective behind the strikes, is a project measured in months, not weeks, a mismatch with Washington’s tolerance for sustained economic pain that has already generated friction inside the coalition. Israel’s own decision to halt offshore gas production at the Karish and Leviathan fields, after Iranian threats, has cut roughly 13 to 14 billion cubic meters of annual gas supply to Jordan and Egypt. That is a reminder that energy infrastructure in this theater carries value well beyond its market price, and that fighting over it will likely outlast any ceasefire in the Gulf. Collateral Damage Beyond the Gulf The steepest cost of this new instrument, though, is falling on countries with no stake in the fight. The World Economic Forum and the IEA describe wide swaths of Southeast and South Asia, including the Philippines, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka, as importing 60 to 95 percent of their crude from the Gulf with no viable alternative in the near term. These are economies that buy oil on the spot market, carry no strategic reserve to draw on, and have none of the institutional access that lets Washington, Tokyo, or Brussels smooth out a shock like this one. When Houthi forces resumed attacks on Suez shipping days after the opening strikes, the same cargoes that might have rerouted around the Gulf lost their fallback route too, forcing tankers onto the far longer Cape of Good Hope passage and pushing freight costs higher still. For a country like Sri Lanka, still recovering from its own recent balance-of-payments crisis , a second oil shock arriving before the first one clears is not a policy problem. It is a fiscal emergency. A Transferable Blueprint This should worry planners well beyond the Gulf. The mechanism Iran has demonstrated, using military signaling to induce a private-market withdrawal that produces blockade-equivalent effects without a blockade, is not bound to Hormuz. The same logic applies to any chokepoint served by a concentrated, risk-averse insurance market: the Strait of Malacca, the Bab-el-Mandeb, or the waters around Taiwan. A state contemplating pressure on Taiwan would not need to declare a quarantine or fire on a single ship to achieve much of the same commercial effect. It would need only to make the risk of doing so credible enough that Lloyd’s and its peers price it out of the market. Any strategy for deterring or responding to that kind of coercion has to start with the insurance architecture itself, not just naval posture. Policy Implications: Closing the Gap None of the standard levers – reserve releases, diplomatic pressure, even a negotiated ceasefire – reach the actual point of failure, which sits in the underwriting departments of a handful of London firms. Reducing the effectiveness of this instrument in future crises will likely require some mix of state-backed reinsurance for critical straits, faster and less conditional International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank support for the developing economies bearing the worst of the shock, and a serious legal debate over whether existing frameworks, the Law of the Sea, the World Trade Organization ( WTO )’s security exceptions, the law of state responsibility , can or should be stretched to reach coercion exercised through private markets rather than state hands. Iran has shown that a determined actor can close one of the world’s most important waterways for a fraction of the cost of a blockade without ever committing what the law recognizes as an act of war. Every future adversary watching this crisis has just been handed the blueprint. The post War By Other Means appeared first on Small Wars Journal by Arizona State University .

title: Man jailed 4 weeks for grabbing passerby by the neck and attempting to kiss her
summary: A Hong Kong man accused of grabbing the neck of a female passerby and attempting to kiss her has been sentenced to four weeks in prison for indecent assault. Eastern Law Courts Building. Photo: Almond Li/HKFP. Fung Ho-yin, 29, appeared at t
content: A Hong Kong man accused of grabbing the neck of a female passerby and attempting to kiss her has been sentenced to four weeks in prison for indecent assault. Eastern Law Courts Building. Photo: Almond Li/HKFP. Fung Ho-yin, 29, appeared at the Eastern Magistrates’ Courts on Wednesday, The Witness reported . He pleaded guilty to a charge of indecent assault stemming from an incident in the early hours of Tuesday in Shau Kei Wan. Fung was sitting on a bench in a park on Nam On Street at around 1am that day when a woman – known to the court as X – walked past him, according to the prosecution. Fung first attempted to take a photo of X. He then stood up and followed her, and wrapped his left arm around X’s neck while using his other arm to touch her chest. He also tried to kiss her, the prosecution said. X managed to escape and screamed for help. Nam On Street Sitting-out Area in Shau Kei Wan. Photo: Wikicommons. She got the attention of a man inside a nearby gym, who ran out and helped her. X then called the police. Officers arrived at the scene and arrested Fung, who admitted under police caution that he had committed the offence out of impulse, The Witness reported. He told police he was attracted to X’s miniskirt and hoped to get close to and speak with her. But X noticed him approach and told him to go away, he said. See also: Hong Kong court acquits gov’t statistician who followed, photographed girl during school open day Handing down the sentence, Magistrate Kestrel Lam said the incident occurred in the quiet of the night, and that the consequences would have been hard to predict if nobody had come forward. He said that even though Fung had no criminal record, this was a serious case that warranted imprisonment, Ming Pao reported . Indecent assault is punishable by up to 10 years’ imprisonment, although jail terms in magistrates’ courts are capped at two years for a single offence.

title: From Mass Detention to Permanent Control: What Zhang Yabo’s Testimony Reveals About the Evolution of the Uyghur Genocide and Forced Labor
source: 乔治华盛顿大学维吾尔族研究中心(每月1到2次）
summary: By CUS Editorial Team For over a decade, the international community has watched the unfolding human rights crisis in East Turkistan (AKA the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). Through satellite imagery, leaked government documents, and ha
content: By CUS Editorial Team For over a decade, the international community has watched the unfolding human rights crisis in East Turkistan (AKA the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). Through satellite imagery, leaked government documents, and harrowing accounts from camp survivors, a picture of systematic persecution, amounting to genocide and crimes against humanity against Uyghur and other Turkic peoples according to multiple governments and international assessments, has emerged. Yet the Chinese communist government has consistently sought to obstruct independent scrutiny, dismissing external findings as Western fabrications and portraying mass internment as voluntary “vocational training” or benign “counter-extremism” measures. Beijing’s narrative has shifted over time. After initially denying the existence of the concentration camps, Chinese authorities sought to justify them as necessary counterterrorism and vocational-training facilities. In recent years, they have claimed or implied that the campaign has ended and that life in the region has returned to normal. To reinforce this false narrative, Chinese authorities have permitted carefully screened Uyghurs to visit the region, allowed a small number of Uyghurs to travel abroad, and arranged tightly controlled tours for foreign diplomats, journalists, and religious figures to visit staged scenes in the region. These efforts have been used to portray the region as being free from repression and to whitewash an ongoing genocide. Uyghurs in the diaspora have consistently rejected this portrayal, warning that repression has not ended but has instead become less visible and more deeply embedded. The testimony of Zhang Yabo provides powerful new evidence supporting their warnings. A Witness from Inside the Chinese Security Apparatus Zhang Yabo is a former Han Chinese police officer who served within the Chinese security apparatus in the Uyghur homeland for nearly a decade, from 2014 to 2023. Unlike camp survivors or outside analysts, Zhang observed and enforced the system from within, serving in various operational roles across Hotan, Aksu, and rural townships. In August 2025, Zhang joined a European tour group, defected upon arrival in Germany, and sought political asylum. In April 2026, Zhang’s evidence was brought to international attention through groundbreaking research published by Dr. Adrian Zenz and the Victims of Communism Memorial […] The post From Mass Detention to Permanent Control: What Zhang Yabo’s Testimony Reveals About the Evolution of the Uyghur Genocide and Forced Labor appeared first on Center for Uyghur Studies .

title: 王天成：走向战略性非暴力对抗

content: （2026年8月31日在达兰萨拉“民主中国与未来西藏论坛”上的发言稿，原文为英文） 致谢：照片为秦伟平先生所提供 究竟如何才能改变中国，这个问题长期以来在中国民主人士、活动人士和知识分子中争论不断。 在这一争论的核心，有一个十分清晰的分歧： 非暴力抵抗，还是暴力行动。 许多人非常坚定地争辩说，面对中国共产党这样一个顽固、强大、残酷的政权，非暴力根本不会奏效。他们认为，推翻这个政权的唯一途径就是暴力。 然而，有一个引人注目的事实： 我们至今没有听到一声枪响。 没有任何有组织的武装起义真正发生过。1989年以来，中国国内从未出现过持续性的暴力运动。 另一方面，非暴力抗争却的确发生过，而且有的是大规模的。1989年的大规模抗议，以及2022年底的白纸抗议，就是最明显的例子。 这两场运动都规模庞大，但都是自发的。它们都不是经过事先的周密策划的。没有经过训练的组织网络，也没有准备好的行动战略。 这一事实，对于我们认识非暴力行动在中国的潜力与局限，意味深长。 如果将中国的这一经历与圣雄甘地在印度所做的事情做个比较，是很有启发的。 甘地领导的运动并不是自发的。它们都是经过精心策划的。以1930年的“食盐进军”为例。这场行动是在数月的准备之后开始的。这是一项经过深思熟虑的战略选择：通过一场漫长的行进，以其象征意义和简单直接的方式，揭露英国殖民统治的不公，同时吸引更多人加入这场运动。 在整个印度独立运动期间，印度人遭到过大规模的殴打、杀害和监禁。但最终，他们赢得了胜利。 许多中国异议人士说，圣雄甘地之所以能够成功，主要是因为他面对的是一个拥有民主制度和相对自由媒体的英国。我认为，这低估了甘地作为一位伟大战略家的能力。 他计算风险，精心选择战术，训练人们进行有纪律的不合作，并且持续不断地保持压力。 英国确实诉诸过暴力镇压。 但不同之处在于，甘地领导的运动已经做好了承受镇压的准备，并且能够把殖民政权的每一次暴力行为，都转化为对其统治合法性的进一步削弱。 我们需要更加重视 战略性非暴力冲突 ——也就是经过周密事先策划的行动，而不是简单地任由抗议停留在自发的层面。自发性的大规模抗议在世界各地都曾发生。有些取得了成功。许多则失败了，被镇压了。 研究表明，良好的战略和实际行动技能——例如周密的计划、广泛的参与、富有创造性的行动战术、维持非暴力纪律，以及根据形势不断调整的能力——都可以显著提高成功的可能性。 而这些能力，是可以通过学习和训练获得并不断发展的。 相当长一段时间以来，我一直在努力说服我的异议人士同道：如果我们希望开展成功的非暴力斗争，就必须深入掌握非暴力行动的知识。 我们需要成为真正的行家——就像将军必须研究战争的艺术一样。 我希望会有越来越多的人认同这一点。 1989年和2022年的两次重大自发性行动表明，中国社会具有进行集体非暴力抗争的能力。 真正缺少的，是将这些机会转化为持续压力所需要的战略深度。 如果我们开始 把非暴力抵抗当作一门严肃的学问 ——一门需要专业知识、战略规划、训练和持续学习的学问 ——那么，我们就能够提高在未来出现机会时，更有效地把握和利用那些机会的可能性。

title: The Pacific Drone Arms Race Has No Rules
source: 亚利桑那州立大学的《小战争杂志》
